#36444. ADE: A Zero-Training Unlearning Method for Latent World Models

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (169 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

ADE: A Zero-Training Unlearning Method for Latent World Models

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (169 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31998v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Latent world models learn compact recurrent dynamics from offline trajectories, yet deployed simulators can retain backdoor triggers or stale transitions from outdated physical regimes. Existing unlearning methods fail in autoregressive physics: gradient updates distort latent manifolds and compound rollout drift, naive output zeroing suppresses valid control responses on trigger onset, and single-step deletion leaves corruption inside recurrent hidden states. We propose Analytical Dynamics Excision (ADE), a deterministic, zero-training closed-form unlearning algorithm for latent world models. Using only cached pretraining moments, ADE recovers retain covariances via single-pass matrix downdating without raw retain data and cascades closed-form edits across the input bottleneck, hidden states, and downstream heads. Pairing orthogonal excision with whitened recurrent damping and mean-preserving affine calibration neutralizes out-of-manifold backdoors and realigns in-manifold shifts without variance collapse. Across four regimes on three MuJoCo benchmarks, ADE outperforms seven tuned baselines on DreamerV1, eliminating HalfCheetah and Hopper velocity-flip triggers $4.4\times$ faster than fine-tuning, and transfers zero-shot to DreamerV3.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, building on the availability of Daybreak models on Amazon Bedrock, GPT‑5.6 Cyber is now available to approved customers in AWS GovCloud (US-East)⁠(opens in a new window) through Daybreak Red. This expansion gives government security teams a new way to apply advanced cybersecurity capabilities within the AWS environments they use to support critical missions.

Daybreak Red provides access to OpenAI’s purpose-trained cybersecurity models for authorized vulnerability research, exploit validation, and security testing. GPT‑5.6 Cyber can help defenders investigate complex software weaknesses, reproduce vulnerabilities in controlled settings, and develop mitigations. Qualified security practitioners should review findings and proposed fixes before implementation.

It has been revealed that for government organizations, adopting advanced cybersecurity capabilities requires more than model performance. Teams also need to work within established security, governance, and operational requirements.

According to recent reports, availability in AWS GovCloud (US-East) gives eligible teams a path to incorporate GPT‑5.6 Cyber into those workflows through Amazon Bedrock. Defenders can use it to reason through security findings, assess their impact, and evaluate fixes, helping connect vulnerability research to practical improvements in defense.

Daybreak Red gives verified defenders greater latitude for authorized cybersecurity work, with fewer refusals for these tasks alongside stronger identity verification, monitoring, and access controls.

For Daybreak Red on Amazon Bedrock, inference data is not used to train models, and customers do not need to share their Daybreak Red data with OpenAI.

Access requires OpenAI Daybreak Red approval and AWS provisioning. To get started, complete the Daybreak application or contact your OpenAI or AWS account team about eligibility. Once approved, work with your AWS account team to enable access. Daybreak Red approval does not automatically enable model access on AWS.

Learn more about Daybreak models on AWS.

Reading, Writing and Repairing Game-Theoretic Policies in Weight Space

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (185 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31979v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can a language model work in the weight space of a policy network for a repeated game? We put four questions to a mid-size open model, on recurrent networks of 1{,}218 weights with exactly checkable answers. Given a population of opponents described in English, write a policy that is optimal: its value is a finite computation over the agent's information state, so a submitted network has an exact gap from the optimum. Given a network's weights, report its action after each of fifteen opponent histories; recover the state machine it implements, judged on every opponent sequence to depth ten; or repair a network whose output was altered in one place and say which round first goes wrong. The model recovers the program in 62 of 66 replies, reports all fifteen behavioral entries correctly in 34 of 36, and attains the optimum in 20 of 20 when it states a policy the evaluator compiles. Repair is the exception: 4 of 18 repaired, 5 of 18 diagnosed, with a median patch covering one of the two entries needed.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that last March, we released Holo3, our state-of-the-art computer-use model.
  • Users want to run the same computer-use capabilities across desktop and mobile environments, with seamless integration with different agent frameworks.
  • Industry observers note that this is why we are releasing the Holo3.1 family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that last March, we released Holo3, our state-of-the-art computer-use model. Adoption was immediate. Developers, enterprises, and partners started deploying Holo3 across a wide range of workflows, from browser automation and business software to internal tools and desktop applications. As adoption grew, we realized performance alone was no longer enough.

Users want to run the same computer-use capabilities across desktop and mobile environments, with seamless integration with different agent frameworks. They want deployment flexibility, from cloud inference to fully local execution on end-user devices.

Industry observers note that this is why we are releasing the Holo3.1 family. Holo3.1 improves robustness across the three dimensions that matter most in production: environments (web, desktop, mobile), agent frameworks, and deployment targets. For the first time, we release quantized checkpoints optimized for local inference, including FP8, Q4 GGUF, and NVFP4.

Holo3.1 is a major step toward our vision of universal computer-use agents: systems that can operate across environments, integrate into any agent stack, and run wherever the workflow lives.

Based on the Qwen family, Holo3.1 was designed to improve robustness across the environments where computer-use agents are actually deployed, while retaining state-of-the-art performance.

As teams moved Holo3 from evaluation to production, we repeatedly observed the same challenge: strong performance in one setting does not necessarily transfer to another. Mobile devices, alternative agent harnesses, and different execution frameworks all introduce their own sources of distribution shift.

Holo3.1 expands Holo3's capabilities beyond browser and desktop control, delivering major gains on mobile environments. On AndroidWorld, our 35B-A3B model improves from 67% to 79.3%, while the smaller 4B and 9B variants improve from 58% to 72%.

To better support teams deploying Holo inside third-party agent stacks, Holo3.1 introduces native support for function-calling protocols in addition to the structured JSON outputs already available in Holo3.

Sources indicate that across OSWorld and our internal benchmark suite covering e-commerce, business software, and collaboration workflows, function-calling and native execution now achieve near-parity performance. Holo3.1 also delivers more than a 25% improvement over Holo3 when evaluated inside our Holotab product harness.

To further enable local and on-device inference, we are also releasing new model sizes including small models (0.8B, 4B, and 9B) for cost-effective and private deployment, in addition to the larger 35B-A3B model for state-of-the-art performance.

Performance versus cost for the Holo3.1 and Qwen 3.5 families. Overall performance averages the four H Corporate benchmarks first (so each family is equally weighted), then takes the mean across OSWorld, AndroidWorld, H Corporate, ScreenSpot-Pro, and OSWorld-G.

This is our first release to ship quantized weights. We’re starting with 35B-A3B checkpoints, available in FP8, Q4 GGUF, and NVFP4.

For NVFP4, we used NVIDIA's Model Optimizer in a W4A16 configuration. These checkpoints enable fast local inference for Computer Use Agents with little to no degradation in model performance. FP8 and NVFP4 achieve the same OSWorld scores, only about two points below the full-precision BF16 checkpoint.

The speedups are substantial: on DGX Spark, NVFP4 W4A16 delivers 1.41× the total token throughput of FP8 and 1.74× that of BF16.

We also release Q4 GGUF checkpoints aimed at local deployment of Computer Use Agents on consumer hardware.

The agent itself runs locally on a Windows or Mac machine, while the model can either run on that same machine—we include reference numbers for Apple Silicon—or on a DGX Spark on the same network. In both cases, execution stays fully private and local, with nothing leaving the user's network.

On Spark, agent harness optimizations we developed with NVIDIA combined with the NVFP4 quantization above deliver a compound ~2× end-to-end speedup over the FP8 baseline, cutting average step time from 6.8s to 3.3s.

Sources indicate that agent request rate across platforms and precisions. On DGX Spark, vLLM with NVFP4 achieves the highest request rate in both Default and Fast modes, followed by Q4 GGUF and FP8. These improvements and more will land in an upcoming desktop agent harness.

The Holo3.1 family is available in four sizes:.

We are also releasing optimized FP8, NVFP4, and Q4 GGUF checkpoints for local and edge deployment.

We look forward to seeing what developers build with Holo3.1.

#36440. Breaking: Distill to Loop: Turning Pretrained Diffusion Transformers into Looped Models with Adjustable Depth

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (227 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Distill to Loop: Turning Pretrained Diffusion Transformers into Looped Models with Adjustable Depth

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (227 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31977v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Looped transformers reuse one block of shared weights along the depth of the network. Recent looped diffusion transformers are trained from scratch, which repeats the full pretraining cost although strong pretrained non-looped diffusion transformers exist. We propose Distill to Loop (Dooop), which distills a pretrained non-looped diffusion transformer into a looped student whose blocks are initialized from the teacher's. We cast distillation as a fixed-point iteration toward the teacher, in which the output after every loop is trained toward the teacher, and each loop is one step of an ordinary differential equation in depth. As a result, one model runs any number of loops at test time without retraining, and the higher-order ODE solvers of diffusion model sampling can be applied along the depth dimension for better results. Meanwhile, because a looped model produces an output after every loop, we also construct loop guidance between the outputs of different loop counts, which improves the generated samples at little extra compute. On SD3-medium, a looped student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matches the teacher on average over GenEval, ImageReward, PickScore and HPSv2.1 with two to four loops, and with two loops it uses about 58% of the teacher's compute. And on a four-step SD3-medium, loop guidance raises the average of the four metrics from 88.2 to 99.2.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Expanding Codex’s tools for building, understanding, and reviewing code.

It has been revealed that today we're announcing that OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer Organization, Inc⁠(opens in a new window). (“Pierre”), the company behind Code Storage⁠(opens in a new window) and a family of standout open-source developer tools. If you’ve browsed files or reviewed a change in the Codex app, you’ve already used Pierre’s Trees and Diffs libraries. We’re excited to work with the Pierre team to build on the Git workflows that developers already rely on and adapt them to how teams work with coding agents.

We’ve seen in our own engineering work how the systems around Git need to evolve as more of that work happens in parallel. Earlier this week, we shared how we’re scaling Git at OpenAI with Pando, our in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. With the Pierre team, we wish to set the standard for modern software development: from the first branch an agent creates to that magic moment when code is deployed to the world. We want to make Codex the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects.

We’ve long appreciated the care Pierre brings to another part of working with Git: how developers review code. You can see that care in the libraries we use in Codex today. Trees lets developers quickly navigate a project’s files, and Diffs makes it easy to see what changed. Both of these tools make it easy to review and navigate large volumes of code with uncompromising performance.

That same attention to detail runs through Pierre’s other work. Diffs’ Edit mode lets a reviewer fix a line of code right where they spot the problem. Pierre recently released Highlights, an extremely fast syntax highlighter that updates as a developer types or an agent streams code. The same small team that put an editor inside a diff also designed the API for Code Storage, a service that lets apps store code and track its history using Git.

Sources indicate that pierre has built tools that developers love, and together, we will ship newly introduced products and platforms that benefit all. Once the acquisition closes, our ambition is to advance the future of source control across the industry. We want Codex to connect the code a firm ships with the decisions its people make, at the scale the future demands.

Pierre’s open-source projects will remain open-source, and we’ll continue to contribute to them. Customers can continue using Code Storage after the acquisition closes while we work to bring its features and functionality into Codex.

The closing of the acquisition is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of regulatory approvals. Until closing, OpenAI and Pierre will remain separate and independent companies.

Latest Update: Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (245 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31962v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI web agents can autonomously navigate websites and complete various tasks. As their capabilities and adoption expand, evaluating bot defenses requires adversarial stress tests. Although prior work demonstrates that existing agents can remain detectable, it remains unclear how effective bot defenses are against adversaries that coordinate evasion across browser fingerprints, automation controls, and interaction behavior. To investigate this threat, we introduce DarkAgent, an autonomous web agent that combines a forked Chromium browser that conceals automation artifacts and generative models that produce human-like mouse and keyboard traces. To address the limitations of existing keyboard mimickers, our keyboard model jointly generates realistic key events and their timings while reliably reproducing the target text. Released agent detectors accept our generated behavior as human, and trained classifiers find it substantially harder to distinguish from human traces than existing mimickers. DarkAgent achieves an 89% page-access bypass rate across a third-party stealth benchmark, exceeding the strongest published baseline by 12 percentage points. To further enhance the measurement of agents, we introduce a benchmark that measures browser fingerprints, interaction behavior, and network activity to assess each channel's contribution to detecting adversarial agents such as DarkAgent. On this benchmark, browser and behavioral modifications are complementary: either alone remains detectable, and only their combination evades all tested checks. Together, our findings expose the gap between passing existing bot defenses and reproducing human behavior, and point to timing between actions as a remaining signal for defenders.

Adding MCP Tools to Reachy Mini

📅 03 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Reachy Mini conversation app can now use tools hosted in public Hugging Face Spaces, called over MCP.
  • Below, we look at what a tool is, how profiles control what the robot can use, and the current limits of the remote path.
  • Recent findings suggest that when you talk to the robot, what you get back isn't only a voice, it's a system that reacts to the conversation: the robot can move and respond non-verbally, when it's applicable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Reachy Mini conversation app can now use tools hosted in public Hugging Face Spaces, called over MCP. You can give your robot a newly introduced ability, like checking the weather or searching the web, by adding a Space from the Hub instead of editing the app. The tool keeps running in the Space itself, so no code is downloaded onto your machine. And you can publish your own tools for other people to use.

Adding a tool takes one command:.

Below, we look at what a tool is, how profiles control what the robot can use, and the current limits of the remote path.

Recent findings suggest that when you talk to the robot, what you get back isn't only a voice, it's a system that reacts to the conversation: the robot can move and respond non-verbally, when it's applicable. The part we want to focus on here is the tools that make that possible. A tool is something the model can do during a conversation: play an emotion, move the head, look through the camera. Each tool has a name and a short description. The model reads those, decides when one is useful, calls it, and uses what comes back.

Today every tool is local and ships inside the app, and most of them are about the robot's body:.

A tool in the code isn't usable until it's enabled in a profile, a folder with two files that matter here: instructions.txt (the prompt) and tools.txt (the tools that are turned on).

The default profile enables the full set:.

If a name isn't in tools.txt, the model can't call it.

You can also write your own tool: add a Python file to the profile (or external_tools/), give it a name and description, and list that name in tools.txt.

Recent findings suggest that today there are built-in tools and custom local tools, and tools.txt decides which are active. This works well for the robot's body and keeps the trusted core small.

Sources indicate that the constraint here is that every tool has to be local Python. For move_head or play_emotion that's right: they talk to the hardware and belong in the app but a lot of useful things have nothing to do with the body, like web search, weather, or lookups. For those, keeping everything local is mostly friction:.

Remote tools add a third kind, alongside the built-in and custom local tools you already have, for capabilities that are easier to publish, share, and update on their own:.

We started with two canary tools, small test tools to exercise the new flow:.

They're enough to exercise the whole feature: install from the Hub, discover the remote tools, enable them per profile, and let the realtime backend call them exactly like built-in tools.

To use both at once, add each Space and their tools stack in the same profile:.

Now the robot can search the web and check the weather in the same conversation, which is exactly what the canary_web_search_weather profile below does.

add validates the Space on the Hub, probes the MCP endpoint, discovers its tools, and by default appends the tool IDs to the active profile's tools.txt. The active profile is default unless you've set REACHY_MINI_CUSTOM_PROFILE. Use --install-only to skip that step.

tools.txt is the gatekeeper: a remote tool is only active if its ID appears in the profile's tools.txt, alongside whatever built-in tools you want.

Installed sources are persisted in:.

Each installed Space gets a local alias derived from its slug, with hyphens, dots, and slashes collapsing to underscores:.

Remote tools are then namespaced with a double underscore:.

This keeps remote tool names from colliding with built-in ones and lets multiple Spaces coexist in the same profile.

Industry observers note that the implementation also strips redundant Space-name prefixes when possible, so a verbose remote tool name becomes a cleaner local ID. If stripping would cause a collision between two tools from the same Space, the code falls back to the fully namespaced name.

According to recent reports, there is also a duplicate safety check at registry level: Tool.name values must be unique across the entire merged tool set. The app fails fast if two sources claim the same name.

For this work we created two focused canary profiles to isolate the MCP experiment from the full embodied tool set.

The first keeps a few expressive tools (emotions, head movement) and adds web search on top:.

The second is the same, plus the weather tool alongside search:.

The small physical tool set means Reachy Mini can still react expressively while answering current questions from the web.

In a recent development, the remote-tool plumbing gets the tools into the model. The prompts decide how the model uses them.

Recent findings suggest that that was especially visible in the search-plus-weather canary. A combined question like:.

Recent findings suggest that can be handled in at least three ways: weather first then search, search first then weather, or both in the same turn. If the prompt is vague, the model serialises the calls and creates unnecessary latency. So the canary prompts became part of the feature, not just incidental configuration.

It has been revealed that two things are worth calling out. First, the Space has to actually behave like an MCP server; if tool discovery fails, the install fails. Second, prompt instructions can encourage parallel calls but cannot guarantee them. If deterministic orchestration matters for a use case, that logic should move from the prompt into code.

According to recent reports, if you want others to use your tool, publish it as a public Gradio Space that exposes the standard MCP endpoint, and keep the tools stateless so they work well over the network. Whether a Space installs depends on this runtime behavior, not on tags.

Tags aren't required for installation, but they help people find compatible Spaces:.

The app now has three kinds of tools sharing one registry: built-in, local custom, and remote MCP tools, and profiles still decide which of them a given assistant can reach. A small, trusted core stays at the center while the optional capabilities around it can be added, tested, and swapped without touching the app itself.

Recent findings suggest that what we're most curious about now is what people build. If you publish a tool Space, tag it reachy-mini-tool and mcp so others can find it. We'd love to see what Reachy Mini ends up able to do!

Acknowledgements: Many thanks to Fabien Danieau for proofreading this post and helping test the workflow, to Andres Marafioti for helping test it, and to Remi Fabre and the Pollen Robotics team for the ideas and feedback that shaped the remote tools workflow.

arXiv:2611.31950v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hands grasp objects with soft skin. A fingertip flattens against a mug, and a palm curves around a bottle. Yet hand-object datasets and estimators represent the hand as a rigid articulated mesh, which hovers above or penetrates the object where skin would press against it. Existing refiners keep the mesh rigid and adjust only the pose, trading pose accuracy for physical plausibility. We ask whether a rigid hand can instead touch the object as skin does while staying close to its original pose. We lift annotated or estimated rigid hands to contact-consistent meshes through an optimization that (i) slightly adjusts the joints and wrist to bring the fingers onto the object, (ii) deforms the skin so that penetrating regions settle onto the surface, and (iii) keeps this deformation consistent over time. Since deformation reaches only skin already near the object, we further train a lightweight head on the lifted annotations to predict where an estimated hand should touch and steer the deformation there. Unlike existing refiners, the lift more than doubles the skin lying on the object surface for three published estimators while barely changing the pose. Guidance from the learned head further improves grasp stability by closing contact gaps that the estimate leaves open. Existing hand-object datasets and estimators can thus adopt contact-consistent hands without changing the hand model or retraining the estimators.

Yet most forecasts for the parameter inference of these systems assume known source parameters, and broad-prior analyses have addressed only simplified versions of the problem. Here we solve it for the augmented analytic kludge model: generative networks narrow the complete prior and reveal a ring of degenerate spin directions, and the exact detector likelihood determines the posterior. The redshifted mass and spin of the massive black hole are determined to two parts in $10^5$, the mass two orders of magnitude beyond any electromagnetic measurement. The compact object's redshifted mass is measured to one part in $10^4$, and its eccentric, retrograde orbit discriminates between capture channels. The 0.8% distance and sub-square-degree localization are sufficient for dark-siren cosmology. Year-long coherent analysis resolves the inspiral driven by radiation reaction itself.

#36434. Breaking: Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots

📅 03 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2908 w)

Breaking: Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots

📅 03 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2908 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in April, we released DharmaOCR, our specialized structured OCR model (available on Hugging Face) along with a paper detailing the methodology behind it and a benchmark demonstrating its superior quality and cost efficiency.
  • Across the tested open-source families, vanilla degeneration rates ranged from below 1% to above 33%.
  • According to recent reports, A second training stage - applied after supervised fine-tuning (SFT), on the same documents, using the same model - reduced text degeneration in every family tested.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in April, we released DharmaOCR, our specialized structured OCR model (available on Hugging Face) along with a paper detailing the methodology behind it and a benchmark demonstrating its superior quality and cost efficiency. The paper benchmarked leading vision-language model families - both open-source and commercial - on a structured document extraction task: OCR on Brazilian Portuguese text. Among the reported metrics was text degeneration rate: the frequency with which a model produces a repetition loop instead of a transcription.

Across the tested open-source families, vanilla degeneration rates ranged from below 1% to above 33%. Supervised fine-tuning reduced those rates for most models - but rarely to production-acceptable levels. The pattern points to a structural limitation: SFT optimizes for correct outputs, but does not explicitly penalize degeneration. There appears to be a ceiling on how much task-focused fine-tuning alone can reduce this failure mode (Text Degeneration Article).

According to recent reports, A second training stage - applied after supervised fine-tuning (SFT), on the same documents, using the same model - reduced text degeneration in every family tested. No exceptions. Average reduction: 59.4%. Best case: 87.6%.

Figure 1: DPO reduced degeneration relative to SFT in every family tested - average reduction of 59.4%, peak of 87.6% (Nanonets-OCR2–3B: 1.61% to 0.20%). The direction is invariant; only the magnitude varies.

That second stage was Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Almost all published DPO applications target chat alignment - models trained on human judgments about helpfulness or harmlessness (example: Rafailov et al., 2023). OCR carries none of that subjectivity: the task is objective, and there is no conversational context. There is, however, a clear preference signal. A correct transcription is chosen; a degeneration loop is rejected. DharmaOCR used that binary to construct a DPO training set, testing the technique not for alignment, but as a direct mitigation tool for a specific failure mode.

The training signal came from the model itself - specifically from the outputs it produced when it failed. How a failure mode becomes a training signal is a structural question about the failure, not the model.

Industry observers note that why SFT has a ceiling on degeneration is still an open question - but the leading conjecture points to loss granularity. SFT trains token by token: each prediction is evaluated in isolation, and a repetition loop is never penalized as a completion-level failure. DPO inverts that logic. The training signal is the full output - chosen or rejected - which means a degenerated completion can be explicitly labeled as the wrong outcome, not just a sequence of locally probable tokens.

In a recent development, when a training objective maximizes the likelihood of observed sequences, it concentrates probability mass in the regions of distribution space those sequences occupy. A model that enters one of those high-probability attractor regions during inference assigns elevated probability to the same token at the next step - which increases the probability further, which sustains the loop until the sequence hits the maximum token limit. Text degeneration is the output of this geometry: a self-reinforcing repetition loop that an autoregressive model cannot exit without external intervention (Holtzman et al., 2020). It is not purely a decoding artifact. The attractor involves the training objective, the learned distribution, and how probability mass concentrates during inference - a systems-level failure rather than a failure localized to any single component.

The geometry of this failure is visible at the token level.

Sources indicate that figure 2: When a token dominates its own conditional distribution, every sampling step deepens the attractor. The decoder samples from this geometry; it does not determine it.

It has been revealed that inference-layer interventions - repetition penalties, temperature adjustments, early-abort logic - operate on the sampling step. They contain the symptom without touching the distribution that produces it. The attractor persists.

Sources indicate that supervised fine-tuning moves the distribution closer to the task domain. For a structured generation pipeline, this means training on domain-specific documents, in the target language, with the required output format. The model gains fluency with longer sequences, constrained syntax, domain vocabulary. What SFT does not do is attack degeneration directly. Its objective - maximizing the likelihood of observed sequences - has no term that penalizes repetition loops. The failure mode is simply outside the scope of what the training signal optimizes for.

In a recent development, one model family in the DharmaOCR benchmark showed an unexpected pattern: vanilla degeneration rate of 0.60%, rising to 3.23% after SFT, before a subsequent DPO stage brought it to 1.41%. It is a single data point - an exception, not a rule - and it would be overstating the evidence to treat it as proof of a mechanism. What it does illustrate is that SFT does not reliably reduce degeneration. Capability and degeneration resistance can move independently.

The distinction matters structurally. SFT and DPO are not interchangeable training stages performing the same operation at different intensities. SFT closes the distance between the model's prior distribution and the task domain. What it does not do is target degeneration as an objective - its effect on the failure mode is incidental, and the benchmark results show it is not consistent. The attractor that produces degeneration is not a problem with the model's proximity to the task - it is a problem with the shape of the distribution space the model now occupies.

Addressing that geometry requires a training signal built specifically to point the model away from its own failure modes. For a structured, non-conversational task with no human preference labels and no conventional "helpful versus harmful" distinction, constructing that signal is a design decision.

The DharmaOCR pipeline's contribution to DPO methodology is specific: it used the SFT model's own degenerate outputs as the rejected examples - not as noise to remove, but as the negative training signal the optimization needed.

DPO requires preference pairs: a chosen output and a rejected output for the same input, with a quality difference clear enough for the optimization to learn from. In chat alignment, human annotators produce those judgments - rating responses as more or less helpful, accurate, or safe. Structured generation tasks have no equivalent annotation source. An OCR pipeline either produces a correct transcription or it does not. Quality differences exist, but they are not produced by human preference rankings - they are produced by the task's own criteria for correctness.

Recent findings suggest that the DharmaOCR pipeline identified a preference signal that structured generation tasks already produce: the range of outputs the SFT model generates in inference. A model capable of performing a structured task is also capable of failing at it in characteristic ways. Those failures - outputs that enter the degeneration attractor - are not noise to filter. They are the most informative negative signal available.

In a recent development, the paper implemented this on 23,726 training documents, generating multiple candidate responses per document with the SFT model and scoring each with an automated LLM judge. The pipeline is shown below.

Figure 3: The critical design decision is not in the pipeline's structure - it is in what the pipeline preserved: outputs displaying text degeneration were deliberately labeled as rejected examples, not filtered out as low-quality noise.

The conventional response when degenerate outputs appear in training data is to remove them. They are low-quality signal; filtering produces a cleaner dataset. The DharmaOCR approach inverted this logic. Degenerate outputs were deliberately retained as the rejected examples in each (chosen, rejected) pair, because they represent exactly the failure mode the DPO stage was designed to suppress. Removing them would have discarded the clearest target available.

The paper describes this as "preference-guided implicit unlikelihood" - the model is trained not only toward better outputs but away from a specific class of failure. Where SFT maximizes the likelihood of high-quality outputs, the DPO stage simultaneously penalizes outputs displaying the degeneration attractor geometry. The direction of the optimization is explicit in a way SFT alone cannot achieve.

Degenerate outputs are particularly well-suited as rejection examples because they represent a consistent failure mode rather than varied low-quality outputs. A transcription that misses words is low quality, but its failure is case-specific. Repetition loops, by contrast, appeared persistently across documents and model families even after SFT - a pattern consistent with a failure mode that likelihood-based optimization does not reliably correct. DPO applies its loss differently: at the completion level, with explicit rejection signals. The post-hoc analysis cannot establish causality, but the evidence suggests that what SFT's objective leaves unresolved, DPO's may address.

This approach requires no specialized annotation infrastructure - only a model capable of producing both acceptable and identifiable-failure outputs, and a scoring model to label preference pairs. A rule-based mechanism could detect repetition loops mechanically - but it could not identify which outputs represented high-quality transcriptions worth preserving as chosen examples.

In a recent development, the scoring model does both: it flags degeneration as the rejected output and validates clean extractions as the chosen one, keeping the model's extraction capability intact while the DPO signal penalizes the failure mode. Whether the resulting training signal successfully moves the distribution in the intended direction - and whether it does so consistently across architectures - is the evidence question.

The DPO stage reduced text degeneration in every model family tested - with reductions ranging from 37% to 88% and an average of 59.4% relative to SFT alone. The result held across architectures, parameter scales, and starting degeneration profiles that differed by more than one order of magnitude. One case in the dataset saw degeneration increase after the SFT stage before DPO corrected it. That case does not complicate the consistency. It confirms the mechanism more directly than any of the others.

Figure 1 reveals the three-stage degeneration rate for each of the five model families tested: Vanilla, SFT, and SFT+DPO. In four of the five families, degeneration falls at each stage. The fifth family's bars move differently - and that difference is the most analytically notable data point in the study.

The Qwen2.5-VL-3B result, read carefully, is not a complication. It is a confirmation. The model's vanilla degeneration rate was 0.60% - not because it was stable, but because it was too generic to produce long structured outputs at all. The model was not entering the degeneration attractor because it was not attempting the task seriously enough to find it.

SFT changed that. After domain adaptation, Qwen2.5-VL-3B became capable of the task - producing longer, more structured outputs with the domain vocabulary and format the pipeline required. That capability brought it into proximity with the degeneration attractor for the first time. Its degeneration rate rose to 3.23%.

This is the mechanism made empirically visible: SFT moved the model toward the task and toward the task's failure geometry simultaneously. These are not necessarily the same operation. A training stage that increases task capability can increase failure-mode exposure as a side effect - particularly when the failure mode lives at the edge of the capability frontier. Treated as the same operation, the Qwen2.5-VL-3B result looks like an error. Treated as distinct operations - which is what the SFT + DPO pipeline formally does - the result is consistent with the hypothesis that SFT and DPO address different failure dimensions.

The DPO stage then brought the degeneration rate to 1.41%. It did not restore the vanilla baseline because it was not designed to: the model after SFT was more capable than it had been, and a return to 0.60% would have required undoing that capability. What the DPO stage did was address the failure geometry the SFT stage had introduced.

Sources indicate that the remaining four model families add quantitative weight to the same conclusion. Figure 1 reveals the SFT-to-SFT+DPO comparison for all five.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1: DPO reduced degeneration relative to SFT in every family tested - average reduction of 59.4%, peak of 87.6% (Nanonets-OCR2–3B: 1.61% to 0.20%). The direction is invariant; only the magnitude varies.

Sources indicate that no model family revealed degeneration increasing after DPO. No family was immune to its effect. The consistency extends to gemma-3–4b-it, which entered the benchmark with the highest vanilla degeneration rate by an order of magnitude - 33.96%, compared to the next highest at 2.62% - and still reached a 75% reduction after the DPO stage. The reduction range - 37.3% to 87.6% - reflects differences in starting configuration and architecture, not inconsistency in the intervention's direction.

This is not a proof of universal applicability. DPO may not transfer to every domain, failure mode, or model family. What the DharmaOCR benchmark provides is evidence across five OCR architectures that the core hypothesis holds: optimizing over complete preference pairs - rather than maximizing token-level likelihood - addresses a failure mode that SFT structurally cannot target. The result was consistent in direction across every model family tested. That consistency, within the scope of this benchmark, is what the evidence supports.

The DharmaOCR approach was possible because this pipeline satisfied a set of structural conditions that allowed a DPO training stage to function as designed - conditions whose presence or absence determines whether the same methodology applies elsewhere (Dharma OCR Paper on ArXiv). It was not possible because OCR is a unique domain.

According to recent reports, the first condition is that the failure mode be identifiable as a distinct class of output, not just a point on a quality continuum. Text degeneration qualifies because a repetition loop is categorically different from a transcription that misses words or misreads a character. The output is not merely suboptimal - it is broken in a specific, behaviorally recognizable way. That categorical distinctness is what allowed the pipeline to construct preference pairs where the rejected examples represented a coherent failure geometry, not noise. A task whose failure modes blend into its range of acceptable variation lacks this property.

In a recent development, the second condition is that a scoring mechanism can reliably distinguish acceptable outputs from failure-mode outputs without requiring human annotation. In the DharmaOCR pipeline, an automated LLM judge scored candidate responses against four task-specific criteria. The scoring did not need to be perfect - it needed to be consistent enough to produce preference pairs with a meaningful quality gap between chosen and rejected. Pairs with ambiguous quality differences contribute noise to DPO training, not signal. The judge's consistency was a design requirement, not an incidental feature.

Recent findings suggest that the third condition is sufficient volume - enough inference outputs to generate a preference dataset with meaningful variance in quality. This is not an extraordinary requirement by fine-tuning standards, but it is a real one.

According to recent reports, when all three conditions are present, the methodological move is structurally available. The design decision at the center of the DharmaOCR pipeline - treating the model's own failure outputs as the rejected examples rather than filtering them - applies wherever a model's failures are categorically identifiable, scoreable, and sufficiently numerous.

In a recent development, the practical implication for ML engineers building structured generation pipelines is direct. SFT is necessary - it closes the distance between a generalist model and a task-capable one. It is not sufficient for structured output reliability, because task capability and degeneration resistance are different properties of the distribution. A DPO stage after SFT is a one-time training investment. In the DharmaOCR results, the degeneration reduction did not come at the cost of extraction quality - the paper's benchmark results show both moving together (Specialization Beats Scale article).

Sources indicate that what makes a failure mode usable as training signal is not the domain - it is whether the failures are consistent enough, identifiable enough, and numerous enough to constitute a legible signal. In the DharmaOCR pipeline, they were. Whether the same holds in another context is a structural question about the task's failure mode, not a question about the model family or the domain.

Industry observers note that the DharmaOCR result does not depend on the domain being special. It depends on the failures being useful.

Sources indicate that text degeneration qualifies as useful because it is categorically distinct from acceptable outputs, consistently produced across inference runs, and reliably scoreable without human annotation. Those three properties - not the OCR context, not the model family, not the language - determined whether the preference dataset was tractable. A failure mode that satisfies them is not noise to remove. It is the most direct evidence available of where the distribution should not go.

It has been revealed that the DPO stage used that evidence. Degeneration fell in every model family tested - in models that entered the benchmark with vanilla rates below 1% and in models that entered with rates above 33%. The direction held. The pipeline did not discard its failures. It trained on them.

In a recent development, interesting explanation of how Direct Preference Optimization can improve model alignment beyond traditional chatbot applications. I think techniques like this are important for making AI systems more reliable and better at understanding user intent. This is particularly relevant when building a customer service chatbot, where accurate, relevant, and helpful responses can make a big difference in the user experience. Consistency and understanding context are just as important as generating natural-sounding answers. I recently came across this article that shares some useful insights into how businesses can use AI chatbots to improve customer service: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-chatbot-for-customer-service. It adds another useful perspective to the discussion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting with equity research, Franklin Templeton is developing AI workflows to help portfolio managers compare views and examine risks.

According to recent reports, franklin Templeton wants AI to help portfolio managers examine different research views and the risks behind an investment idea. Codex is one of several tools our investment teams are using to develop workflows for investment research.

When Franklin Templeton first tried using AI, the team put data in a database and connected the models to it. But it didn’t produce the answers the teams needed because the models didn’t understand how the data fit together. When the team added agents and a semantic layer, a structured model of what the firm’s data means and how it’s connected, the results changed. The team is using Codex and other tools to develop this connected intelligence layer. "We've been able to build what we think of as a connected intelligence layer," Dudley notes. "We're bringing the data into the tools, and we're surfacing insights that make a difference.".

Research, risk, compliance, and trading offer different perspectives on an investment. Franklin Templeton’s ambition is to bring those inputs together for portfolio managers. “We're able to bring that all in and then use that to surface insights to the people who are making decisions, which are our portfolio managers,” Dudley claims.

Industry observers note that dudley describes the earlier equity-research workflow as human-led and sequential: an analyst performs first-pass stock analysis, reviews earnings calls, and studies competitors in each business line. The goal is to surface useful information as analysts prepare new ideas to be pitched to portfolio managers or provide updates on existing positions in the portfolio. As she puts it, “It's just continuous intelligence combined with that human judgment.”.

In the workflow Franklin Templeton envisions, its investment teams will have access to a governed, reusable intelligence foundation that brings together trusted connectors, portfolio and workflow context, and agentic capabilities that surface actionable insights for its analysts and portfolio managers.

Franklin Templeton has used Codex in hackathons, bringing experts alongside investment practitioners as they develop their own tools. Its Investment AI champions are working to turn experiments into production-ready workflows, with security review, expert support, and data controls as part of that process.

Dudley says, “We have moved from augmenting our research process to reimagining the investment research workflow.”.

It has been revealed that some of what makes AI helpful in other settings doesn't work in asset management. Many tools learn a user's preferences and show them more of the same, so if someone favors one research provider, the tool surfaces more of that provider's reports. For an investment team, that narrowing potentially brings a biased perspective into the investment process. Franklin Templeton wants the opposite. "We want to make sure that they're accessing that diversity of research and diversity of opinion," Dudley says.

Franklin Templeton wants its AI systems to emphasize investment risks. “We need AI to understand that a great investment idea is one that is well reasoned, but it also has analyzed the risks and makes our portfolio managers aware of the risk,” Dudley indicates. “If you’re looking at a research note, focusing on the fact someone has identified the investment risks is not a bad thing from our perspective. It makes for a more informed investment decision.”.

Franklin Templeton's experience points to some investment management best practices:.

In a recent development, “Our message from leadership is consistent: we encourage innovation and experimentation with AI within clearly defined risk guardrails. Not every initiative will succeed, but each should generate insights that strengthen our capabilities, inform future decisions, and drive continuous improvement,” Dudley indicates.

Get new tools into people's hands: Dudley says Franklin Templeton has brought practical labs to teams swiftly after new technology debuts, so they can test how it fits their work.

Help teams learn the tools: Dudley says, "The goal is getting them to actually understand the power of the technology.".

Build with appropriate controls: Security review, expert support, and data agreements are part of Franklin Templeton’s path from experimentation toward production-grade tools.

Dudley’s longer-term goal is to make that connected intelligence accessible across investment teams, from analysts to the leaders of each investment group.

According to recent reports, she wants analysts to spend more time in the field, speaking with many different experts and professionals, including executives at private companies, and bringing what they learn back to their investment teams. For Dudley, that human perspective remains essential as the tools develop.

arXiv:2611.31909v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GUI grounding requires resolving fine visual details within the context that gives them meaning. Additional views can improve localization, but their value depends on what evidence they expose and how much context they preserve. We explore a capability of vision-language models (VLMs): even when their coordinate predictions are incorrect, they can describe visual evidence worth inspecting. We introduce \textbf{SPARK}, \textit{\textbf{S}emantic \textbf{P}robe-guided \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{R}egion see\textbf{K}ing}, a training-free framework that turns this semantic guidance into targeted visual observations. Exploration probes describe relevant context and distinguishing target details, while verification probes identify evidence needed to assess emerging hypotheses. Their spatial attention guides view placement, contextual responses determine crop extent, and observation history encourages complementary inspection. The resulting predictions are combined through uncertainty-weighted voting. On ScreenSpot-Pro, SPARK improves grounding accuracy over single-view inference by 13.9, 25.2, and 16.1 percentage points with Qwen3-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, and UI-TARS, outperforming all compared test-time methods for each backbone. Consistent gains across four additional benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness across diverse interfaces and grounding tasks. These results establish semantic probing as an effective mechanism for turning a frozen VLM's understanding of what to inspect into more accurate GUI grounding.

Breaking: Designing the hf CLI as an agent-optimized way to work with the Hub

📅 04 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2219 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub.
  • It has been revealed that the hf CLI has been primarily built for our owners over the years.
  • According to recent reports, we started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub. Anything you can do on the Hub from the Python SDK, you can do from your terminal: download and upload models, datasets and Spaces; create and manage repos, branches, tags and pull requests; run Jobs on HF infrastructure; manage Buckets, Collections, webhooks and Inference Endpoints.

It has been revealed that the hf CLI has been primarily built for our owners over the years. But it's now increasingly used by coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more. So we rebuilt it to make it work for both audiences at once. This blog post summarizes what we did, and how we benchmarked it. We found that on complex, multi-step tasks the no-CLI baseline (an agent hand-rolling curl or the Python SDK) uses up to 6× as many tokens as the hf CLI.

According to recent reports, we started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026. The hf CLI (and the huggingface_hub Python SDK it's built on) detects when a coding agent is driving it by reading the environment variables agents set: CLAUDECODE/CLAUDE_CODE for Claude Code, CODEX_SANDBOX for Codex, plus Cursor, Gemini, Pi, and the universal AI_AGENT. That single signal does two jobs: it shapes the CLI's output (more on that below) and it tags each Hub request with an agent/ user-agent, so we can attribute traffic to the agent driving it. The two largest by distinct customers are Claude Code and Codex, well ahead of everything else, and they're the two agents we benchmark later in this article.

The bars count distinct users per agent; request volume is the sub-label. Claude Code alone is ~40k users and nearly 49M requests, with Codex close behind. These are early numbers (we only began attributing agent traffic in April 2026), but the scale is already significant, and we expect it to keep growing as coding agents become a standard way to work with the Hub.

In a recent development, humans and coding agents expect different outputs for the same hf commands. A human wants rich terminal output: ANSI color, padded tables truncated to fit the screen, a green ✅ on success, ✔ for booleans, progress bars, prose hints. An agent wants the inverse: no ANSI, nothing truncated, every value in full since an agent can handle far denser output than a human, kept compact and structured to stay light on tokens. It also can't answer a CLI prompt and will happily re-run a command after a timeout. The rest of this section is how hf gives each side what it needs. We introduced agent-mode output in hf v1.9.0 and have been migrating the rest of the CLI to it gradually in the following releases.

When hf auto-detects agent use (via the environment variables mentioned above), it renders the same command differently. It optimizes output format for humans or agents without passing a flag:.

A human gets an aligned table, truncated to fit the terminal, plus a hint on how to see more, with color cues for status (a green ✓ on success, red on error). An agent gets the complete record as TSV: full repo ids, full ISO timestamps, every tag, no ANSI codes, nothing truncated, clean to parse and light on tokens.

According to recent reports, in practice, we've implemented logging methods like .table(...), .result(...), .json(), etc., which take raw data as input and handle the formatting. In addition to human and agent modes, we've introduced --json and --quiet options to make it easier to pipe commands together. The default mode is automatically chosen based on context, but users can always force the format of their choice with --format human | agent | json | quiet.

Industry observers note that CLI commands rarely run in isolation: one step usually implies the next (git add, then git commit). Many hf commands now end with a hint: the exact next command to run, pre-filled with the IDs you just used, so a user or agent can chain straight to the next step instead of working it out from scratch. Start a Job in the background and it points you to its logs; create a Space and it points you to its boot status:.

For a human that's a convenience. For an agent it's a rail: the next action is named, parameterized with the right ids, and ready to run, so it takes fewer steps working out what to do. Errors behave the same way, naming the fix instead of just failing:.

Hints, warnings and errors all go to stderr while data goes to stdout, so none of this guidance pollutes the output the agent is parsing.

hf never sits on an interactive prompt waiting for a key an agent can't press. A destructive command still asks a human to confirm, but in agent mode it fails fast with the fix in the message (Use --yes to skip confirmation.), and -y/--yes skips it. And because agents retry on timeouts and lost context, operations are built to be safe to repeat: hf repos create --exist-ok is a no-op if the repo already exists, and re-running an upload re-commits cleanly. Separately, the commands that move real data take a --dry-run that shows exactly what they'll transfer before they run, which proves handy for humans and agents alike, since neither has to commit to a long download or blind sync:.

hf is built to be probed: run hf to see the resource groups, run --help on the one you need, and every --help ends with real, copy-pasteable examples (which an agent matches against far faster than it parses a description):.

Industry observers note that the command tree is consistent, resource + verb with the obvious aliases (hf models ls, hf repos create, hf jobs ps, hf collections delete; list/ls, remove/rm), so once an agent learns one command it can guess the rest. And the output composes: -q prints one id per line to pipe into the next command, --json gives you something to hand to jq.

To find out whether the hf CLI is really more efficient for agents, we measured it. We built a small evaluation harness and ran the same set of Hub tasks through each way of driving the Hub, many times over, grading every run against the live Hub. Here's the headline before the methodology: across both agents the hf CLI comes out ahead, most clearly on complex, multi-step tasks where it uses far fewer tokens.

It has been revealed that (self-report error = the agent reported success on the 17 solvable tasks but the Hub said otherwise. The hf CLI rows are the CLI with its skill installed; what the skill adds on top of the bare CLI (chiefly fewer tool calls) is broken out in the skill section below. Representative transcripts are published in this bucket.).

Recent findings suggest that we defined 18 non-trivial Hub tasks. Not "download a file", but the kind of thing you'd actually ask for: aggregate a trending org's models, inspect a repo's files and their sizes, upload a folder with include/exclude rules, delete files, copy files across repos, open a PR that adds a license, create a repo with a branch and a tag, sync and prune a bucket, build a collection. Each task goes to a fresh coding agent with exactly one way to talk to the Hub:.

Sources indicate that we run the hf CLI in two configurations, with and without its skill (a generated command reference we come back to in its own section). But the headline comparison below is simply hf CLI vs curl / the SDK; the skill's incremental effect is small enough that we break it out on its own rather than crowd it into the main results.

According to recent reports, the config is deliberately clean: a fresh instance per run, no custom MCP servers, no CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, nothing in context to nudge behavior. The task and the tool go into a single prompt, and the agent finishes with a TASK_COMPLETE or TASK_FAILED marker, but we don't trust that marker (an agent will report success on work that never landed), so we grade every run independently by re-querying the live Hub: did the branch really get created, is the file actually gone, does the bucket exist? Each task/tool combination is run 10 times, since coding agents are non-deterministic, about 520 runs per agent (18 tasks × 3 tools × 10 reps, minus a cap on one billable Jobs task) and ~1,000 graded runs in total. We ran the whole thing twice, on the two most popular coding agents (Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI Codex with GPT-5.5).

It has been revealed that the two charts below unpack the table above. First, task success on Sonnet, the agent where curl and the SDK struggle most:.

Without the CLI, curl and the SDK trail by ten points, because on Sonnet they simply can't finish parts of the job (the writes, mostly), while the hf CLI clears them.

Industry observers note that the second image indicates token impact on GPT-5.5, broken down per task. Each bar is the curl/SDK tokens divided by the CLI's on the same task, so 2.4× means the non-hf version burned 2.4 times as many tokens to do the same thing:.

Sources indicate that on a one-shot read (count dataset rows, batch metadata) curl and the SDK are fine, and sometimes lighter. But as tasks get more complex and involve several dependent steps, the agent has to hand-roll the entire chain of REST calls (or dig through the SDK) and the cost blows up: 2.4× to 6× the CLI's on creating a repo with a branch and tag, deleting files, copying across repos, or syncing a bucket. The hf CLI lets the agent express the task as a few higher-level commands, rather than crafting a complex workflow.

In a recent development, hf ships a skill: a compact reference of the whole command surface that an agent loads as context. It's auto-generated from the live hf command tree, one line per command (its signature, a one-line description, and the flags that matter), grouped by resource, with a short glossary of common options. It deliberately skips the self-explanatory flags so it stays terse and light on context, and it's regenerated every release. Run hf skills preview to print it, or install it with:.

What does it buy you? Mostly, the agent stops guessing. The clearest single view is how many commands each run takes, with the skill and without:.

On both agents that's about ten commands per task down to about seven, roughly 30% fewer tool calls. That's because the agent isn't probing --help to find the right command and argument. The skill won't cut your token bill, because it prepends a fixed slice of info to the context, so tokens remain about the same or slightly tick up for the same task. The Skill won't make the CLI more reliable either, but it will help the agent spend time running your task rather than finding out how the tool works. This could be particularly helpful when using hf with local models.

Recent findings suggest that we ran each task in a fresh session, so the skill pays its context cost on every task. In a real multi-task session that cost amortizes (the agent learns the command surface once), so the token picture likely improves there; we didn't measure that case.

We benchmarked all this because we think it matters. Agents are becoming real users of the Hub: they train models, build and clean datasets, and ship demos as Spaces, almost always on behalf of a person. A Hub that works well for agents is also a Hub that works better for the people using them. The better an agent's tools are, the more it can do for you.

If your agent interacts with the Hugging Face Hub, we recommend giving it the hf CLI:.

Then hand it the skill, so it knows the whole command surface from the first turn:.

In a recent development, then point your agent at the Hub and let it work. Make sure you're logged in (hf auth login), then hand it a prompt like:.

It'll work out the commands on its own and come back with something useful.

The full command reference lives in the hf CLI guide.

It has been revealed that building an agent harness? Get it registered! That's how hf learns to detect it, and how the Hub attributes its traffic to your harness. You simply need to open a small PR adding an entry to agent-harnesses.ts. Read the Register your agent harness guide for more details.

It has been revealed that giving AI agents access to command-line tools can make them more capable because they can interact with real development resources instead of relying entirely on generated text. The vital part is setting appropriate permissions, defining task boundaries, and checking the results of commands before allowing consequential changes. I also think repeatable workflows make these integrations easier to manage, especially when the same development tasks occur frequently. This guide onhttps://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-development/ai-workflow-automation-cursor-claude-commands is relevant to that idea, as reusable commands can help standardize routine coding activities. Combining tool access with clear safeguards is key to building dependable AI-assisted workflows.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.31902v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Flow-based policies provide expressive action distributions for continuous-control reinforcement learning. In online actor-critic learning, off-policy value estimates can be unreliable in poorly covered action regions, where expressive policies may shift probability mass toward critic-favored actions. We propose MIFLOW, which calibrates online flow-policy learning with a recency-adaptive flow-matching prior fitted to recently executed actions. Inspired by canalization as a qualitative analogy for path-dependent stabilization, we use the prior as a moving density reference for value-guided policy improvement. MIFLOW uses the approximate recent-action log-density in a dimension-normalized correction to both actor updates and critic targets. This correction increases the cost of low-density actions while keeping them available. Across six MuJoCo continuous-control tasks and five random seeds, MIFLOW achieves competitive mean return curves and higher late-training mean returns than the evaluated baselines on several tasks. In a Walker2d-v4 case study, MIFLOW demonstrates a lower proportion of actions assigned low density by the learned reference, both overall and among high-Q actions. Prior-family and prior-buffer comparisons show task-dependent differences in returns and prior-defined diagnostics. These results support dynamic recent-behavior priors for reference calibration in the evaluated settings. The diagnostics measure how sampled actions align with the learned reference. True action support and critic extrapolation error remain unmeasured in these experiments.

arXiv:2611.31895v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Knowledge-intensive video generation remains challenging because prompts often omit the facts, appearances, and temporal relationships required for accurate generation. While search-based workflows can retrieve missing evidence, manually designed strategies limit adaptive planning, and conventional training suffers from costly video-level feedback and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment. In this paper, we present Loupe, a video generation agent that retrieves and verifies textual and visual evidence to construct evidence-grounded temporal video prompts with reference images. We further introduce Rubric-Based Credit (RBC), which leverages prompt-specific factual, visual, and temporal requirements to evaluate intermediate search and planning decisions before video rendering. Building on RBC, RBC-SFT reweights assistant-token learning by step quality, while RBC-GRPO incorporates step-level credits alongside a final planning reward, without rendering videos during RL. To address the lack of dedicated search-oriented evaluation, we construct Search-VBench, which contains 150 held-out prompts across seven categories. Experiments show that Loupe improves all four evaluation dimensions across three video generators, raising the overall score of MiniMax-H3 from 32.80 to 70.67 and outperforming an untrained search workflow. Ablation experiments show that full RBC training outperforms standard SFT followed by trajectory-level GRPO by 5.27 points. Human evaluations and results on Sci-VBench and KIVI-Bench further demonstrate improved generation quality, scientific grounding, factual precision, and helpfulness. Our project page is available at https://zengkaiya.github.io/Loupe/.

In a recent development, flipsnack⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) helps teams turn static documents into interactive digital experiences. Its customers use the platform to create product catalogs, sales presentations, brochures, internal communications, and training materials.

Industry observers note that for Flipsnack, that range of applications creates a marketing challenge: helping people recognize how the product fits the work they need to do. As the company increased its focus on business customers, it wanted to reach people with needs that its product category alone might not clearly describe.

According to recent reports, flipsnack had relied heavily on search advertising. Its ChatGPT Ads test became an opportunity to learn which customer needs could translate into product signups.

Because Flipsnack is a visual product, prospective customers often want to experience it before speaking with sales. Its campaign landing pages directed people into a signup flow, making completed registration the first meaningful step the team could measure and optimize for.

According to recent reports, to help business customers see where the product could fit their work, Flipsnack expanded beyond its original, broader Flipbook campaign. Separate campaigns for Magazine, Catalog, and Brochure addressed specific document needs, while campaigns for Sales Enablement, Employee Benefits, Real Estate, and Hospitality connected the product to business applications and industries.

In a recent development, “A sales team and an internal communications team can use the same product for very different jobs. We want our campaigns to help each see where Flipsnack fits.”.

In a recent development, flipsnack’s initial click-focused campaigns brought in traffic and signups. After seeing better delivery and registration efficiency in conversion-focused campaigns, the team rebuilt existing campaigns with a conversions objective and bidding set to maximize conversions.

Flipsnack created conversion-focused versions of five existing US campaigns that had used a clicks objective with fixed bids.

Reach people as they explore options, compare choices, and make decisions in ChatGPT, with relevant ads that fit naturally into the experience.

Industry News: Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety: Customizable Multimodal Safety for Global Enterprise AI
