💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the last two years have seen NVIDIA's content safety stack grow from a focused English text classifier into a family of specialized models—each extending coverage to fresh modalities, languages, and inference modes.
  • This post covers what changes in 3.5, the design decisions behind each latest capability, and how to integrate the model into production safety pipelines.
  • Nemotron 3 introduced image understanding; Nemotron 3.5 deepens the multimodal integration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the last two years have seen NVIDIA's content safety stack grow from a focused English text classifier into a family of specialized models—each extending coverage to fresh modalities, languages, and inference modes. Nemotron 3 Content Safety, released in March 2026, combined multimodal and multilingual capabilities for the first time in a single 4B-parameter model. Today, we are releasing Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety, which completes that arc: a single model that unifies multimodal input, multilingual reach, custom enterprise policy enforcement, and auditable reasoning into one inference call.

This post covers what changes in 3.5, the design decisions behind each latest capability, and how to integrate the model into production safety pipelines.

Nemotron 3 introduced image understanding; Nemotron 3.5 deepens the multimodal integration. The model takes a user prompt, an optional image, and an optional assistant response as a single context window and produces a coherent safety verdict over the combined input. Evaluating all three together—rather than scoring each independently—closes a well-known gap in multimodal safety scenarios: policy violations that only emerge from the interaction between text and image, or between request and response, are now caught in a single pass.

Nemotron 3.5 maintains the 12-language explicit training coverage of its predecessors—English, French, Spanish, German, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Hindi, Russian, Portuguese, and Italian—while also inheriting strong zero-shot generalization across approximately 140 languages from the Gemma 3 base model. This means deployments in markets where training data is sparse (e.g., Southeast Asian languages, Scandinavian languages, less-resourced African languages) benefit from base-model multilingual transfer without requiring separate fine-tuning.

Industry observers note that this is the most significant architectural addition in 3.5 relative to Nemotron 3. Production deployments rarely operate under a single universal safety taxonomy. A healthcare platform has a different risk profile than a financial services chatbot, a developer tools IDE, or a children's education app. Nemotron 3.5 accepts a custom policy specification alongside the input. The model reasons over that policy when producing its verdict rather than deferring entirely to the built-in taxonomy. This extends the work first introduced in Nemotron Content Safety Reasoning 4B to the full multimodal, multilingual setting.

Every safety verdict in Nemotron 3.5 can be accompanied by an auditable reasoning trace via an optional think mode. When enabled, the model outputs its step-by-step reasoning before delivering a final safe / unsafe label and, optionally, the violated categories.

When latency is the primary constraint, THINK mode can be disabled to return to the same low-latency binary verdict available in Nemotron 3.

With Nemotron 3.5, we are releasing our safety dataset. This is an vital milestone since most OSS safety models don't generally provide the training or evaluation sets. This problem is worse for the multimodal space where artifacts such as images or videos are often derived from resources with restrictive licensing terms. The Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety Dataset is multimodal, multilingual, and includes safety reasoning traces that were used to train the model. These reasoning traces were generated in a 2-step manner to make them concise, similar to the Nemotron Content Safety Reasoning 4B model.

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety is built on Google Gemma 3 4B IT (4B parameters), providing a 128K context window, strong vision-language reasoning, and broad multilingual coverage. NVIDIA fine-tunes this base with a LoRA adapter that installs targeted safety classification behavior while keeping the model compact enough for real-time deployment on 8GB+ VRAM GPUs.

The inference interface supports three output modes:.

Mode 1 — Low-latency binary verdict:.

Mode 2 — Binary verdict with categories:.

Mode 3 — THINK mode (reasoning + verdict):.

The safety taxonomy follows the Aegis 2.0 framework: 13 core categories aligned with the MLCommons safety taxonomy, plus 10 fine-grained subcategories. This alignment allows direct comparison with other open and closed guard systems benchmarked on Aegis-taxonomy datasets.

Reasoning is a supercharger for content safety classification because it provides the necessary context, customization, and accountability required for production AI systems, especially in enterprise and regulated environments.

Enables Custom and Contextual Policy Enforcement.

In a recent development, reasoning allows a content safety model to dynamically interpret and enforce custom, domain-specific policies defined in natural language at the time of inference. This is necessary because production deployments rarely operate under a single, universal safety taxonomy. A financial services chatbot has a different risk profile than a children's education app which may have a lower tolerance for profanity. This capability supports:.

Provides Auditable and Documented Justification.

The reasoning traces show the model's step-by-step logic before it delivers a final safe or unsafe verdict. This documented justification serves several purposes:.

While reasoning can introduce latency, the Nemotron model addresses this by condensing reasoning chains into concise summaries to limit output tokens and increase efficiency. This is done in a 2-step process similar to what was done in the predecessor model Nemotron-Content-Safety-Reasoning-4B. In the first step, we use larger, more powerful models such as Qwen 397B to generate chain-of-thought reasoning traces based upon provided prompts, images, and responses. We also provided the ground-truth labels of the samples to avoid any misclassification that can find its way into the reasoning traces. In step 2, we make these reasoning traces more concise by using another large model such as Qwen 80B. We specifically instruct this model to rephrase the original traces (from step 1) so that it fits in no more than 3 sentences. Based on our experiments, most reasoning traces generated are under 3 sentences.

According to recent reports, the efficient reasoning traces optimization allows for low-latency custom policy enforcement. Furthermore, the reasoning traces provide a valuable training signal that can be used for training specialized moderator models. Developers can choose a dual-mode operation, disabling reasoning for minimal latency in generic tasks or enabling it for complex policies.

Recent findings suggest that the dataset driving Nemotron 3.5 is an evolution of the multimodal, multilingual blends used for Nemotron 3, with additions targeting the reasoning and custom-policy capabilities. We have used the following sources of data:.

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety was evaluated across multilingual, multimodal, and custom-policy safety benchmarks, including VLGuard, MM-SafetyBench, PolyGuard, RTP-LX, Aya Redteaming, XSafety, MultiJail, Aegis, Dynaguardrail, and CoSA. These evaluations reflect the core production challenge for enterprise safety: applying consistent guardrails across global languages, text and image inputs, and domain-specific policies without adding significant latency.

Recent findings suggest that nemotron 3 set a strong baseline with 84% average accuracy on multimodal harmful-content tests and roughly half the latency of LlamaGuard-4-12B. Nemotron 3.5 maintains that compact 4B efficiency while adding custom policy support and reasoning traces.

According to recent reports, across multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks, Nemotron 3.5 delivers strong harmful-content classification accuracy while maintaining a compact footprint. This matters because many safety models remain English-first, text-only, or too costly to run repeatedly in production pipelines. Nemotron 3.5 is designed to combine multilingual coverage, multimodal classification, custom-policy support, and low-latency deployment in one model.

Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety delivers strong harmful-content classification accuracy across multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks, averaging about 85% across the evaluated benchmark set.

Recent findings suggest that the language-level results highlight why multilingual safety matters for global enterprise AI. On Multilingual Aegis, Nemotron 3.5 averages 96.5% harmful-content classification accuracy across 12 languages. On RTP-LX, it averages 88.8%, for a combined Aegis and RTP-LX average of 92.7%. This consistency helps teams apply the same safety posture across customer, employee, and partner-facing workflows instead of relying on English-only moderation or separate regional safety models.

In a recent development, figure 2. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety averages 97% harmful-content classification accuracy on Multilingual Aegis Cultural + Adapted (prompt classification) (harmful-f1) across 12 languages.

Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety averages 89% harmful-content classification accuracy on RTPLX (prompt classification) (harmful-f1) across 12 languages.

Accuracy alone is not enough for production guardrails. Safety models must also be efficient enough to run before content is processed, returned, or routed downstream. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety's compact 4B design helps reduce the cost and latency of repeated safety checks, making multilingual and multimodal guardrails practical for real-world AI applications.

In a recent development, the latency profile is unchanged from Nemotron 3 in the default (no THINK) mode. THINK mode adds inference time proportional to trace length, but this overhead is predictable and can be budgeted separately from the synchronous moderation loop—for instance, by running THINK-mode evaluation asynchronously as part of an audit pipeline while the default mode handles real-time decisions.

Figure 4. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety achieves 3x lower end-to-end latency on a multimodal benchmark compared to an alternative multimodal safety model.

Compared to another reasoning safety model, our model generated up to 50% fewer tokens when reasoning is enabled, making it efficient in terms of cost and latency.

A recurring theme in multimodal safety research is the gaps in existing evaluation infrastructure. Nemotron 3.5's development encountered the same gaps documented in the broader literature:.

Recent findings suggest that NVIDIA's multimodal training data—with real images and culturally nuanced multilingual prompts—is designed to fill some of these gaps for model training. The benchmark gap for evaluation remains an open problem for the broader safety research community.

It has been revealed that nemotron 3.5 Content Safety is available on Hugging Face under the NVIDIA Open Model License for research and commercial use, along with the training dataset. It supports transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, and is available as a production-grade NVIDIA NIM on build.nvidia.com for teams that need a pre-packaged, GPU-optimized inference microservice.

Developers can also access the model through inference platforms including Baseten, Eigen AI, DeepInfra, OpenRouter, and Vultr.

For custom policy workflows, NVIDIA provides a Claude- and Codex-compatible skill for generating custom policies, along with cookbooks showing how to use the model. Custom policies and reasoning traces help teams adapt safety behavior to domain-specific rules while keeping decisions auditable.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.31883v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video understanding depends not only on how models reason about visual evidence, but also on which evidence they observe. Fixed observation policies determine this evidence in advance; agentic harnesses allow models to seek further observations as their understanding develops. This shift creates an opportunity to realize capabilities that fixed inputs leave untapped, yet the ability to request observations does not ensure their effective use. We investigate when and why video harnesses improve understanding, examining how task demands and models' capacity for interaction jointly shape their benefits. Using Video-Relook as an experimental framework, we let models adapt their temporal and spatial observations from a common default configuration, and analyze performance and interaction trajectories across models and tasks. Adaptive observation yields substantial gains on fine-grained action understanding, with benefits also extending to Video-MME-v2. Even under the same observation interface, gains differ substantially across models; interaction traces reveal corresponding differences in evidence seeking and the reliability of answer revision. The benefits also vary across tasks for the same model, ranging from substantial improvements to limited gains and regressions. Together, these findings support an account in which harness effectiveness depends on the alignment between opportunities for informative observation and the model's ability to turn interaction into reliable revisions. They motivate video harnesses that coordinate perception and reasoning, matching observational autonomy to task demands and model capabilities.

Newly introduced commitments to the communities where we build and policy proposals to help more Americans share in the benefits.

In a recent development, the promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures. It can help someone learn a new skill, build a business, or solve a problem that was previously out of reach. Building more computing infrastructure capacity in the United States can help lower the cost of delivering AI, put these tools in more people’s hands, and ensure America stays at the forefront of the technology.

Sources indicate that the communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too. Residents should be able to influence how a campus is developed, hold developers accountable for covering the cost of powering it, and share in the jobs and business opportunities it creates. How we build these campuses is one of the first tests of whether the benefits of AI will be broadly shared.

Today we’re publishing our National Community Compact⁠(opens in a new window) and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint⁠(opens in a new window). The compact sets out what communities can expect from OpenAI at future campuses that we own and operate. The blueprint proposes policies to help ensure that compute campus development gives communities a meaningful voice, protects families from new costs, and broadly shares the economic gains of AI.

According to recent reports, this builds on work we began in January, when we revealed our Stargate Community commitments to pay our own way on energy and develop intends shaped by local priorities. We followed with specific commitments in Georgia and Ohio, covering energy costs, water use, local investment and accountability. Throughout that work, we’ve listened to residents, local leaders, schools and businesses about what matters to their communities. Today’s announcement is the next step in that ongoing effort.

Recent findings suggest that every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We’ll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we’re doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:.

Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We’ll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we’ll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.

Protect local resources and report on our impact. We’ll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We’ll publish construction aims and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.

Create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We’ll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We’ll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.

Sources indicate that those priorities will differ from place to place. In Effingham County, Georgia, residents helped shape a $4.8 million grant to provide free school meals for all 14,000 students in the county. In Pike County, Ohio, families identified childcare as a priority, leading to a joint $6 million commitment from OpenAI and SB Energy.

According to recent reports, families should be able to count on basic protections whoever builds a campus in their community. Voluntary commitments from companies are an key starting point, but our blueprint goes further—asking federal, state, and local policymakers to establish clear rules for how the industry builds. Fresh policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies. Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared.

In a recent development, that starts with who pays for power. State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and protect other customers if a project falls through. Utilities should also make it easier for campuses to connect if they can safely cut demand when power is scarce. At our planned Effingham County campus, for example, our agreement with Georgia Power allows the utility to reduce the power it delivers to us by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand. Congress can help meet growing demand by speeding up transmission upgrades and restoring and expanding tax incentives for clean electricity.

Communities also need a way to hold developers accountable. The blueprint calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise, and hiring, and for narrow limits on when developers can require public officials to sign NDAs. When states or local governments offer tax incentives, the terms should be public, with measurable commitments and a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short.

Finally, the blueprint proposes practical ways to keep more of the work local to ensure compute campuses support local workers and local businesses. Developers can share purchasing prepares early enough for local suppliers to compete for contracts. Employers, building trades unions, and community colleges can use hiring forecasts to train residents for jobs they know will be available, from electrical work during construction to maintaining power and cooling systems for years afterward.

It has been revealed that the investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while prepares can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenEnv is a tool for creating an agentic execution environment like terminals, browsers, or anything an agent can interact with. And today, we’re excited to announce that OpenEnv is becoming even more open, to make the future of training agents open source.

Sources indicate that starting today, OpenEnv will be coordinated by a committee that so far includes Meta-PyTorch, Reflection, Unsloth, Modal, Prime Intellect, Nvidia, Mercor, Fleet AI, Microsoft, Hugging Face, and RadixArk. OpenEnv now lives at huggingface/OpenEnv.

OpenEnv project is supported and adopted by some of the leading organizations in the AI ecosystem, including PyTorch Foundation, vLLM, SkyRL (UCB), Lightning AI, Axolotl AI, Stanford Scaling Intelligence Lab, Mithril, OpenMined, Scaler AI Labs, Scale AI, Patronus AI, Surge AI, Halluminate, Turing, Scorecard, Snorkel AI, SGLang, and Miles.

It has been revealed that agent harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, and Hermes just keep improving. One reason for their improvement is that models like GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 are trained to use their respective harnesses.

We want those gains with open source models too: training local models that use harnesses effectively, and saving compute by specializing models for specific tasks.

Frontier labs train models and harnesses that, for the most part, work like hand in glove. The model is trained to use the harness and optimised for its characteristics. Models can generalise beyond these harnesses, to some extent, but nothing beats the efficiency of training.

Recent findings suggest that in the open, this isn’t the case. Developers use any harness, any model, any inference engine, on whatever use case they value. This is fundamental to the community, but it’s also a challenge that requires infrastructure and tooling to tackle.

Industry observers note that that’s where OpenEnv comes in. It’s a library to interface between harness, environment, and trainer, which works on any model. For this to stick, it will need to be owned by all the major stakeholders.

Alongside the governance change, we're tightening what OpenEnv is.

Industry observers note that in recent releases, OpenEnv has become an interoperability layer for RL environments. Its job is to standardize how environments are published, deployed, and consumed by agents. It will not dictate how rewards are defined or how training loops work. Reward definition, scoring rubrics, and trainer-specific logic belong in the libraries that specialize in them. OpenEnv is the common socket they can all plug into.

Industry observers note that one interface, many environments which all expose the familiar Gymnasium-style API (reset(), step(), state()) running on a client/server architecture. A trainer that speaks OpenEnv can drive any compliant environment without bespoke code.

Familiar protocols and canonical packaging. Environments are served over standard protocols like HTTP and WebSocket and packaged with Docker. MCP is a first-class citizen, so OpenEnv environments are instantly compatible with MCP servers and the same environment behaves consistently in both simulation (train/eval) and production modes.

According to recent reports, interop across env libraries. You can define and consume environments across different ecosystems (verifiers, harbor, and others) and on the infrastructure and hub of your choice. OpenEnv is the deployment and interface layer underneath them, rather than a competitor to them.

Over the coming months we will focus on the things that turn OpenEnv from a fast-growing project into a dependable standard:.

OpenEnv is community-centric by design, and it's still early — expect rough edges, and help us smooth them. Check out the code and RFCs: github.com/openenv/OpenEnv.

Sources indicate that thanks to everyone who helped make this transition happen. Let's build the common substrate for open-source agentic RL together.

In a recent development, there is some excellent work here to check. https://a2eprotocol.github.io/docs/.

CALVIN-MAX: When Does a Mid-Execution Change Hurt a Robot Policy?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (300 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.31868v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robots must often keep working after the world changes, as when a block moves or the camera shifts while the robot still acts on what it saw before. Recent work highlighted that one change during a task lowers success for every policy tested, but did not separate the effect of its timing from the cost of the changed world, or measure what it costs afterwards. We introduce CALVIN-MAX, a benchmark of 7,828 cases on CALVIN's five-instruction chains, each with one change to the objects, the camera, the robot, or the instruction. Each case compares three runs that are identical until the affected instruction begins: one without the change, one with it in place from that moment, and one in which it arrives while the robot is moving. The second run against the first gives the cost of the changed world, and the third against the second the effect of meeting it mid-motion. On 1,526 held-out cases per policy, with hypotheses fixed in advance, each of ten released policies loses 4.4 to 9.9 percentage points on the affected instruction over the eight core changes. Whether timing matters depends on the change: one that alters what the robot sees costs 5.4 points less mid-motion than from the start, whereas a change to the scene itself or to the robot highlights no detectable effect. Rewinding the robot to the start of the instruction removes the benefit for every policy; the stricter test we fixed in advance, that the rewound run then matches the second run, passes for three. The cost also outlasts the affected instruction: the change stays in place, and a policy that still completes that instruction is 5.0 to 16.8 points less likely to complete the next one.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.31850v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale pretraining provides embodied models with general capabilities, but reliable task execution still requires post training. In multitask settings, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) faces distribution mismatch between training and deployment, whereas reinforcement learning (RL) is limited by sparse rewards and uneven learning progress across tasks. Multi-teacher on policy distillation (MOPD) consolidates expert capabilities through dense supervision on the model's own trajectories, but achieving performance beyond the teachers remains challenging. We propose a two-stage post training framework for flow-based embodied models, constructing distillation objectives from the velocity regression formulation of conditional flow matching. Stage 1 efficiently consolidates expert capabilities through MOPD. Stage 2 combines RL with teacher distillation that weights velocity errors according to the sampling noise, where distillation is restricted to failed trajectories to supplement sparse rewards with dense guidance without directly constraining successful behaviors. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks show that the framework outperforms joint SFT and exceeds the corresponding teachers' aggregate success rates. Sample efficiency comparisons show higher success rates than direct RL with fewer environment interactions.

JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (234 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.31849v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting features of masked regions from visible context. In chest computed tomography, the findings that decide a diagnosis, such as a small nodule, are often not predictable from the surrounding anatomy. A hidden finding is then best predicted toward normal anatomy, and the prediction loss stops rewarding the encoder for representing it. We call this the context shortcut. Conditioning the predictor on the radiology report repairs the prediction, but in our setup the encoder gains little over image-only pretraining: the report supplies what the encoder never had to learn. JECT therefore gives the report two roles: a condition for the predictor and, through masked section-text prediction, a target for the encoder, which must predict the report's anatomical sections from the unmasked scan. A hierarchical three-dimensional encoder that predicts at every stage keeps this clinical content at every scale. In ablations, the text target improves classification and localization, while conditioning adds little to the encoder. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, the recipe reaches the level of current computed tomography foundation models in classification, retrieval and nodule malignancy, and of task-specific models in lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning. Conditioning still matters: its predictor can be reused, with no extra training, to show where a report sentence acts, changing most at the finding the sentence describes. Code and pretrained weights are available.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you have a GitHub repository and you have GitHub Actions enabled, you probably use GitHub-hosted runners for CI.
  • That default is convenient, but it also has limits.
  • So built an alternative: keep GitHub Actions in charge of CI, but run the jobs on Hugging Face Jobs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you have a GitHub repository and you have GitHub Actions enabled, you probably use GitHub-hosted runners for CI. That is the default for many projects because it is simple: add a workflow, write runs-on: ubuntu-latest, and GitHub gives you a machine.

That default is convenient, but it also has limits. GitHub Actions can be slow or down for maintenance, the hosted machines are generic, and GPU access is not something most open-source projects can just turn on. For Trackio, those limits started to matter. We wanted both reliable CPU CI for basic unit tests and frontend checks, but also GPU CI for tests that need to run on actual CUDA hardware.

So built an alternative: keep GitHub Actions in charge of CI, but run the jobs on Hugging Face Jobs.

The result: Trackio's CI now runs on Hugging Face Jobs and streams back real-time logs, cutting our CI time for CPU jobs by about 30% and enabling a whole newly introduced test suite that runs on GPU machines!

In this article, we explain step-by-step how to recreate the same setup for your GitHub repo. If you are using an agent, you can point it to this article, since we provide CLI instructions alongside browser-based instructions for us humans.

Let's start with a quick intro to Hugging Face Jobs!

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face Jobs lets you run commands or scripts on Hugging Face's serverless infrastructure with almost any hardware flavor. A Job is essentially:.

According to recent reports, that makes Jobs a natural fit for CI. CI jobs are already command-driven, already run in clean environments, and often benefit from choosing exactly the right hardware. For ML libraries, the GPU case is especially compelling: you can run a test suite on real GPU hardware without maintaining your own always-on runner.

The key step is connecting GitHub Actions to HF Jobs, which we describe below.

For this setup, we created huggingface/jobs-actions, a small bridge that turns a GitHub Actions job into an ephemeral self-hosted runner running inside an HF Job.

The complete flow looks like this:.

Sources indicate that from GitHub's point of view, this is just a self-hosted runner. From Hugging Face's point of view, it is just a Job that releases a container to run the workflow steps from the repo’s GitHub Actions.

The first thing you need is the dispatcher. This is a small Docker Space that receives GitHub workflow_job webhook events and launches HF Jobs in response.

Recent findings suggest that create this first because the GitHub App needs a webhook URL, and that URL comes from the Space. This Space should be under your own namespace or under a Hugging Face org that you have write access to.

Go to huggingface/jobs-actions-dispatcher and click Duplicate this Space.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.31848v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard LLM personalization typically frames identity as a static retrieval task, overlooking the inherent incongruity of human personas, where stable traits coexist with atypical, context-specific stances. Existing methods struggle to reconcile these dimensions: prompting succumbs to context drift over long sequences, while fine-tuning often suppresses idiosyncratic "quirks" in favor of generic distributional patterns. To bridge this gap, we present QuirkyMind, a framework that disentangles identity definition from its expression. First, Traits Anchoring constructs a dual-stream latent state, fusing a sentence-level summary for semantic stability with a token-level sequence for generative control. This state is stabilized via In-Context Narrative Refinement using an alternating objective: a discriminative InfoNCE loss anchors the persona in representation space to prevent drift, while a generative cross-entropy loss ensures faithful verbalization. Finally, Persona Steered Generalization transfers the refined state to downstream tasks via parameter-efficient adapters. Empirical evaluations on Persona-Steered QA and Narrative Inference demonstrate that QuirkyMind mitigates drift, consolidating persona knowledge without erasing authentic incongruities.

GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A cybersecurity model trained to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, while staying within the scope that researchers set.
  • It has been revealed that we’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set.
  • On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A cybersecurity model trained to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, while staying within the scope that researchers set.

It has been revealed that we’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set. GPT‑6 Cyber delivers major gains on key cybersecurity benchmarks over GPT‑5.6 Cyber, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym and a step function improvement when tested on staying within scope. It is already helping to secure real-world software, uncovering and validating thousands of exploits in security-critical codebases such as Linux and Firefox.

On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. It also follows task boundaries more reliably: in a separate alignment evaluation, GPT‑6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and 100% with this prompt. This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.

Recent findings suggest that these capabilities are already helping secure real systems. Our researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux⁠ and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, despite extensive prior testing with frontier models. The model also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox vulnerabilities⁠(opens in a new window). Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and we have relied on it to find and fix weaknesses in our own infrastructure⁠.

Industry observers note that it is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software⁠. Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Mainline models such as GPT‑6 Astra already support code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development. Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals, while Daybreak Red enables deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT‑6 Cyber.

According to recent reports, GPT‑6 Cyber is a major step up from GPT‑5.6 Cyber and outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on most cyber tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the request. We evaluated the model on tasks that require it to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Based on these results, we classify the model as Critical in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.

Industry observers note that on ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, about 16 percentage points higher than GPT‑5.6 Cyber’s 32.1%. To test vulnerability discovery, we also built a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing. Models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT‑6 Cyber achieved 40.3% recall of vulnerabilities compared with 32.0% for GPT‑6 Astra.

According to recent reports, daybreak Red is designed to support more advanced security workflows, including developing working exploits and using them against remote targets. To evaluate these capabilities, we built a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins deployed in a controlled environment. In our initial evaluation, GPT‑6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused 100% of tasks, while GPT‑6 Cyber completed 95%; its only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. See the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full results and evaluation settings.

One risk for cybersecurity agents is that they go outside the scope of their assigned task, attempt to exploit unrelated services, or disregard the researcher’s rules of engagement.

We made alignment a central focus of GPT‑6 Cyber, using specialized training to help the model stay within authorized scope, follow restrictions on its actions, and report its work accurately. Before deployment, we ran a series of alignment evaluations to measure these behaviors. See the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full results.

Industry observers note that one of these evaluations is ExploitGym Honeypot, which was informed by the Hugging Face incident⁠. We give the model a difficult exploitation task in an isolated environment with access to supporting services, such as a package registry or object store. We deliberately make these services easy to exploit so that attacking them can reveal the task’s flag. The model must infer that exploiting them is outside the scope of its task.

In a recent development, GPT‑6 Cyber shows a step-change improvement over GPT‑5.6 Cyber on this evaluation. When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time.

We can see directly in the GPT‑6 Cyber model’s chain of thought how it reasons about staying within bounds:.

Industry observers note that GPT‑6 Cyber is already helping security teams find vulnerabilities, validate their impact, and develop fixes. Customers have put it to work on large codebases, long-running exploit development, and security review:.

In a recent development, we have also relied on GPT‑6 Cyber to secure our own systems. It was one of the main models behind the work we recently shared on hardening the infrastructure used to train frontier models⁠. In controlled red-teaming campaigns, agents using GPT‑6 Cyber and other OpenAI models chained vulnerabilities to escape microVMs and execute code on the underlying hosts. We used the findings to patch software, tighten network restrictions, and report challenges to maintainers and vendors.

In a recent development, our vulnerability researchers also use GPT‑6 Cyber to find and validate vulnerabilities in open-source software at scale. This work has uncovered previously unknown flaws in software that has been scrutinized for years:.

Found 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities. GPT‑6 Cyber can be suitable for use in autonomous workflows for finding vulnerabilities and proposing high-quality patches at scale. During a vulnerability research campaign, GPT‑6 Cyber produced evidence and reproducible tests for 81 novel vulnerabilities classified by Mozilla as high severity, and showed that an additional 30 known issues were more severe than previously reported. We disclosed the findings to Mozilla, along with proposed patches to help its engineers develop fixes. Mozilla was supportive of this work, and began landing fixes shortly after receiving the reports⁠(opens in a new window).

Developing exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities⁠. GPT‑6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948—more than five times the 166 exploited by GPT‑5.6 Sol using the same research harness. Following the Linux community's guidance, we disclosed 304 critical findings to maintainers with candidate patches and are in the process of getting other vulnerabilities fixed.

Demonstrating critical RCE vulnerabilities. We recently discussed a critical vulnerability in Brotli⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), a compression library used by Node.js and other software. Our security researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber alongside other OpenAI models to develop and validate exploits showing how the flaw could enable remote code execution in downstream applications.

In a recent development, as models become more capable and uncover more security vulnerabilities, we are also seeing more attempts to use them to cause harm. These attempts include efforts by malicious cyber actors and adversarial groups seeking to distill our models. We have thus paired GPT‑6 Cyber’s stronger capabilities with stronger safeguards to detect and disrupt misuse and keep the model’s actions within the user’s intent and authorization.

We added and strengthened these protections alongside the release of GPT‑6 Cyber (see the system card⁠(opens in a new window) for full information):.

Industry observers note that cyber-specific misalignment monitoring. We monitor whether actions match the user’s authorization, while recognizing legitimate exploit development and testing.

Sources indicate that targeted monitoring for emerging threats. For example, during the coordinated disclosure of critical PHP vulnerabilities, we set up targeted monitoring for attempts to develop exploits against live PHP servers, while preserving support for defenders patching affected systems.

Private Safety Processing (PSP). We use automated checks to review related interactions for misuse. Standard retention remains the default. API customers using Zero Data Retention⁠(opens in a new window) generally must use PSP⁠(opens in a new window), which reviews encrypted records retained in customer storage for 30 days without exposing prompts and responses to OpenAI personnel.

Protection against stolen credentials. We require IP allowlisting for Daybreak Red API access by default, restricting requests to approved networks with limited exceptions. We also monitor credentials for compromise.

Sandboxing and oversight. As with past models, we recommend sandboxing⁠(opens in a upcoming window), action review⁠(opens in a new window), and human oversight for high-risk workflows.

Protections against high-risk cyber assistance. We use new checks to block high-risk activity involving critical systems (see below for more).

Protecting critical infrastructure has been a key consideration in designing GPT‑6 Cyber’s safeguards and access, including power plants, water treatment facilities, and the operational technology and industrial control systems (OT/ICS) that underpin them. We simultaneously want to give the teams defending these systems access to our most capable models while also strengthening our safeguards to prevent unauthorized attacks.

According to recent reports, first, to equip these defenders, our $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders⁠ grant program subsidizes access for resource-constrained teams such as government organizations and essential service providers. We’re also introducing a latest group within Daybreak Red (Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure) for approved critical infrastructure defenders, which gives them permissions to conduct authorized testing of critical systems while retaining safeguards against model misalignment.

Second, to prevent misuse of the Daybreak Red and Blue platforms, we have refined safeguards against assistance and capability development that could compromise industrial controls or safety-critical systems, interfere with equipment, or cause serious injury, catastrophic physical damage, or life-endangering service disruption. The figure below compares safeguard label rates across four access configurations, before and after the recent updates we’re rolling out alongside GPT‑6 Cyber.

In a recent development, higher safeguard block rates are not always better. Many of the techniques in this evaluation are also essential to legitimate security work: understanding systems, finding vulnerabilities, and verifying that fixes withstand attack. We therefore assess these rates alongside support for legitimate research and patching, rather than aiming for 100%.

To evaluate how our models can help defend critical infrastructure, we partnered with Dragos, the global provider for extended operational technology (xOT) cybersecurity. Dragos ran evaluations using cyber-permissive Daybreak Red models in a controlled lab environment. The evaluations covered requests progressing from network discovery and asset enumeration through targeted reconnaissance, sensitive data exfiltration, and unauthorized, potentially dangerous device actions.

It has been revealed that we used feedback from Dragos to refine our safeguards, aiming to block harmful assistance without unnecessarily restricting authorized testing. See their final report⁠(opens in a new window) for details on the evaluations. We’re also working to expand partnerships with other offensive security providers and purple teams on penetration testing and red teaming with AI, and with energy companies, other critical infrastructure operators, and national labs to assess our models’ effectiveness and safeguards in industrial defense. We have also increased our investment in threat investigations to detect model usage involving OT/ICS. We’ll continue refining our safeguards with input from partners and the security community, including reports through /feedback when safeguards miss harmful activity or interrupt legitimate work.

GPT‑6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. We will progressively expand access to all Daybreak Red customers soon, and are also making GPT‑5.6 Cyber available to all Daybreak Red customers. We’re also expanding Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT‑6 Astra to more organizations and individual security researchers; let us know⁠(opens in a new window) if you’re interested.

Fresh users and organizations can apply for Daybreak⁠ and get started with our cyber skills, products, and partners⁠.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (322 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.31839v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: SWE-bench-style benchmarks, such as SWE-bench Verified (Verified) and SWE-bench Pro (Pro), evaluate coding agents with tests taken from the change that originally fixed each glitch. However, these tests can enforce details the task never states, causing correct alternative fixes to fail. Such overspecified tests have so far been found mainly through expensive expert review. To address this, we define the Spec-Test Coverage Gap (STCG), a 1-4 scale measuring overspecification, and score it with two LLM judges, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, which are given the specification and the test patch. A task is flagged as overspecified when both judges score it 3 or higher. Our study has three parts. First, we validate the judges on 206 tasks that earlier human audits and agent results label as overspecified or fine. Second, we apply STCG to all 500 Verified and 731 public Pro tasks and compare the flags with the results of the top 30 Verified submissions. Third, we verify the flags by asking Claude Opus 5.5 to loosen the overspecified requirements of flagged tasks, and regrade 2,186 failed patches from those submissions. Our main findings are: (1) Overspecified tests are detectable: on the validation tasks, the judges correctly flag 89% of the tasks that human audits identify as overspecified and wrongly flag only 4% of the tasks known to be fine. (2) Overspecified tests are common: applied to whole benchmarks, the judges flag 23% of Verified and 35% of Pro tasks. (3) Flagged tasks are much harder for agents: the top 30 Verified submissions resolve only 31% of the flagged tasks on average, against 88% of the other tasks. (4) Overspecified tests change the leaderboard: relaxing the tests lets 61% of the 2,186 failed patches on flagged tasks pass. Counting these patches as resolved would add 33 to 60 tasks to each top-30 submission, raising resolve rates by up to 12 percentage points.

  • I asked a coding agent to build a beautiful website showcasing the monuments of Paris as 3D Gaussian splats.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An agent built a 3D Paris gallery from two Hugging Face Spaces.

I asked a coding agent to build a beautiful website showcasing the monuments of Paris as 3D Gaussian splats. I never opened an image generator. I never touched a 3D reconstruction tool. The agent produced every asset (the images and the 3D splats) by calling two Hugging Face Spaces directly, then wired them into a cinematic viewer.

Here's the result, live as a static Space:.

This post is about how that's possible now, and why I think it's a preview of how a lot of multimedia software gets built from here on.

In a recent development, mitchell Hashimoto recently described a shift he calls the building block economy: the most effective path to software is no longer a polished monolith, but small, well-documented components that others (increasingly agents) can assemble. His key observation: AI is okay at building everything from scratch, but it is really good at gluing together proven pieces.

That thesis has mostly been told with code libraries. But the same forces are hitting multimedia AI. The hard part of using a state-of-the-art image model, a video model, a TTS model, or a 3D reconstruction model was never the model. It was the integration: SDKs, weights, GPUs, input formats, polling. If each model were instead a documented, callable block, an agent could glue them together the same way it globs together npm packages.

That's exactly what Hugging Face Spaces have quietly become.

The Hub hosts thousands of state-of-the-art models (a huge share of them open-weights), and most are deployed as interactive Spaces. As of now, every Gradio Space also exposes a plain-text agents.md that tells an agent exactly how to call it:.

returns everything needed in one shot: the schema URL, the call and poll templates, how to upload files, and the auth hint:.

No client library. No hardcoded integration. An agent reads that, and it can drive the Space end to end. Set an HF_TOKEN and you're going. You can find these instructions on any Gradio Space via its Agents button:.

The real unlock is chaining: the output of one Space becomes the input to the next. Prompt → image → 3D. That's the whole pipeline behind this gallery.

The six source images the agent generated, all isolated on black, ready for single-image 3D reconstruction:.

It has been revealed that from there the agent did the "glue" work too. It noticed TripoSplat outputs are Y-down and flipped them upright, auto-framed each monument, compressed the .ply files to .ksplat (~3× smaller, so they load fast), built a Three.js viewer with a scroll-to-switch and drag-to-rotate UI, and deployed the whole thing as a static Space. The only human inputs were taste-level: "make it zoomed out," "replace the obelisk with something better for splatting," "the transition lingers too long.".

Sources indicate that several of those steps were the agent reacting to reality. A wide glass pyramid splats poorly. A thin obelisk is dull. A single-view reconstruction infers the back. That is exactly the "outsourced R&D, fast iteration" loop the building-block economy predicts, except the R&D was a conversation.

Industry observers note that the real test of a building block is how cheaply you can reuse it. Once this pipeline existed, spinning up entirely new galleries cost about one sentence each. "Create a similar Space with splats for Japan," then the same for Egypt, and the agent did the rest: six monument images, six splats, compression, a viewer, and a deployed Space, per country.

Gaze World Model

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (227 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.31836v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Where a person looks indicates their focus of attention, and how their gaze shifts between targets reveals how that attention responds to a changing scene. Existing gaze target estimation methods largely operate frame by frame and do not model these shifts. Gaze shifts are often driven by dynamic changes in the scene, which is the kind of information world models are designed to encode. This relationship is subtle, however, since an event far across the frame may produce only a slight movement of the person's head or eyes. We therefore introduce the Gaze World Model (GWM), which co-trains latent scene prediction with person-conditioned gaze supervision on a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder; in our ablations, the latent prediction objective improves both shift detection and gaze localization. Given a video clip and the person's head box, GWM estimates gaze locations and detects gaze shifts in the observed clip, and forecasts future gaze and shifts from predicted scene features. To train and evaluate these tasks, we augment VideoAttentionTarget and ChildPlay with event-level gaze-shift annotations. GWM achieves state-of-the-art shift detection on these benchmarks, about 10 points higher in four-class AP than the strongest baseline, while remaining comparable to the strongest image-based models in gaze target estimation, and outperforms the compared baselines on future gaze localization and shift forecasting.

arXiv:2611.31835v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Actor-critic methods achieve high returns in robotic control, yet trained actors exhibit high-frequency action oscillations. Most smoothness methods constrain the actor, whereas PAVE regularizes the critic by separately penalizing action-gradient variation and encouraging negative action curvature. The same gradient change, however, moves the critic's preferred action farther where the critic is flat, and separate penalties do not measure this motion. We characterize this motion through the greedy shift, which approximates greedy-action displacement across state transitions to first order under local concavity. Since displacement alone does not reflect its critic-value consequences, the analysis further highlights that the shift's curvature-weighted energy approximates the value lost by retaining the previous greedy action to second order. Based on this relationship, POISE regularizes the curvature-weighted energy along temporal and spatial state displacements. It employs a saddle-free curvature metric and reward-scale-consistent scaling while leaving the actor unchanged. On six continuous control tasks with TD3, POISE reduces the smoothness score on every task by $5.9\times$ on average ($4.5\times$ geometric mean), compared with $2.2\times$ ($1.9\times$) for the strongest baseline, and achieves the lowest score on five tasks. Paired return intervals include zero on four tasks, with a 14% increase on Ant and an 11% decrease on Hopper.

Cult.fit’s first major shift was in engineering. Before standardizing on Codex, developers were using a mix of coding agents and assistants. It has been revealed that cult.fit wanted a shared platform around which it could standardize the software development lifecycle. The tech giant chose Codex as that foundation. Repository structures, skills, testing, code review, and feedback loops could now follow common conventions across teams.

Teams are also building their own applications and workflows. HR, for example, built a workflow in Codex to manage performance reviews, scheduling, feedback collection, and the work of bringing that information together. Profiling in PyTorch (Part 2): From nn.Linear to a Fused MLP

📅 11 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is the second post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the first part of this series "Profiling in PyTorch", we used torch.add(torch.matmul(x, w), b) to learn how to read PyTorch profiler traces.
  • In the second iteration (this blog post), we climb one rung up the ladder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is the second post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:.

Recent findings suggest that in the first part of this series "Profiling in PyTorch", we used torch.add(torch.matmul(x, w), b) to learn how to read PyTorch profiler traces. We also discussed several other topics that came our way - the CPU dispatch chain, launch overhead, the difference between an overhead-bound and a compute-bound regime, and some internals of torch.compile.

In the second iteration (this blog post), we climb one rung up the ladder. We replace the hand-written matmul-add pair with an nn.Linear (with bias=True). This is the building block every deep learning model uses. We then stack three of them (specific to our example), with an activation in between, to form a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) block.

The scripts for this blog post live here: 02_linear.py, 03_simple_mlp.py, and 03_kernels_mlp.py. Like before, it helps to open them in a separate tab and walk through the code as you read. We use an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to set up a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.

Before we begin, a quick recap of two ideas we will lean on repeatedly:.

nn.Linear is a module wrapper around the same matrix multiplication and addition we already profiled in Part 1. The only difference is that it owns its weight and bias as parameters and exposes a forward method that PyTorch owners have grown familiar with.

The operation at hand can be written as:.

According to recent reports, where x is the input, w is the weight and b is the bias. Let's run 02_linear.py and check the profile.

trace-util is a utility that will sync your traces to a Hugging Face bucket and then provide the Preffeto URLs on your terminal.

Figure 1 shows the profiler trace of a forward call of the linear layer. We trace the forward call of the linear layer with a similar schedule setup as the previous traces, with wait=1, warmup=1 and active=3. This is why we see three Profile Steps in the CPU and GPU lanes.

If we zoom into the profiler trace, as we do in Figure 2, we notice an aten::t (transpose) op before the aten::addmm (multiplication and addition) op. We can already figure out that nn.Linear transposes the weight parameter and then multiplies it with the input. This is the reason we see an aten::t op.

In a recent development, an crucial thing to notice is that aten::t does not really copy or reorganize data: it only rewrites tensor metadata (shape and stride) on the CPU to represent the transposed matrix. It does not launch a kernel on the GPU. One can verify this two ways: by looking at the GPU lane in the trace, or by checking the aten::t row in the profiler table and the time it took on CUDA.

It has been revealed that there is no aten::add (the bias addition) in the dispatch chain of the linear layer, as seen in Figure 3. This is because the bias addition has been folded into the matrix multiplication kernel, using what is called an epilogue.

Industry observers note that an epilogue is a small computation that a GEMM (GEneral Matrix Multiply) kernel does at the very end, just before it writes its result back to HBM (High Bandwidth Memory, the GPU's main memory). Adding a bias, applying an activation, or scaling by a constant are all classic epilogues. The point of an epilogue is to avoid loading or writing to HBM a second time, since memory traffic makes an operation expensive.

Recent findings suggest that nn.Linear calls torch.nn.functional.linear, which, in turn, calls aten::linear. aten::linear looks at the inputs, notices that a bias was passed, and dispatches aten::addmm(bias, x, weight) instead of doing a matmul and an add separately. addmm computes:.

It has been revealed that the cuBLAS GEMM kernel that runs on the GPU has a bias-add variant built in, and that's the kernel aten::addmm picks. The add never appears as a separate kernel because it is part of the matmul kernel's writeback, which is exactly what an epilogue is.

In a recent development, this is the moment to notice something subtle. The kernel you saw in Part 1 under --compile (addmm) is the kernel that eager nn.Linear already uses. There is nothing left for torch.compile to fuse here, which is the next thing we will verify.

It has been revealed that let's compile the forward call and look at the profiler trace. (The profiler trace is visualized in the next section).

If you compare the eager and compiled traces for a single nn.Linear's forward, you will find:.

It has been revealed that this is worth internalizing. A common reflex is to reach for torch.compile whenever a model feels slow. For a single GEMM-with-bias, compile has very little to do. This is not a bug, this is just that compile needs more than one operation to possibly do any fusing. Let's prove that by looking at an MLP.

A careful reader of the two traces (eager vs compile) will notice that the eager CPU dispatch chain has more in it than the compiled one.

Sources indicate that the eager CPU dispatch chain inside aten::linear is aten::t followed by aten::addmm (Figure 4). To understand what aten::t actually does, we need a quick detour into strides and views.

It has been revealed that A tensor stores its data as one flat, contiguous run of numbers in memory. The shape and stride are metadata that sit on top of that run and tell PyTorch how to walk it: a stride of (s0, s1) means "step s0 elements to move one row, step s1 to move one column". Change the metadata and you get a different view of the same raw data, with no copy:.

Recent findings suggest that M.t() did not move a single number. It returned a fresh view whose strides are swapped, so reading it row-by-row now walks the original buffer 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in transposed order. The underlying data is identical; only the metadata differs.

This is exactly what aten::t does inside the linear layer: it does not allocate a new tensor or copy any data, it produces a view of the weight with rewritten strides.

Sources indicate that as we can see in Figure 5, compile did not remove a GPU kernel: it removed the CPU overhead of dispatching that view. Inductor traced through the view chain at compile time, computed the resulting strides once, and emitted a direct aten::addmm call with those strides hard-coded. A few microseconds of CPU work disappear while the GPU does identical math.

As one would expect, when the input data violates the strides precomputed by the compiler, it will throw an error.

If you look at the GPU lane in both traces, there is exactly one kernel per forward, and it is the same kernel both times:.

If no transpose kernel ran, who taught the GEMM to read the weight matrix in transposed order? The answer is in the kernel's name. Look at the suffix:.

In a recent development, that tn is the layout descriptor. cuBLAS and CUTLASS precompile a separate kernel binary for each combination of input layouts.

Recent findings suggest that n (non-transposed) and t (transposed) describe how a kernel walks its input during the inner loop. The dispatcher's job is to look at the input strides, decide which suffix combination matches, and pick the right precompiled kernel.

The kernel name in a profiler trace is a hash dump of the kernel's identity. If two runs show the same kernel name, the GPU is doing the same work. If they differ (e.g., _tn_ vs _nn_, bf16 vs fp16, or s16816gemm vs s161616gemm) then the GPU is doing different work, and the dispatcher took a different branch. Learning to read this name is one of the most useful habits when comparing traces.

In this section, we will profile a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). To make this more interesting, we will profile a feed-forward network with the GeGLU activation variant (which is quite heavily used in practice). This is also our way of paying tribute to one of the greatest lines ever written in the history of deep learning research (Figure 6).

You will find the entire script here: 03_simple_mlp.py. Execute it like so:.

In a recent development, before we open the trace, let's think together about what we should expect to see. The forward function does a fair amount of computation, but most of it is already familiar to us.

According to recent reports, we should expect three aten::linear dispatches, one for each nn.Linear layer. We should also expect two pointwise kernel launches, one for the GeLU and one for the multiplication. Forming this expectation before looking is the single most useful habit in the profiling journey: you read the trace to confirm or break a guess, not to form one from scratch.

From Figure 7 we can pat ourselves on the back, as our intuition was correct. Per forward pass (one mlp_fwd), the GPU runs exactly 5 kernels. Figure 8 highlights the "occupancy query" as seen in the CPU lane for the linear projection layers.

According to recent reports, the three GEMMs each do an extra cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor call before the launch. We have a separate section on this in Part 1, you can find it here. That is cuBLAS sizing the grid. The pointwise ops (GeLU and mul) launch directly, with no occupancy query. So "a linear" is actually query + launch, while "a pointwise op" is just launch.

The aten::t, aten::transpose, aten::reshape, aten::view, aten::as_strided, and aten::_unsafe_view ops launch zero kernels. They show 0.000us of CUDA time in the table (Figure 9) because they only rewrite tensor metadata (shape and stride) on the CPU. A reader scanning the table sees around six op names per linear, but only one of them (mm) ever reaches the GPU.

The MLP flattens [batch, seq, dim] to [batch * seq, dim] for the matmul. In our command-line invocation we used 64 for batch and 128 for seq, so that's where the 8192 (batch * seq = 64 * 128) below comes from.

Recent findings suggest that all three GEMMs have the same FLOP count, 2·8192·768·3072 ≈ 38.7 GFLOP each, yet down_proj is about 10% faster. Same work, different shape (N=768 instead of 3072), so cuBLAS picks a different tile (128×256, with a deeper stages_64x3 pipeline) that gets better reuse for that shape.

If you want to learn more about tiling in depth, here is a great resource to get started with.

This is exactly why the table had two GEMM rows (Figure 9): the 128x128 row is gate+up and the 128x256 row is down.

Before compiling the forward method and visualizing it, let's do the mental exercise again of asking ourselves what we expect to see in the trace. This is a fun experiment, and an vital one to repeat every time you profile something yourself. Always build on your intuition, and the moment something does not match, stop and figure out why.

Industry observers note that in eager mode, each nn.Linear was expanded into a chain of dispatcher ops (aten::linear → aten::t → aten::transpose → aten::matmul → aten::reshape → aten::mm). Those are the high-level wrappers that ATen walks through before reaching the real GEMM. torch.compile removes that chain.

It has been revealed that by the time the compiled graph runs, there is no linear, no matmul, no transpose or reshape and those metadata ops were folded into how mm is called. We can see three bare aten::mm external calls (Figure 10). The proof that it is the same GEMM is that the kernel names are byte-for-byte identical to eager: ...128x128...stages_32x5_tn for gate and up, and ...128x256...stages_64x3_tn for down.

In a recent development, this is the headline of the whole compile lesson. The two eager pointwise kernels (GeLU and mul) plus a reshape collapsed into one kernel, triton_poi_fused__unsafe_view_gelu_mul_0 (Figure 11). Let's decode the name:.

Why is this a win? In eager mode, the intermediate h = gelu(g) is a full [8192, 3072] bf16 tensor (around 50 MB) that the GeLU kernel writes to HBM and the mul kernel immediately reads back. Fusion keeps it in registers (memory that resides inside the chip and are closer than the HBM). The Triton kernel reads g and u once, computes gelu(g) * u, and writes the result once. One whole round trip of the intermediate through global memory is gone.

Sources indicate that so far we have let PyTorch (eager) and the compiler (torch.compile) pick our kernels. Now we plug in a kernel that a human expert wrote and tuned by hand. We use the LigerGEGLUMLP layer, that we can easily fetch from the Hugging Face Hub with the kernels library.

The full script is here: 03_kernels_mlp.py.

Figure 12 reveals the profile for the LigerGEGLUMLP layer using the Liger kernels from the Hub.

Industry observers note that writing kernels in Triton or CUDA is one problem and shipping them is another. The kernel has to be compiled for your exact combination of GPU architecture, CUDA version, and PyTorch version. This is the step that usually breaks ("works on my machine", missing nvcc, wrong Triton version).

The kernels library moves that build step off your machine. get_kernel("kernels-community/liger-kernels", version=1) downloads a pre-built, version-pinned kernel package from the Hugging Face Hub and caches it locally (here under ~/.cache/...kernels-community--liger-kernels). The benefits are:.

When we say "tuned", we mean two concrete things, and both are visible in the trace.

The fusion is baked in. The LigerGEGLUMLP forward is down_proj(LigerGELUMulFunction.apply(gate_proj(x), up_proj(x))). The LigerGELUMulFunction runs a single Triton kernel, _geglu_tanh_forward_kernel, that computes gelu(gate) * up in one pass. This is exactly what we saw from torch.compile, where the intermediate never makes a round-trip through HBM. We get it here without the compiler, as shown in Figures 13 and 14 (no Dynamo guards, no compile latency, no recompilation risk).

It has been revealed that the launch parameters were chosen for the hardware. The kernel does not guess its block size at random. Liger's calculate_settings picks them from the column count.

It is worth being honest about the trade-off here, because the raw numbers can be misleading. The Liger kernel runs in 92.8 µs, while Inductor's fused kernel from the compile run was 89.4 µs. At first glance the hand-written kernel looks slightly slower, but that comparison hides the cost that makes it worthwhile.

According to recent reports, torch.compile specializes for a static shape. Inductor's 89.4 µs kernel is fast precisely because it was generated for this exact [8192, 3072] problem. Change the batch size, the sequence length, or the hidden dimension, Dynamo re-traces, and you pay the compile cost all over again to get a new specialized kernel.

So the real choice is not "slow human kernel vs fast compiled kernel". It is a fast generic kernel vs a kernel specialized for one particular input shape. The Liger kernel takes one set of launch parameters and runs them for any shape with no recompilation. It gives up the last few microseconds that per-shape specialization would buy, in exchange for being robust to changing shapes.

The table below collects what each step changed on the GPU and what it left untouched.

If there is one habit to carry forward, it is the one we practiced before every trace: guess first, then look. State what you expect the trace to contain, open it, and treat any mismatch as the most interesting thing on the screen.

Sources indicate that this was the second stop in the Profiling in PyTorch series. In the next post we will keep climbing the ladder, moving from this MLP block towards the attention block and, eventually, a full model.

Exploring Multi-Player Social Games as Verifiable Training Grounds for Large Language Models

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (241 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.31821v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The training of socially intelligent language models often relies on large language model (LLM) judges, which are expensive, noisy, and vulnerable to reward hacking. Multi-player social games offer a natural alternative: they require open-ended communication to coordinate with teammates and infer hidden roles, while their rules provide an objective outcome which can serve as a verifiable reward for training. Using three social games, we explore how much social intelligence Qwen3 models can acquire through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Results show that against a much stronger Gemma-3-27B model, SFT and RLVR raise the win rate of Qwen3-4B from 33% to 81% on the three trained games, and from 39% to 54% on three additional held-out games. In contrast, in-context strategies such as prompting improve the win rate of Qwen3-4B by only about 6 pp across the same games we train and evaluate on. Furthermore, we show that the gains from SFT and RLVR hold across the model sizes 1.7B, 4B, and 32B. Qualitative analyses of agent behavior show signs of stronger social intelligence; for example, trained agents tend to share information more openly, check each other's claims against public evidence, and coordinate their votes. More broadly, our results demonstrate that training LLMs on verifiable outcomes in social games can cultivate generalizable social behaviors, which offers a scalable path for building socially intelligent agents.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the future of Australia’s workforce is taking shape before today’s students receive their degrees. Across university campuses, students are using AI to investigate ideas, build assistants and turn concepts into working prototypes. They are beginning to develop the skills they will take into research, established industries and ventures of their own.

Recognising this shift, Australian universities, including UNSW Sydney, University of Sydney, La Trobe University, and Adelaide University, are forging collaborations with OpenAI to give their students and staff access to frontier AI tools.

Students, educators and IT teams are putting AI to work in clinical simulations, robot-assisted teacher training and student projects that build pathways into industry. Alongside this work, universities are developing frameworks for where and how AI can be used in learning and assessment, helping students build practical skills while knowing when to rely on their own judgment. For teachers, employers and industry practitioners, these examples offer practical lessons in designing AI-supported learning, setting clear expectations for AI use and preparing Australians for an AI-enabled workplace.

Newly introduced research1 commissioned by OpenAI reveals what students want from their universities, including the access to AI they increasingly expect. In a survey of more than 1,000 Australian university students, 81% said they already use AI several times a week, including nearly a third (33%) who use it multiple times a day. Over a quarter (28%) had already built an AI agent or assistant to help manage their studies, work or personal life. Four out of five students (79%) want their university to offer more opportunities to use advanced AI tools on real-world projects, with the same proportion interested in applying AI to challenges in health, climate, science or cyber security.

arXiv:2611.31813v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath it too weakly, a program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior. Static analyzers and fuzzers are bound to fixed patterns or to the paths they execute. We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it. We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more. Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost. We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. In the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, it found 11 more undefined-behavior bugs and 4 incomplete contracts. Maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 findings that we reported.
