📅 17 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1116 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if you build with agents today, you probably know three protocols.
  • The Agentic Resource Discovery (ARD) specification is the discovery layer that sits in front of them.
  • In this post, we'll explore the specification, how Hugging Face has implemented it, and how you can start building on ARD.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you build with agents today, you probably know three protocols. MCP gives agents a standard way to call tools. Skills give agents a way of consuming instructions. A2A gives agents a way to call other agents. All three assume the user already knows which tool, instruction, or agent they need. The user is still responsible for discovering, integrating, and maintaining those capabilities.

The Agentic Resource Discovery (ARD) specification is the discovery layer that sits in front of them. It is a draft, open specification developed by contributors from Microsoft, Google, GoDaddy, Hugging Face, and others, with broad participation across the industry. It defines how agents and tools are cataloged, indexed, and searched across federated registries, so an agent can find capabilities at runtime instead of needing them pre-installed. It is not a product or a marketplace. It is a shared standard that any firm can implement independently, and that any agent or tool can participate in.

In this post, we'll explore the specification, how Hugging Face has implemented it, and how you can start building on ARD.

In a recent development, the current model for agent capabilities is install-first, use-later. A developer hardcodes an MCP server URL into a config file. A user connects a service to their AI app via a plugin and reuses it. This works for the handful of tools an agent uses every day, but it doesn't scale to thousands of ad-hoc surfaces.

Sources indicate that the fallback is to dump every available tool description into the LLM's context window and let the model pick. This is limited by the context budget. There are search-based strategies here too, but the descriptions are often too thin to disambiguate well.

Sources indicate that ARD moves selection outside the LLM. A registry indexes capabilities with richer signals such as publisher identity, representative queries, compliance attestations, and tags. It exposes a REST endpoint. The client searches in natural language, and the model invokes whatever the search returns. The shift is from manually installed, static catalogs to intent-based search that lets an agent find the right capability dynamically, and reach a growing ecosystem of MCP tools, A2A agents, and other services without pre-configuring each one.

The specification defines two things:.

In a recent development, the Hugging Face Discover Tool is our reference implementation of ARD. It provides search access to thousands of Skills, ML applications, and MCP Servers — on Hugging Face and across other ARD discovery services.

Industry observers note that it works by combining the Hub's existing semantic search over Spaces, alongside our Agent Skills, and serving the results as ARD catalog entries. The Hub already hosts a catalog of Spaces running Gradio apps, MCP servers, and demos. Its semantic search supports an agents=true flag that returns Spaces ranked by agent-oriented metadata, and Discover translates that search into the ARD specification.

Recent findings suggest that the adapter applies two filters. First, the response includes only Spaces whose runtime stage is RUNNING. Second, the response media type is driven by the request. Three media types are supported:.

According to recent reports, the skill type involves an additional transformation. Many Spaces ship an agents.md file describing how an agent should interact with them. Discover reads that file and wraps it with the frontmatter a skill consumer expects: name, description, and source metadata covering the Space ID, Hub URL, app URL, and original agents.md URL. The result is a skill any skill-aware client can install or load through its normal skill flow.

It has been revealed that for MCP-tagged Spaces, the adapter generates a catalog entry pointing at the Space's Gradio MCP endpoint over HTTP transport. The URL uses the Space's runtime domain when the Hub provides one, otherwise the standard .hf.space slug convention.

discover is built into the Hugging Face CLI (hf). To get started and give you or your agent access:.

You can also Search the catalog directly using either the REST API or an MCP Server.

The Hugging Face catalog is published at its well-known URL:.

Alternatively, connect any MCP Client to search via MCP endpoint using https://huggingface-hf-discover.hf.space/mcp to search the catalog.

ARD separates discovery from execution. The static manifest format is driven by media type, so any artifact protocol can ride the same envelope without specification-level changes. The registry API is plain HTTP REST, so any client can federate against it. Discover is one of several reference implementations of the specification across the ecosystem, and because federation is built into the protocol, a search through one service can surface capabilities hosted by another.

The Discover Tool is a working test of that design. It does not invent a newly introduced artifact format. It wraps an existing search backend, the Hub, in the specification's envelope, and lets the same Spaces surface as skills or MCP servers depending on what the client asked for.

Next steps are tighter integration with the specification's federation modes (auto, referrals, none) and Hub-side support for static ai-catalog.json manifests on user and organization profiles. Once that lands, any Space publisher will be able to advertise their capabilities through the standard well-known URI mechanism.

In a recent development, google just published Agentic Resource Discovery — an open standard (with the Linux Foundation) for how AI agents find and connect to capabilities across the web. Think DNS + a phone book for agents.

The model is simple: you publish an ai-catalog.json at a well‑known path on your domain → registries crawl it → an agent searches by intent → it verifies the publisher → then it connects (over MCP, A2A, or a plain API). Publish → crawl → search → verify → connect.

It has been revealed that most of the coverage will fixate on discovery. I want to flag step 4, because it's the one that actually matters: verify. The agent is about to act on what it finds — call a tool, pull data, make a decision. "I found a capability" is worthless if it can't check who published it and whether it's been tampered with. Discovery without verification just industrialises trusting strangers.

That's the half we've been building the whole time — so when the spec dropped this week, we shipped our catalog the same week. Dynamic Feed is now a verifiable ARD publisher: domain‑anchored identity, every datapoint Ed25519‑signed and checkable against our public key.

Industry observers note that the agentic web is going to be discovered and verified. Good to see the standard treat the second half as a first‑class citizen.

According to recent reports, if you publish an API, an MCP server, or an agent — you can host an ai-catalog.json today. It's a single file. Spec's open: github.com/ards-project/ard-spec.

Tech Report: How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (291 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.31811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We now live in the age of machine-generated mathematics: AI systems produce research-level proofs faster than the human mathematical community can read them. Verification is only part of the challenge. We also need to know whether a "fresh proof" is indeed new, whether a thousand generated proofs contain one idea or many, and where each sits relative to human mathematics. All of these require measuring distances between proofs. Following Hilbert's 24th problem and the identity-of-proofs problem, we ask how far apart two proofs of one theorem are, and what shape the proof space they inhabit has. We define 19 dissimilarity measures in 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties, which we argue are the conditions for safely optimising a measure. In a Curry-Howard kernel, 5 machine-checked proofs that the primes are infinite show that raw syntax cannot tell a rewrite from a new argument, that dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), and that semantic measures invert it: Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. A replication in Lean 4/Mathlib (3 theorems, 19 proofs, 18 measures) confirms that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, and shows that equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, that proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and that proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs. We argue for reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile, extend the measures to proofs of different theorems, and discuss uses, from detecting duplicated AI proofs and orchestrating prover agents to interpreting AI proofs via their nearest human-understandable counterparts. Code, Lean sources and data are released.

Breaking: GLM-5.2: Built for Long-Horizon Tasks

📅 17 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1839 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're introducing GLM-5.2, our latest flagship model for long-horizon tasks.
  • Supporting long-horizon tasks starts with making long context engineering-usable: the model must maintain quality across long, messy coding-agent trajectories, not just accept more tokens.
  • This capability is reflected in GLM-5.2's performance on three long-horizon coding benchmarks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're introducing GLM-5.2, our latest flagship model for long-horizon tasks. It marks a substantial leap in long-horizon task capability over its predecessor GLM-5.1 and, for the first time, delivers that capability on a solid 1M-token context. GLM-5.2's newly introduced capabilities include:.

Supporting long-horizon tasks starts with making long context engineering-usable: the model must maintain quality across long, messy coding-agent trajectories, not just accept more tokens. A 1M context is easy to claim, but much harder to keep reliable under real engineering pressure. To this end, we substantially expanded 1M-context training for coding-agent scenarios, covering large-scale implementation, automated research, performance optimization, and complex debugging. The result is a long-context system that is not only wide in scope, but solid in execution: a practical substrate for sustained engineering work.

This capability is reflected in GLM-5.2's performance on three long-horizon coding benchmarks. FrontierSWE measures whether an agent can complete open-ended technical projects at the scale of hours to tens of hours, spanning systems optimization, large-scale code construction, and applied ML research. On this benchmark, GLM-5.2 trails Opus 4.8 by only 1%, while edging out GPT-5.5 by 1% and Opus 4.7 by 11%. On PostTrainBench, where each agent is given an H100 GPU and evaluated by how much it can improve small models through post-training, GLM-5.2 outperforms both Opus 4.7 and GPT-5.5, ranking second only to Opus 4.8. On SWE-Marathon, an ultra-long-horizon software engineering benchmark covering tasks such as building compilers, optimizing kernels, and developing production-grade services, GLM-5.2 still has room to grow, trailing Opus 4.8 by 13% while remaining second only to the Opus series. Across all three benchmarks, GLM-5.2 is the highest-ranked open-source model, showing that its 1M context has translated into practical long-horizon delivery capability.

In a recent development, on standard coding benchmarks, GLM-5.2 is the strongest open-source model, improving on GLM-5.1 by a wide margin: 81.0 vs. 63.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 62.1 vs. 58.4 on SWE-bench Pro. It also closes much of the gap to the closed-source frontier — on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (81.0) it lands within a few points of Claude Opus 4.8 (85.0) — while staying ahead of Gemini 3.1 Pro.

GLM-5.2 also introduces effort level control, enabling people to explicitly balance model capability against task execution speed and computational cost. As shown in the figure, GLM-5.2 delivers substantially stronger agentic coding performance than GLM-5.1 at comparable token budgets, with its capability roughly positioned between Claude Opus 4.7 and Claude Opus 4.8 under similar token consumption. Moreover, the Max effort level allows users to allocate additional computation when higher performance is required in challenging tasks, further extending the model’s coding capability. This design gives users greater flexibility when using GLM-5.2 for coding tasks, allowing them to select the most suitable reasoning mode for different scenarios.

Sources indicate that to support 1M context length, in GLM-5.2, we apply IndexShare to reduce the computational cost of the indexer in DSA. Specifically, in GLM-5.2, every 4 transformer layers share a lightweight indexer. The indexer is placed at the first of 4 layers and topk indices are used for 4 layers. This reduces the computation of indexer dot product and topk operation in 3/4 layers. GLM-5.2 is trained with IndexShare from mid-training with 128K sequence length, outperforming GLM-5.1 on long-context benchmarks with less computation.

We improve the MTP layer of GLM-5.2 for speculative decoding with two objectives: 1) Minimize the cost of the MTP layer as draft model; 2) Maximize the acceptance rate of speculative decoding.

It has been revealed that for the first objective, we also apply IndexShare on the mtp layer. In multi-step MTP, the indexer is placed on the first step and topk indices are used for all the following steps. However, different from the backbone, the input tokens of different mtp steps are different. As the following figure highlights, if we reuse the topk indices of $h_4$ for $h_5$, $h_5$ can only attend to $h_1$ to $h_4$, but not $h_5$. We will show that the property can help us achieve the second objective, by eliminating the training-inference discrepancy in GLM-5.1's mtp layer.

Industry observers note that in the above figure we show the inference of a two-step MTP layer. In the first step, inference is consistent with training, with all the hidden states coming from the target model. However, in the second step, $h_{1:4}$ come from the target model and $h_5$ comes from the mtp layer. Therefore, the KV cache of $h_5$ is a mixture of $kv_{1:4}$ computed from the target model and $kv_5$ computed from the mtp layer. Instead, with IndexShare, the KV cache of $h_5$ includes only $kv_{1:4}$, all from the hidden states of the target model. For training, we reuse both kv cache and topk indices of the first mtp step. Note that the same as GLM-5.1, the parameters of different MTP steps are also shared. Furthermore, inspired by https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.12370, we introduce rejection sampling for speculative decoding, and use end-to-end TV loss for training.

The table below shows the ablation of techniques by acceptance length on the coding scenarios. In the experiment we use the backbone and training data of GLM-5.1. The number of MTP steps is set to 7 for both training and inference. Compared with the baseline, the acceptance length of the final MTP layer increases by 20%.

As GLM-5.2 extends the maximum context length from 200K to 1M tokens, coding workloads are expected to shift substantially toward longer prompts. This shifts the primary inference bottleneck from computation to KV-cache capacity, long-context kernel overhead, and CPU-side overhead. Although the fresh GLM-5.2 architecture reduces per-token computational FLOPs, it does not proportionally reduce per-token KV-cache size. As a result, supporting longer contexts, higher concurrency, and higher token throughput under limited GPU resources becomes a central challenge for inference engine optimization.

To address this challenge, we optimize the inference engine along three directions. First, building on LayerSplit, we introduce finer-grained memory management and parallelization strategies to increase KV-cache capacity and provide more usable cache space for ultra-long-context requests. Second, we optimize kernels whose cost grows with context length and better coordinate them with the cache transfer pipeline, minimizing the impact of cache transfer on both prefill and decode performance. Third, we optimize CPU-side cache management, request scheduling, and runtime execution paths to reduce bubbles in the GPU execution pipeline and improve end-to-end throughput. As shown in the figure, GLM-5.2 achieves an increasingly larger throughput advantage as context length grows, demonstrating stronger scalability in long-context inference scenarios.

The agentic RL post-training of GLM-5.2 involves tasks at larger scale, across more domains, and with more complex execution patterns. Heterogeneous data and tasks need to be organized within a unified training process, while long-horizon interactions, tool use, sub-task decomposition, and multi-turn environment feedback all impose higher requirements on rollout and training orchestration. To support this process, slime serves as an integrated infrastructure layer from training to large-scale inference rollout. It supports multiple training and task organization modes, including white-box rollout, black-box rollout, compact trajectory, and sub-agent workflow, enabling the same system to scale to larger and more complex RL and OPD training workloads. In the post-training process of GLM-5.2, we used the slime framework to conduct parallel OPD training, efficiently merging more than ten expert models into the final model. The entire OPD training process took approximately two days, demonstrating high training efficiency.

Agentic RL also places higher demands on system resources and inference infrastructure. slime provides a highly open and flexible interface to inference systems: the training side can connect to inference services in different forms, and flexibly adapt to different parallelism strategies, routing policies, PD disaggregation setups, and deployment patterns. At the same time, the configuration experience, scheduling strategies, and optimization paths accumulated during RL rollout can be reused and further refined in the production serving stage, allowing the training side and the serving side to reinforce each other. This creates a more direct path from post-training to production deployment. Together with flexible training-inference resource organization and KV-cache FP8, slime provides critical infrastructure support for GLM-5.2’s large-scale agentic RL training, further improving system efficiency, rollout throughput, and large-scale inference concurrency.

Recent findings suggest that RL for Long-Horizon Tasks. For GLM-5.2, long-horizon tasks produce substantially longer execution traces, and once a super-long trajectory is split by compaction into multiple sub-traces, different rollouts under the same prompt yield different numbers of trainable traces with highly variable lengths. We therefore move from group-wise optimization to a critic-based PPO formulation that learns from individual rollouts, relying on a critic to estimate token-level advantages rather than group-relative comparisons. This single-rollout formulation fits compaction naturally, as it places no constraint on how many traces a prompt produces or on their relative lengths: we bring compaction into training by including all compacted sub-traces as trainable trajectories, and apply a token-level loss to address their length imbalance.

Anti-Hack in Coding agents. Coding RL is especially vulnerable to reward hacking because the reward is typically a verifiable pass/fail signal. We find that GLM-5.2 reveals more potential hacking behavior than GLM-5.1. This makes the verification signal easy to optimize, but fails to actually improve the fundamental capabilities of the model. An agent can read protected evaluation artifacts, copy answer content from references or upstream commits, or directly fetch the target source in GitHub-related tasks. For example, the agent may download solution via curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ or even chained leakage like.

It has been revealed that these behaviors inflate rewards and corrupt the training signal, requiring a clear mechanism to separate real task-solving from shortcuts. To address this, we introduce an anti-hack module for both RL training and evaluation. The detection process has two stages: a rule-based filter first catches potential hacks to maximize recall, and then an LLM judge checks the intent of these flagged actions to keep precision high. We use an online strategy that monitors the tool calls at each step. If a hack is detected, the system blocks the call and returns dummy information as the result. Importantly, this online guard allows the model to continue the rollout even after a hacked action is caught. By handling the specific invalid behavior instead of rejecting the entire trajectory, this approach helps prevent the training instability and model collapse that can happen when rollouts are abruptly stopped.

According to recent reports, prefer a GUI? We offer ZCode —a desktop agent powered by GLM-5.2, with /goal for long-horizon tasks, SSH remote development, and mobile control. Special offer: use GLM-5.2 through Coding Initiative inside ZCode and get 1.5x effective quota until June 30.

arXiv:2611.31801v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Brainprint authentication enables continuous identity verification, but EEG data are privacy-sensitive. Existing feature-level encrypted authentication (FLEA) schemes protect extracted features under a trusted-client assumption. We show theoretically and empirically that a compromised client with access to plaintext query features and continuous authentication scores can exactly recover a registered template after finitely many interactions. To address this risk, we propose TopoCryptoEEG, a homomorphic-encryption-based framework that encrypts preprocessed EEG data at the client and performs feature extraction, template matching, score computation, and threshold centering on ciphertexts at the server. This extends protection from extracted features to preprocessed EEG data and removes the client-side plaintext-feature interface exploited by the attack. For efficient encrypted authentication, we develop Multi-Window Topology-Aware Encoding (MWTE) and a Topographic Branch Model with Linear Fusion (TopoFuse-MLP) to preserve EEG spatial information while limiting multiplicative depth. Query-Patch Coordinate Packing (QPCP) and Lane-Preserving BSGS Evaluation (LP-BSGS) further reduce ciphertext operations. Experiments on HGD and BCICIV-2a show high authentication accuracy, with homomorphic computation taking 1-2 s on CPUs and about 14 ms on GPUs. TopoCryptoEEG achieves over 18x average speedup over the EER (IMWUT 2025) baseline, supporting practical privacy-preserving brainprint authentication.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing BioBasicsBench, a benchmark measuring how well AI agents interpret raw experimental data across 100 routine wet-lab tasks.

Sources indicate that our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. As part of that mission, we want to help scientists accelerate biological research—from understanding disease to developing new treatments. For AI agents to contribute, they need to reliably interpret the experimental evidence scientists work with every day in wet labs, where they run experiments with biological samples. Everyday wet-lab work involves failed experiments, ambiguous images and conflicting observations. Existing benchmarks are built around charts and images selected for scientific papers may miss this ambiguity and the troubleshooting it requires. That’s why we’re introducing BioBasicsBench, a new benchmark developed with Ligo, a biotech organization focused on enzyme design, to measure how well agents handle routine wet-lab analysis.

Industry observers note that the benchmark’s 100 tasks test whether agents can interpret raw experimental data, identify errors, and recognize when the evidence cannot support a conclusion. Getting these tasks right matters because misreading an image or overlooking a problem with the controls used to check an experiment’s results can lead scientists to draw the wrong conclusion and spend time on experiments that won’t help answer their question.

According to recent reports, at the ‘xhigh’ setting, which allows more reasoning per task, GPT‑6 Astra earned an average of 66.7% of the available credit, compared with 43.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. The results show progress on routine lab analysis, with room for further improvements in interpreting images, checking controls and applying experimental context.

BioBasicsBench uses raw experimental evidence, from gel images and colony plates to microscopy and instrument readouts.

According to recent reports, bioBasicsBench has 100 tasks across five areas of routine wet-lab work: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. Tasks range from simple requests, such as reading the molecular weight of a DNA sample in a gel, to detailed assay analysis, but all involve routine work that wet-lab scientists should be able to complete reliably.

Industry observers note that scientists created the tasks using data from their own experiments, pairing each question with expert-written grading criteria. Each task underwent an internal review by a Ligo scientist who had not written it, an external review by a PhD-level scientist working in a wet lab, and a final internal review.

Recent findings suggest that agents return a structured answer with the requested conclusion, measurement or recommendation and, where required, supporting reasoning. Answers receive credit against individual rubric criteria, allowing the benchmark to distinguish a correct conclusion from a partially correct analysis. Most tasks test several skills together, including biological knowledge, interpretation of images and other data, error detection and protocol understanding.

Recent findings suggest that “Unique tasks” counts each task once. The skill columns count tasks with each skill tag. These categories overlap: one task can appear in several columns, so the skill counts should not be added to obtain a task total. Color identifies the domain; stronger shading indicates a larger share of that domain’s tasks testing a skill.

Industry observers note that the inputs preserve the forms of evidence scientists work with: gel and blot images, plate photographs, microscopy stacks, sequencing reads, plate-reader exports and videos of bench work. A task can include several kinds of data. Reference sheets, such as ladder charts and plasmid maps, support the interpretation of the experimental evidence.

Sources indicate that scientists wrote the tasks using data from their own experiments, pairing the experimental evidence with a question and an expert-written grading rubric. Reviewers checked the prompt, experimental evidence, rubric, author notes and a graded model attempt.

Recent findings suggest that answers are scored against the task’s rubric, which assigns credit to individual criteria. Depending on the task, these criteria assess the conclusion, numerical results, supporting reasoning or recognition that the evidence is insufficient.

We evaluated seven models on BioBasicsBench: GPT‑5.2, GPT‑5.4, GPT‑5.5, GPT‑5.6 Sol, GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6 Luna and GPT‑6 Astra. The evaluation covers 37 model and reasoning-effort settings, with five attempts on each of the 100 tasks per setting, for a total of 18,500 results.

We report mean reward: the average task score, expressed as a percentage of the available credit. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals calculated by resampling whole tasks, keeping the five attempts for each task together.

Dashed orange lines show GPT‑5 models, and solid blue lines show GPT‑6 models. Faint whiskers show 95% whole-task bootstrap confidence intervals. Each setting includes all 100 tasks and five attempts per task. Effort settings differ across models.

According to recent reports, GPT‑6 Astra substantially improves on GPT‑5.6 Sol, even at low reasoning effort. These gains suggest that stronger native multimodal capabilities may be key to improving performance on everyday wet-lab analysis.

Recent findings suggest that xhigh is the highest reasoning-effort setting reported for all seven models. Each row includes all 100 tasks and five attempts per task. Max-effort results, where available, are included in the chart above.

A common trap in science is over-interpreting the data, especially given the nature of bias that occurs when testing a hypothesis. Astra demonstrated a better ability to discern the limit of what the data shows and not draw unwarranted conclusions.

In this example, GPT‑5.6 Sol classified cells as dead based on the signal from a dye used to detect dead cells. But the detector could also pick up light from a second dye, so brightness alone could not justify that conclusion. Astra recognized this ambiguity and called for better controls to separate the signals.

Brightfield · transmitted light.

In a recent development, the same cell regions in three channels; the detection windows overlap at 525–540 nm. The shared window permits interference; its amount has not been measured. Each channel is displayed with a separate linear intensity scale, fixed across both regions; brightness cannot be compared quantitatively between channels.

Sources indicate that scientific research is highly multimodal, requiring constant visual interpretation and decision making. Astra displayed a significant improvement at handling multimodal data which was given in the form of photos and videos, as well as raw outputs from sequencing, plate-reader assays, microscopy and flow cytometry.

It has been revealed that at the most basic level, this improvement was noticeable through GPT‑6 Astra’s ability to pick up on finer detail from images taken during experiments and therefore draw more accurate conclusions as shown in this example. This task asked agents to draw conclusions from a DNA cloning experiment, where controls are essential. GPT‑5.6 Sol saw no colonies on the negative control plate and based its conclusions on that observation. GPT‑6 Astra noticed that the plate was labeled with the wrong antibiotic and correctly rejected it as a reliable control.

The original benchmark photograph, with the rim label circled and enlarged. “LB Kan50” identifies kanamycin, a different antibiotic from the ampicillin used in the experiment.

Scientists must be able to hold tacit biological knowledge and experimental context in mind whilst analysing data in order to correctly interpret what it highlights. Astra demonstrated an improved ability to maintain this context and apply it throughout its analysis.

Industry observers note that one task demonstrated cells coming into and out of focus in a series of microscope images. While GPT‑5.6 Sol looked for a biological explanation for the cells’ apparent disappearance, GPT‑6 Astra correctly recognized a z-stack: a series of images taken at different depths.

Six frames from the original recording. Dashed boxes mark the same location as the microscope scans through depth. Times refer to playback position in the supplied video.

In a recent development, higher benchmark scores do not yet mean models can make reliable judgments in the lab. These Astra examples show how assumptions, expected answers and supplied labels can override the evidence, and how a correct intermediate observation can fail to guide the final decision.

Industry observers note that astra lets a familiar assumption override the interpretation supported by the experimental controls. It can distinguish the two groups of colony bands, but assumes that a larger PCR product would identify successful cloning. On that condition it proposes lanes 4, 6, 7 and 8; the reference’s control comparison instead selects lanes 5, 9 and 10.

The reference selects colonies 5, 9 and 10; Astra proposes 4, 6, 7 and 8.

1: marker · 2: cloning mixture · 3: original plasmid · 4–10: colony samples.

Lane 3 contains only the original plasmid PCR. Its band provides the old-plasmid reference position.

In the reference interpretation, lane 2 contains both patterns: incomplete assembly leaves old template/backbone alongside the fresh product.

Industry observers note that the resulting colonies can carry either old or newly introduced plasmid. Compare their bands with these reference patterns.

Reference selection: 5, 9 and 10.

Astra’s selection: 4, 6, 7 and 8. Astra nominates this group suggesting the larger PCR product represents the intended construct.

According to recent reports, the visual grouping is correct but the experimental identities attached to those groups are reversed relative to the reference. Astra therefore selects the wrong colonies from the colony PCR results which would result in the down-stream purification of the incorrect plasmid.

It has been revealed that astra discounts observations that contradict its preferred interpretation. It concludes that vacuoles, compartments inside cells, are generally darker than the surrounding cell, even though some appear lighter in the same image. Both appearances matter: changing the microscope’s focus can reverse the contrast, so the darker examples do not establish a general rule.

Astra’s darker-vacuole generalisation omits the lighter vacuoles visible in the same field.

Some cells have an opposite contrast. Both appearances occur because different focal depths can reverse the contrast.

Astra inspects several regions and even comments that contrast varies with focus. It then gives greater weight to the cells it calls better focused and retains only their darker-vacuole description in the final answer. The contradictory lighter regions have been inspected but are not considered in the conclusion.

Astra’s counting marks do not reliably correspond to individual colonies: it fails to resolve close neighbours, misses visible colonies and marks empty agar. The net result on this plate is an overcount of approximately 12% relative to the benchmark reference.

A: one counting mark between neighbouring colonies. B: two visible colonies left unmarked. C: empty agar counted as a colony. Red circles indicate Astra’s counting positions. Black arrows are editorial guides.

An inaccurate colony count directly affects estimates of how efficiently DNA was introduced into cells. With the plated volume and dilution held fixed, an overcount inflates that estimate by the same proportion.

Sources indicate that accelerating biological research requires getting the everyday work right. BioBasicsBench makes that work a target for improvement: interpreting raw experimental data, checking controls and recognizing when a conclusion is not supported. Progress on these tasks could help scientists spend less time troubleshooting and more time deciding which experiments to pursue next. Tracking these capabilities will also help us understand their implications for biosafety and biosecurity.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.31800v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents commonly use the full interaction history as a proxy for state, retaining all past observations and actions regardless of whether they remain relevant. We instead ask what information an agent actually needs to carry forward. We define agent state as a compact abstraction of interaction history that preserves the competence of a fixed reference agent, with the minimal such abstraction as the ideal. Because matching the reference agent's behavior is unnecessarily restrictive and difficult for black-box policies, we define sufficiency through task performance rather than behavior matching. We represent state abstractions as deterministic recursive programs and search over them using an LLM-guided genetic algorithm. Across ALFWorld and ScienceWorld, the learned abstractions preserve near-reference task success while reducing mean policy input by up to 71% and 57%, respectively. The resulting programs are directly inspectable, providing an explicit account of what information is retained, updated, and discarded during interaction.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A walkthrough of the LeRobot integration in Strands Robots - one agent loop, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot, with sim-to-real datasets in the same on-disk format and policies you swap with a string.
  • Updated for Strands Robots 0.6, which rewrote the library around three classes: Simulation, Robot and Policy.
  • You have a robot, a folder of demonstration data on the Hugging Face Hub, and a new task you want it to learn.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A walkthrough of the LeRobot integration in Strands Robots - one agent loop, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot, with sim-to-real datasets in the same on-disk format and policies you swap with a string.

Updated for Strands Robots 0.6, which rewrote the library around three classes: Simulation, Robot and Policy.

You have a robot, a folder of demonstration data on the Hugging Face Hub, and a new task you want it to learn. Today that takes five separate tools: one to record new demonstrations, another to train, a third to test in simulation, custom code to deploy on hardware, and yet another to coordinate when you have more than one robot. The pieces work on their own. They don't talk to each other.

It has been revealed that strands Robots is an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that gives you a robot, its simulation, and the LeRobot stack behind agent tools that you hand to a single Strands agent. The integration is deliberately thin: LeRobot's own scripts handle hardware recording and calibration, and Strands Robots comes in for the parts an agent actually orchestrates. A robot in simulation records LeRobotDatasets with LeRobot's own writer, in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware. A Policy loads LeRobot checkpoints in-process behind one interface, including ACT, SmolVLA, pi0, GR00T and MolmoAct2. A peer mesh fans the agent out to remote robots. The dataset format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it; the agent loop is the glue.

Industry observers note that this post walks you through five steps inside a single agent: build the agent over the robot's tools, record a demonstration as a LeRobotDataset in simulation, run a policy from the Hub on the same robot, deploy the same agent code to a physical SO-101 with one keyword argument change, and reach the robot over the Zenoh mesh. At the end, you can clone the working sample from GitHub and run it on your laptop in simulation. No hardware, no GPU, no Hugging Face credentials needed for the default path. The runnable companion to this post is the notebook notebooks/11_hub_to_hardware.ipynb.

Sources indicate that strands Robots gives you the LeRobot stack behind agent tools that you hand to one Strands agent. The example agent in this post does four things: drive a simulated SO-101 while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hub as a LeRobotDataset, run a policy from the Hub on that robot, and deploy the same agent code to a physical robot with one keyword argument change. When you have more than one robot, the agent can coordinate the whole fleet through a built-in peer mesh. For hardware recording and calibration, LeRobot's own CLIs (lerobot-record, lerobot-calibrate) handle the bring-up; the agent picks up from there.

Figure 1. Robot("so101") is an SO-101 in a MuJoCo world by default; Robot("so101", port=...) drives the physical arm through the same safety chain. The agent holds the robot's tools, run(record=...) writes a LeRobot v3 dataset with LeRobot's own writer, and a Policy loads a checkpoint from the Hub by name, so a dataset captured in sim and a dataset captured on hardware use the same on-disk format.

Two design choices make this work. First, Robot("so101") is a robot in a simulated world by default (no hardware, no risk), and Robot("so101", port=...) is the same class driving a physical arm. The agent code is identical across both, and every command from the agent passes the robot's safety chain: a target outside a joint's range is refused, never clipped. Second, recording goes through LeRobot's own dataset writer on both the simulation path and hardware, so a dataset captured in MuJoCo and one captured from a physical SO-101 are in the same format.

The whole workflow in five lines of Python:.

What follows is what's actually happening inside that call, step by step.

It has been revealed that that's it. The example in this post runs end-to-end on a laptop with these three.

Install Strands Robots and get the example files:.

It has been revealed that sign in to Hugging Face if you want to push datasets to the Hub. This is optional for the default simulation path in this post; the example runs end-to-end with a placeholder motion and writes the dataset to a local folder without needing Hub access.

The runnable example lives at notebooks/11_hub_to_hardware.ipynb, with the same code as a script in notebooks/scripts/11_hub_to_hardware.py, in the strands-labs/robots repository alongside the other numbered notebooks. The notebook is the recommended starting point: open it in JupyterLab and run cells top-to-bottom in simulation without any hardware connected.

A robot in simulation records LeRobotDatasets in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware. No hardware required. robot.run(policy, record=...) writes a LeRobot v3 dataset through LeRobot's own writer, one episode per run: same parquet schema for joint states and actions, same per-camera MP4 layout. Recording is an argument your code passes, not something the agent decides, so the operator chooses what is kept:.

Pass a folder (record="data/cube_picking_sim") instead to keep the dataset local.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. The recording scene in MuJoCo simulation: the SO-101 arm and a red cube on the ground plane, captured to a LeRobotDataset. No hardware, no GPU, no Hugging Face credentials needed for this default path.

Industry observers note that the placeholder motion is intentional: it moves the arm so the workflow runs end-to-end without a trained checkpoint. The robot waves rather than completing the grasp, and the recording is structurally complete (valid joint states, valid camera frames, a well-formed LeRobotDataset episode), but the demonstration itself isn't useful as training data. Step 3 below swaps in a trained policy from the Hub; the recording call, dataset format, and agent code stay the same.

According to recent reports, the proof is what happens next. LeRobot's own dataset loader reads the sim-recorded data with no Strands-specific code path:.

According to recent reports, these features are the same as any LeRobot dataset on the Hub: same column names, same parquet+MP4 layout, same loader path, plus time.measured, the time each frame was actually read, so a stall shows up in the data. Training scripts that consume hardware-recorded data consume the sim-recorded data without modification. Datasets pushed from sim sit alongside hardware recordings in the same Hub repository if you want them to.

A single episode from a recorded LeRobotDataset, played back from the per-camera MP4 LeRobot's writer produced, the same on-disk video a training script reads.

To record demonstrations on a physical SO-101 instead of simulation, use LeRobot's record CLI directly. Strands Robots doesn't wrap that command because LeRobot already does the job cleanly:.

The dataset that lands on the Hub from this command is in the same format as the simulation recording. To fine-tune a policy on it, run LeRobot's training CLI (lerobot-train); training itself is out of scope for this post and follows the standard LeRobot workflow. From Step 3 onward, the agent picks up either the original or a fine-tuned checkpoint interchangeably. For full SO-101 hardware setup, calibration, and cameras, see the hardware guide.

Industry observers note that with the dataset on the Hub, the next step is to run a policy. A Hub repo id is a policy: Policy("/") loads a LeRobot checkpoint in-process with LeRobot's own loader. You hand it to the robot's tool by name, and the agent runs it the same way it would run any other policy:.

It has been revealed that under the hood, the agent calls the robot tool's run action with policy="act". The robot steps the simulation with the policy's action chunks, and every action passes the same safety chain as a command from the agent. norm= states the units the checkpoint was trained in, and the library checks it against the checkpoint's saved statistics before the first step, naming the joint and the fix if they disagree. The chain applies to the policy too: in one of our runs it stopped the checkpoint after 1.3 seconds, when it asked for the gripper 0.0002 rad past its range, and the robot refused the step instead of clipping it. To run inference on a separate GPU machine instead, serve the checkpoint with LeRobot's lerobot-policy-server and point the robot at it with Policy("zenoh://gpu-box:7447/").

Figure 3. The Hub ACT checkpoint driving the simulated SO-101. It was trained on a real SO-101 with a wrist camera, so here it moves the arm; a checkpoint trained on your own demonstrations swaps in by changing the string.

A different checkpoint is a different string. Policy runs ACT, Diffusion, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T and MolmoAct2 checkpoints, anything LeRobot's own policy registry can load. The policy guide lists the families and the options.

Industry observers note that note: Loading a checkpoint runs code its publisher chose. A Policy your own code builds loads directly; a Hub checkpoint the agent asks for by name loads only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS (for example STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS=lerobot/smolvla_base,my_user/*). Only load checkpoints from organizations you trust.

This is the same code as Step 3, with one keyword argument changed. port= gives the same Robot class a Feetech driver for the physical arm, with LeRobot's calibration file:.

Recent findings suggest that the same agent prompt now runs against a physical arm. The camera names are the image keys the policy sees, and on a real arm nothing moves without the operator: operator= is asked once for every move a tool requests, and once for a policy run's strategy. The same checkpoint, loaded in-process, generates the action chunks.

Recent findings suggest that before this runs against your SO-101, calibration for both follower and leader has to be in place. Run LeRobot's calibration command (lerobot-calibrate) once per device; the files land under ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/calibration/ and Robot(..., id=...) reads them from there. If a calibration is missing, the robot claims which file it looked for.

Up to now we've driven one robot at a time. The mesh is how Strands Robots handles more than one. Picture five SO-101s running the same warehouse task in parallel, a humanoid coordinating with a mobile base, or an arm in another room that an agent on your laptop drives. All of those are mesh patterns. The mesh is built on Zenoh, an open source peer-to-peer protocol, and you don't manage IP addresses, write discovery code, or pick a broker; robots show up on the mesh the moment they're mounted, and the agent can talk to all of them at once.

A robot joins a mesh when you mount it, and the agent reaches every robot on the mesh through one tool, use_mesh:.

Industry observers note that the agent lists the devices on the mesh, reads each one's manifest, and invokes the same actions the robot's own tool has: observe, act, run, stop and estop. Use Mesh("iot://us-west-2") with the iot extra to route the same calls over AWS IoT Core for cross-network fleets; the agent code doesn't change.

It has been revealed that safety goes with the robot, not the transport. An agent can always press e-stop, on one robot or with a broadcast to all of them, but it can never resume one: only a named operator can, with resume(approved_by=...). A plain zenoh:// mesh is one any machine on the network can join, so a real robot on it is observe-only until you give the lab certificates (python -m strands_robots.mesh ca and cert); simulated robots take commands on it freely.

According to recent reports, the transport scales without touching agent code. On the LAN, Zenoh peers find each other with no broker. Across subnets, run a zenohd router with its own certificate, and for cloud fleets the iot:// mesh carries the same calls over AWS IoT Core with an X.509 certificate per robot.

The full sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in the notebooks/ folder. Notebook 11 packages all five steps, with the same code as a script in notebooks/scripts/11_hub_to_hardware.py. It runs in simulation with a placeholder motion and a small ACT checkpoint from the Hub. No GPU, no Docker, no Hugging Face credentials needed.

It has been revealed that the agent steps use Amazon Bedrock with your AWS credentials; set STRANDS_MODEL_ID to the model you want. The recorded dataset lands in a temporary folder the notebook prints. To push it to the Hugging Face Hub instead of keeping it local, set HF_USER= after hf auth login with write scope.

Recent findings suggest that the code snippets shown in this setup represent a “hello world” example of setting up Strands Robots with HuggingFace. For more serious, production-ready use cases there are some important considerations users should be aware of:.

Supplying untrusted data into agents can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. Given the actuation of these robots in physical space, this is an important risk to track. To mitigate this behavior, developers should be careful to feed the robots only data that comes from a trusted source. If not all input data can be trusted, developers should restrict the tools available to the agent to prevent the robots from making safety-critical actions.

It has been revealed that A plain zenoh:// mesh, as in the snippets in this post, has no access control: any device on the same network can join it, and the peer id in a request is only a claim. That is why a real robot on it answers only describe, observe, stop and estop. For untrusted networks or production environments, give each machine a lab certificate (python -m strands_robots.mesh ca, then cert), so the mesh runs over mutual TLS and only machines with a certificate can reach a robot. On AWS IoT Core, give each robot its own X.509 certificate and an IoT policy limited to its own topics.

On a real robot, operator= is the gate: one function answers every move a tool, the dashboard or the mesh asks for, and every policy run's initiative, once, before anything moves. The agent's approval never comes from its own tool arguments, so a prompt-injection attempt that slips an approval into a command cannot bypass it. An agent can always press e-stop but can never release one, calibrate, record, push, or choose a policy address on the network, and it loads a Hub checkpoint by name only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS.

Industry observers note that the preceding workflow opens serial ports on hardware and writes a local dataset cache. To return your environment to a clean state:.

The integration's central design choice is that Strands Robots doesn't reimplement what LeRobot already provides. Calibration, the dataset format, and the policies stay upstream. Strands adds the agent tools, the safety chain and the mesh that make them composable from natural language.

Sources indicate that two consequences follow. For users, every dataset on the Hub is an asset an agent can extend, fine-tune from, and deploy against with no conversion step. For developers, simulation data and hardware data share a single file format, so training scripts written for one consume the other unchanged. The line between sim and real becomes a deployment detail, not an architectural divide.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4. The Strands Robots catalog spans arms, humanoids, mobile bases, and hands, all in the same MuJoCo simulation and behind the same Robot class. The SO-101 in this post is one of its 76 robot presets.

According to recent reports, the full Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policies, recording, and the mesh in depth. For larger workloads, Strands Robots also runs GPU simulation: MuJoCo-Warp with Simulation("mujoco", physics="newton") and Isaac Sim with Simulation("isaac"). Both sit behind the same Robot class shown in this post, so the agent code stays the same as you scale up.

Industry observers note that contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this workflow, open an issue with what worked and what didn't. The SDK improves fastest when developer feedback lands directly on the surface that needs it.

Cagatay Cali is a Research Engineer at AWS focused on Agentic AI and robotics. He designs interfaces that connect AI agents to physical robots, enabling developers to control robotic systems through natural language and making agents and robotics development accessible to builders at any skill level.

Industry observers note that sundar Raghavan is a Sr Solutions Architect at AWS on the Agentic AI Foundations team. He leads the developer experience for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, owning the SDK and CLI, and drives the framework and ecosystem integrations strategy. He focuses on how developers build, deploy, and scale production AI agents on AWS. He is currently extending that focus into physical AI, collaborating on Strands Robots to bring the same agent developer experience to robotics.

Fantastic to see! The single-kwarg flip from MuJoCo sim to mode="real" (same agent code, same LeRobotDataset format end to end) is exactly the friction-removal that gets robotics agents into real labs. Work like this lifts all the ships: the easier and more open we make agent-to-hardware control, the faster the whole industry moves. The Device Connect team at Arm is excited to collaborate!

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31780v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent time-series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast a distribution over futures, and multimodal time-series (TS) forecasting further exploits other modalities to improve forecasting accuracy. However, existing works have two limitations: 1) TSFMs reduce the predictive distribution to its median or mean, flattening diverse futures into a calm line, and 2) multimodal TS forecasting models incorporate text into the forecaster through TS-language alignment, which is substantially weaker than vision-language alignment. To address these limitations, we propose the VIsion-language SelectOR (VISOR), a multimodal TS forecasting framework that selects one plausible future instead of averaging across candidates, leveraging the alignment capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to select the most suitable candidate based on textual information. VISOR consists of two components: 1) a text-free stochastic predictor that samples diverse candidate futures, and 2) a VLM selector that reads the candidates as a single chart image and selects one based on the text. To avoid overly calm forecasting paths, we train the selector with a shape-aware target that evaluates each candidate based on both point-wise error and path shape. Across three benchmarks covering ten datasets, VISOR achieves the best average ranking in both point and volatility errors compared with TSFMs and multimodal TS forecasting models. As AI agents connect services in upcoming ways, that combination of skills becomes even more valuable. Working alongside Hacktron will help us test those connections more deeply and use what we learn to strengthen our defenses.

We’re grateful to Hacktron and other independent researchers who put time into finding and reporting weaknesses to help strengthen the security that protects all our users. To see which systems are in scope or submit a finding, visit our Security Bug Bounty program⁠(opens in a newly introduced window).

Is it agentic enough? Benchmarking open models on your own tooling

📅 18 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Benchmarking transformers revisions across different metrics.
  • Recent findings suggest that coding agents increasingly work with our software instead of us: describe a task, and the agent picks the library, writes the calls, runs them, and debugs its own mistakes.
  • It has been revealed that most benchmarks just look at the final answer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benchmarking transformers revisions across different metrics.

This is a human-made, agent-focused blogpost.

Recent findings suggest that coding agents increasingly work with our software instead of us: describe a task, and the agent picks the library, writes the calls, runs them, and debugs its own mistakes. When the library gets in the way, it will happily bypass it and rewrite the logic from scratch. This introduces a fresh concept in library development: the code should not only be correct and fast, but should be designed so that an agent can drive it effectively. A clunky API or stale docs annoy us developers, but it now also sends the agent down a longer, more expensive path.

It has been revealed that most benchmarks just look at the final answer. We wanted the whole process instead: not just whether the agent got it right, but how much work it took to get there, and how that shifts across models, library revisions, and tasks. We measured exactly that, using transformers as our case study.

Here, we will introduce a tool specific benchmark focusing on how the answer was found, and provide a simple implementation of one such harness, running entirely on open models driven by the pi coding agent, with the full sweep of models × revisions × tasks fanned out across Hugging Face Jobs so every run sees identical hardware.

But, how do you optimize software for agents?

We're strong believers in the following two software principles:.

This remains the same within the realm of agentic-optimized tooling, and, for once, the two are directly tied to each other.

You want your tool to exist for an agent: it needs to be discoverable. The API needs to be clear and the docs need to be extensive. They need to be structured in a way that the agent has rapid access to the useful files and examples. If you want your tool to work for an agent, then you should test it for agentic-use.

We'll use transformers as an example throughout this blogpost: agents using it to solve ML tasks (classifying text, captioning images, transcribing audio), not contributing code to it; though the harness was designed to work with any tool that can be operated from the command line.

According to recent reports, our intuition on transformers was that usage could be dramatically simplified with a few changes: a CLI, a Skill, and self-contained, task-specific examples. This is the same recipe recently applied to the hf CLI, redesigned to be agent-optimized, where agents used 1.3–1.8× (and up to 6×) fewer tokens. We wanted to know whether that kind of win generalizes, and whether it could be useful for transformers as well.

It has been revealed that intuition is a powerful tool, but we wanted more evidence before we opened PRs that add several thousand lines of code to such a widely used codebase as transformers. We set out to measure what success looks like.

Two agents can both produce the correct label for a sentiment-classification task, but one:.

Both reach POSITIVE (0.9999), and here are the two paths an agent actually took on this exact task:.

Both methods reach the same result. But they have very different profiles in cost, latency, token usage, and failures.

If your evaluation only checks the final string, you're blind to these as well as whether a change you shipped to the library (a CLI improvement, better error messages, a Skill) actually helped agents.

Our goal with this harness is to evaluate how much work an agent has to do to perform a given task, and whether changes to the library improve performance.

A few words on how we'll evaluate agents here.

We run every task under three variants (or "tiers"); three different ways an agent can come at transformers:.

These aren't nested: skill doesn't contain clone (it ships curated docs, not the source tree), and neither strictly contains the other, each gives the agent a different kind of help. As we'll see, a model can sometimes do better on clone than on skill.

Not all models driving agents are equal, and their difference changes what you should look at when running them.

At one end, you have the largest, most capable open models. On reasonably common tasks, these should get the right answer, eventually. For them, task completion saturates near 100% and stops telling you much about your tool; a more relevant benchmark is the effort it took the agent to get there: how many turns, tokens and seconds it took, and whether they walked a clean path or used deprecated APIs.

Local models vary widely in size, and so do their abilities. Metrics such as "match %" are more relevant than for their larger counterparts, as you can see how model sizes/capabilities affect results on your specific tool.

This harness not only provides guidance to library maintainers on how to improve a repository for agent interactions, it also helps assess how different agents and models perform on the tasks consumers care about.

The harness scores every run on several axes, so that you can ask what actually matters for each class of model:.

All of it lands in a report you can directly examine:.

The live report: Overview, Coverage, and Results, all client-side.

And because it captures the native agent trace of every run, numbers are just the beginning: you can read exactly what the agent did, command by command. The traces are shareable through the Hub's agent-traces viewer:.

A run rendered in the Hub's agent-traces viewer: MiniMax-M2.7 on the answer-question task. Open this trace on the Hub ↗.

Before the results, a quick recap of the setup. Each run varies four things: the model driving the agent, the transformers revision it runs against, the task, and the tier (bare / clone / skill). As discussed, we look at different metrics for the two different model categories.

Industry observers note that since a large open model will usually get to the correct result, what you're really measuring is the effort it took to do so. Did it take ten turns or one? Did it follow an API path you deprecated because it trusted obsolete documentation? Did it hit an error you hadn't foreseen?

The natural experiment is to fix one strong model and vary the tool's revisions: the successive git versions of transformers we test against, from released tags like v5.8.0 and v5.9.0 to the specific commit that introduces the CLI and Skill. We want to watch whether the load it puts on the agent goes up or down. We used the harness on transformers to check whether adding a dedicated CLI and Skill actually lightened the agents' work.

For the three large models we used in our tests, the average time spent on all tasks indicates that the Skill commit results in less time spent working on the tasks:.

Median time per revision, by tier: the skill commit (green dot) is the fastest.

On the other hand, in the experiments in which we cloned the repository, we can see a significant increase in token consumption due to the commit that introduced the CLI and examples, as we'll see in a moment.

Median newly introduced tokens per revision, by tier: the clone variant jumps once the CLI lands in the repo.

Reading the clone-variant traces explains why. The commit adds a command, but it also ships the CLI's implementation and a set of cli/agentic/*.py usage examples into the repository directly.

Sources indicate that on the clone variant the agent has a full transformers checkout in front of it, and roughly a third of the runs go read the new surface (the /cli/ tree and the example scripts) to learn the interface before calling it. This raises the median input from ~4k to ~6.4k tokens.

The two charts are then two sides of one tradeoff: the commit buys the large models less time (they reach for the CLI instead of debugging Python) at the cost of more tokens (they read the code that taught them the CLI). A tradeoff worth knowing about before merging PRs.

One caveat works in the CLI's favor, though, which isn't benchmarked yet: the cost of reading it is amortized with successive runs. Our setup is built for one-off experiments. Each run is a fresh agent that rediscovers the CLI from scratch, so it pays the discovery cost every time. In real usage an agent learns the interface once and then solves task after task within the same session, amortizing that cost across many requests. The token bump we measure here is closer to a worst case than to what a user would see day to day.

It has been revealed that open models give us fine-grained control over the variables that matter most here: size, configuration, quantization, provider, training, and anything that would differ from one model to the next. They're also where a good tool surface matters most: a small model asked to "use transformers to do X" on a bare environment can guess an API that changed some releases ago, may do unnecessary tool calls, and can get the wrong answer.

So here the experiment is the opposite of the above: hold the revision and sweep the model. This helps see which models actually take care of the task, not just by token count and time, but down to which ones can't reliably handle the tool calls. Our intuition is that the smaller the model, the harder both tool use and the task get; we ran the harness across a range of model sizes to test exactly that:.

Match % across models, by tier: the skill tier lifts the larger models but drops the smaller ones.

which also seems to be correlated with the number of tokens ingested.

Median newly introduced tokens across models, by tier.

A note on fair comparison: naively averaging across tasks is misleading when coverage is uneven (a model that only finished the quick tasks looks fast). The report has a "shared tasks only" toggle (across models and/or revisions) so you compare like-for-like, and a Coverage heatmap so you can see exactly which task × revision × model cells actually ran.

Two things come together here: how to look past whether the agent succeeded to what it did and how it did it; as well as the first results we pulled out of the harness.

Match %, tokens, and time tell you the cost of a run but don't tell you much about what happened under the hood.

Industry observers note that this is why we've introduced the concept of markers. A marker is a named pattern the profile (the small per-tool plugin that teaches the harness how to build and drive a given library) matches against a run.

It is a one-line label for a behavior you care about, checked against the shell commands the agent ran, the code it wrote, the files it read, or its final answer. A run can fire several markers or none; the report demonstrates how often each one fired, per model and per revision.

For transformers we declare a handful but we'll only look at the two most relevant ones:.

It has been revealed that these are what we watch to see whether a change actually shifted the agent's behavior. Interestingly here, the larger the model, the more it leverages the newly introduced context instead of using its memory; therefore leveraging the newly introduced CLI.

CLI adoption by tier across models: only the skill tier reaches for it, and more so as models grow.

In a recent development, CLI adoption is upcoming: the CLI lands in a single commit, isn't in any model's training data, and is only lightly documented. The effect is clear: it's the Skill variant, the one that ships the CLI's documentation, that actually reaches for it, at 55.3%.

According to recent reports, comparing the commit across model sizes, the CLI + Skill helps the bigger models: on the skill tier, Kimi and the other large agents reach for the CLI and finish in fewer turns. (On clone they spend more input tokens first, reading the new CLI code, as we saw above, so the win highlights up in time and turns, not raw tokens.).

Kimi-K2.6, GLM-5.1, and MiniMax-M2.7 across revisions.

Sources indicate that but in some smaller-model settings, it appears to hurt performance. One plausible explanation is that small models lean on memorized API patterns, reproducing pipeline(...) snippets they've seen in their training data. The new concepts are then a larger surface for them to get wrong. You can watch this directly on the harness: lower match %, more retries, the cli marker barely firing. It is particularly striking on the Qwen3-4B model: the Skill barely changes its match rate yet its cost distribution is significantly affected.

It has been revealed that almost all of that comes from the clone tier. The checkout now contains the CLI's implementation and cli/agentic/*.py examples, and the 4B agent reads them in bulk: its median new tokens jump from ~2.4k to ~23k, with time and output skyrocketing as well, for no gain in accuracy.

Qwen3-4B across revisions. The CLI + Skill commit fans the cost distribution wide open, on the clone tier the agent reads the newly-shipped CLI source in bulk (~10× the new tokens), for no gain in match %. (repeat tokens stays flat: this setup uses no prompt caching.).

Sometimes, though, the Skill breaks correctness outright. Reading the traces shows how, for example for Qwen3-14B: adding the Skill drops its overall match rate from 67% (bare) to 43%, and on the simplest tasks the collapse is very visible: classify-sentiment goes from 100% on the clone variant to 0% with the Skill.

Qwen3-14B on classify-sentiment, by tier: clone (blue) holds at 100% across revisions, but the Skill variant (green) collapses to 0% at the CLI + Skill revision.

Looking at the traces, the model mistakes the CLI for a tool it can call directly (as in an agentic-harness tool, like web-search). The Skill is not an executable tool: it's documentation loaded into the agent's context, and the transformers CLI is only ever meant to be run from the shell (via bash); so this will not work.

Recent findings suggest that qwen3-14B reads the Skill and, in 39 of its 56 Skill runs, either emits a transformers(command="classify", ...) tool call (a tool that was never registered) or, finding nothing like it among its read/bash/edit/write tools, concludes it can't run a model and gives up. Either way, rather than fall back to the one-line pipeline(...) that scored 100% on the clone checkout, it declares the task impossible.

Qwen3-14B on classify-sentiment (Skill variant): it reasons that read/bash/edit/write can't run a model, and gives up.

This is exactly what we built the harness to catch: the same change that speeds the large models ends up breaking the small ones, which seemed a bit counterintuitive to us at first and something we'd likely have shipped as-is. The takeaway for maintainers: agent-facing APIs should be evaluated across model sizes, because a new affordance can reduce work for strong models while adding ambiguity for smaller ones. It also hints at a fix: rather than hand-write a Skill and check it after the fact, you could generate and validate one against the weaker models up front.

This is exactly what Upskill does: it turns a strong model's solution into a Skill only when it measurably helps the smaller ones.

Industry observers note that the harness is one CLI, agent-eval. Install it, run a suite, fan it out across models × revisions on HF Jobs, and publish the report as a Hugging Face Space.

Trusted local use only. The harness runs a coding agent with bypassed permissions and executes code from whatever revision you point it at, and traces can contain prompts, output, and local paths. See SECURITY.md before pointing it at code you didn't write or sharing results.

The full, kept-current setup and usage instructions live in the README.

Sources indicate that checking the final answer tells you whether an agent can use your library. It doesn't tell you what it costs: the turns, tokens, errors, and the path it took to get there. This harness measures that, across the revisions and models you pick.

On transformers, it caught something we'd have shipped on faith: the CLI + Skill helps the largest open models and hurts the smallest ones. Worth knowing before merging!

It's profile-based, and designed to be adaptable: point it at your own library, define a few tasks and their expected answers, get the same report. Code and tasks are in the repo, traces are on the Hub. Let us know if you use it for your project!

This harness stands entirely on pi, Mario Zechner's coding-agent CLI: it drives every open-model run, and only needs an HF_TOKEN to serve a model, which is what made the open-model sweep practical at all.

It has been revealed that thanks to the model builders and inference providers behind the models we swept. Across the board they performed well above what the bare baseline would suggest.

Tech Report: SPARQL-Planned Single-Hop Traversal over a Live Knowledge Graph for Multi-Hop Question Answering

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (262 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31771v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semantic retrieval struggles with multi-hop question answering on both recall and precision: gold passages are buried among distractors that degrade the reader's answer, and retrieving them requires reasoning over the query rather than matching it. GraphRAG techniques expand semantic retrieval by connecting passages to graph nodes and performing one or more hops of expansion after initial retrieval. This improves recall, but multi-hop expansion becomes expensive and brings additional noise into the retrieved set. We break this tradeoff by \emph{interleaving} dense retrieval with knowledge-graph traversal for complex multi-hop questions. Dense retrieval locates the first relevant regions of the search space at good recall, while traversal of a pre-existing external KG (Wikidata) restores precision and improves recall by confirming retrieved passages against a reasoning path through the KG. To keep traversal both question-adaptive and reliable, we have an LLM blueprint it as code generation task for graph traversal in SPARQL format but \emph{parse rather than execute} the query. On full 1{,}000-question splits under a shared corpus and reader, and with a single configuration applied identically to every dataset, we reach \textbf{62.5 / 75.1} EM/F1 on HotpotQA, \textbf{73.5 / 81.0} on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and \textbf{37.1 / 50.0} on MuSiQue, ahead of reproduced HippoRAG2, T\textsuperscript{2}RAG, and IRCoT on all three benchmarks. A second, token-matched setting stays ahead of T\textsuperscript{2}RAG on HotpotQA and 2Wiki while spending roughly its per-query budget. Executing the generated SPARQL instead of parsing it costs up to 11.4 EM, mostly because raw queries return empty results, not because of syntax errors.
