For decades, VistaPrint has helped small businesses bring ideas to life, from business cards and signage to a wide range of branded merchandise. But small business needs do not always start with a specific product in mind. A customer may be launching a business, preparing for an event, refreshing their brand, or looking for ways to market themselves more effectively.

Industry observers note that that creates an opportunity to reach customers as they explore what they need and evaluate the different ways to bring their ideas to life. It was this opportunity that drew VistaPrint to the ChatGPT Ads pilot.

Industry observers note that “What excites us about ChatGPT is where it sits in the customer journey—at the point where intent is still forming. When a potential customer doesn’t yet know what they need, and they’re in a conversation working that out, that’s exactly where we want to be. Discovery is where we can help inform the decision, not just respond to it.”.

VistaPrint’s early campaigns leaned on product-oriented messaging. The team shifted the focus to what small business owners could do with them, like using signs to draw people to a booth or handing out branded merchandise at an event.

In a recent development, this became the foundation of an evolving playbook. Creative could help customers see how a product fit their needs; the team also wanted its campaign optimization to reflect what happened next. For VistaPrint, the business goal was to turn that interest into orders.

VistaPrint explored that next step with two successive US campaigns for one of its popular product categories. The first used click-focused bidding. In July 2026, the team debuted a conversion-optimized campaign. VistaPrint selected ‘Order Created’ as the conversion event and paid per valid click.

As the campaign learned from conversion data, the team evaluated performance and adjusted maximum bids. VistaPrint reported that cost per attributed order was approximately 90% lower in the conversion-optimized campaign than in the preceding click-focused campaign.2 The conversion-optimized campaign recorded a 5.9x return on ad spend.1.

Sources indicate that those results gave VistaPrint the confidence to expand the approach across its remaining US campaigns and into the UK, Canada, and Australia. The experience added a practical lesson to the team’s creative learning: allow time for conversion-focused bidding to learn, then keep evaluating performance as the campaign develops.

Recent findings suggest that product feeds added another way to connect customer needs with VistaPrint’s range. Alongside its standard campaigns, the team introduced catalog-based campaigns using product information from its feed to populate ads.

Industry observers note that “ChatGPT Ads isn’t about choosing between text or catalog formats—it’s about the synergy between the two and having a balanced campaign structure. While our standard campaigns allow us to engage in broader conversations about a customer’s business goals, our dynamic product feeds instantly provide them with the right products they are looking for.”.

It has been revealed that vistaPrint used its catalog results to guide spend allocation and expanded feed campaigns to other markets. Its recommendation to other ecommerce advertisers is to invest in a clean, well-structured feed alongside creative tailored to the conversational context.

Industry observers note that reaching newly introduced customers was central to VistaPrint’s original goal for the channel. From July through September, a majority of the US site conversions VistaPrint traced to ChatGPT Ads came from new customers.3.

It has been revealed that these results have given VistaPrint the confidence to expand its approach across campaigns and markets. For the team, the opportunity is to connect with small businesses as their ideas take shape—and help them discover the products that can bring those ideas to life.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (289 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31767v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign. We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.

#36392. Beyond LoRA: Can you beat the most popular fine-tuning technique?

📅 18 Jun 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2390 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Beyond LoRA: Can you beat the most popular fine-tuning technique?

📅 18 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you want to fine-tune an open model on your own data, you are probably interested in so-called parameter-efficient fine-tuning, in short PEFT.
  • Industry observers note that there are countless open models available, but they often aren't quite good enough for your use case.
  • Recent findings suggest that fine-tuning, however, is memory-hungry: you generally need enough memory to fit the whole model several times over.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you want to fine-tune an open model on your own data, you are probably interested in so-called parameter-efficient fine-tuning, in short PEFT. This term describes techniques that significantly reduce the memory requirement to fine-tune a model. Although there are dozens of these techniques, almost everyone chooses one called “LoRA”. In this blog post, we explore whether LoRA is really the best choice, what tools are available to make an informed decision, and how you can benefit from extending your horizon beyond LoRA.

Industry observers note that there are countless open models available, but they often aren't quite good enough for your use case. Prompting may help, but it usually isn't enough. Rather than training a newly introduced model from scratch, you should consider fine-tuning an existing one.

Recent findings suggest that fine-tuning, however, is memory-hungry: you generally need enough memory to fit the whole model several times over. Quantization reduces a model's memory footprint, but quantized models can't be fine-tuned directly. So a set of techniques emerged to cut the memory needed for fine-tuning, called "parameter-efficient fine-tuning", or PEFT.

With PEFT, you can fine-tune a model using only a fraction of that memory and even fine-tune quantized models. It offers other advantages, such as tiny checkpoint sizes, greater resistance to catastrophic forgetting, and the ability to serve multiple fine-tunes from the same base model.

At Hugging Face, we develop the PEFT library, which implements many PEFT techniques behind a unified API and integrates well with the ecosystem, for example Transformers and Diffusers. It also supports multiple quantization methods, enabling further accessibility in parameter-efficient fine-tuning. PEFT provides a good starting point, whether you want to fine-tune on your own data or you're researching a new PEFT method.

It has been revealed that one parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that emerged early and proved to be quite effective is called “Low Rank Adaptation”, or short “LoRA”. It works by adding a handful of parameters on top of the base model, freezing the base model weights, and only training those few parameters.

It has been revealed that among all PEFT techniques, LoRA is by far the most popular. Here are a few estimates:.

Although these estimates are not perfect, the conclusion is nonetheless that LoRA is almost certainly by far the most common PEFT technique.

According to recent reports, this could just mean that LoRA works best for everyone, and this fact is reflected in its usage statistics. There is, however, another possibility: LoRA was one of the earlier, popular PEFT techniques. So maybe its usage became self-reinforcing: LoRA has the highest visibility, the highest number of tutorials/examples, and it has the best support in downstream packages. Thus LoRA's popularity feeds on itself.

This all leads to the question: Are we all leaving performance on the table by shunning better techniques? After all, there are countless researchers whose papers claim their technique beats LoRA. Isn't that sufficient proof that we should go beyond LoRA in favor of newer techniques?

There are dozens of papers that investigate fine-tuning techniques other than LoRA. Just in the PEFT library, there are more than 40 distinct PEFT techniques at the time of writing (and numerous more when counting variations of PEFT techniques). For almost all of them, you will find researchers claiming that their technique beats LoRA according to their benchmarks.

Sources indicate that the trouble with these claims is that researchers are under pressure to provide results that beat the existing benchmark. Even without ill intent, this can bias the results, e.g. by spending less time tuning the alternative techniques compared to the one proposed by the researchers. One study found, for instance, that LoRA can match supposedly better PEFT techniques by tuning the learning rate.

According to recent reports, another complication is that each paper chooses a different set of PEFT techniques to compare to, and a different set of benchmarks to run. And even if the same technique is compared on the same benchmark, the code is often not available or not easy to run yourself, which makes results hard to reproduce.

In a recent development, overall, it's difficult to figure out the PEFT technique that works best for you by only checking paper results. Therefore, you might be tempted to just go with the default, LoRA.

At Hugging Face, we thought about how we can help users make informed decisions about which PEFT technique to use. With the PEFT library, we already provide a package that implements many PEFT techniques and exposes them with the same API. The next step is to provide benchmarks that can shed more light on the discussed concern.

Industry observers note that we already had a benchmark that checks fine-tuning of LLMs on a math dataset for some time. This benchmark takes an LLM and fine-tunes it on chain-of-thought reasoning to produce the result to a mathematical question using a base model that is not instruction fine-tuned. The benchmark thus checks if the model can learn to perform mathematical reasoning and also to adjust the generated output to the expected format.

Recent findings suggest that to extend our findings on another modality, we also added an image generation benchmark. This one tests whether the model can be fine-tuned to learn a new concept, a cat plushy, and generate it in new contexts without forgetting existing concepts.

All PEFT techniques are evaluated according to the exact same conditions: same base model, same dataset, same training and evaluation code, same hardware. As different consumers have different needs, we track more than just test performance. Besides VRAM usage, we track metrics like forgetting/drift, runtime, and checkpoint size. The results are designed to run on consumer hardware, and adding a upcoming experiment only requires adding a new PEFT config and running a script.

According to recent reports, since we compare all PEFT techniques on equal footing and have no horse in the race, we believe that these benchmarks can draw an objective picture of how well different PEFT techniques work. We argue that if you have your own dataset, you can take a similar approach and take advantage of the PEFT library to evaluate multiple PEFT techniques.

In a recent development, after finishing the benchmark runs, we found that although LoRA works well, other PEFT methods can beat it on one or multiple axes and should thus be considered. Check the image below that compares the performance of LoRA and five other PEFT techniques.

One way to interpret the results above is to think in terms of tradeoffs, for example: How well does the model perform on the test set vs how much memory is needed to train it? If a PEFT technique cannot be beaten on both of these metrics at the same time by any other technique, it is on the Pareto Frontier. In other words: If you want better test accuracy, you need more memory, and if you want more memory efficiency, you have to give up on accuracy.

Industry observers note that let's take a closer look at the results for the LLM Math dataset benchmark. When it comes to test accuracy vs memory, we find that LoRA is indeed on the Pareto frontier. It achieves 53.2% test accuracy and requires 22.6 GB of VRAM at the peak. There are, however, other PEFT techniques on the Pareto Frontier. For instance, BEFT achieves 32.9% test accuracy and requires only 20.2 GB of memory at max. On the other end, we have Lily, which achieves 54.9% test accuracy but requires 25.6 GB of memory. Depending on what's more important to you, you may conclude that LoRA does not present the best tradeoff for you.

According to recent reports, it is also worth noting that even though LoRA does well on this task, we're not talking about vanilla LoRA. On one side, we have LoRA with rank stabilized initialization, which is a technique to scale the LoRA contribution differently from the default initialization and provides very good test accuracy (53.2%). On the other end, we have LoRA-FA, which uses an optimizer specialized for LoRA that freezes part of the LoRA weights and is thus more memory efficient (20.2 GB). Normal LoRA only achieves an accuracy of 48.1% at 22.5 GB memory and should thus be avoided in favor of the alternatives.

Sources indicate that next let's take a look at the image generation benchmark. In the Hugging Face Space, choose “image-gen” in the “Select Task” dropdown to show the results. The goal of the task is to learn a upcoming concept, namely a cat plushy, and generalize it to new prompts.

For this task, the main metric is “dino similarity”, which measures how much a generated image resembles the picture from a holdout test dataset, with higher values being better. As always, we also want to keep an eye on memory usage. When plotting the Pareto Frontier of these two metrics, we find that LoRA is below that frontier. Let's get concrete numbers: LoRA achieves a similarity score of 0.697 whereas OFT achieves 0.708; in terms of memory, LoRA requires 9.97 GB, and OFT requires 9.01 GB. Therefore, OFT strictly dominates LoRA on these metrics.

According to recent reports, of course, you should also check the other PEFT methods that are close to the Pareto frontier, as metrics can be subject to small variations due to randomness. Also, you should explore other metrics: is runtime performance notable to you or do you care about the size of the checkpoints? Choose the relevant metric from the dropdown and the picture can change considerably. For the image generation benchmark, do inspect the generated sample images to get a vibe of the fine-tuned model's capability.

Objection: But the benchmarks favor one method over another!

One criticism that could be leveled at the PEFT benchmarks is that the choice of hyper-parameters may favor one technique over another. This is true, doing an exhaustive and fair hyper-parameter sweep with this many techniques is difficult. It is, however, very easy for everyone to contribute their own experiments to PEFT: If you believe that a specific PEFT technique can be improved by choosing different hyper-parameters, create a PR! We added instructions on how to do that. In a similar vein, if you want to contribute a completely upcoming benchmark, reach out to us to discuss your idea.

Another problem with the benchmarks is that they may not fully reflect the capabilities of a specific PEFT technique. We make it possible to compare the techniques along many different dimensions and discover the best ones according to these tradeoffs. But it's impossible to capture all facets this way. For instance, one PEFT technique called Cartridges was developed to compress long prompts, which is not measured in the benchmarks. Other factors can also influence the choice, for instance:.

The benchmarks cannot fully lift the responsibility to do your research, but they can be reasonable pointers.

Objection: But llama.cpp/vLLM/... only supports LoRA.

According to recent reports, A limitation of using a PEFT technique other than LoRA is that they don't get the broad support in downstream packages that LoRA sees. For example, if you want to serve the model using vLLM, only LoRA checkpoints can be loaded. Thankfully, PEFT now supports converting other adapters into LoRA. That way, you can convert a non-LoRA checkpoint into LoRA and use it in vLLM or other downstream packages.

To test this, we converted an image adapter using the GraLoRA technique into a LoRA checkpoint. The test scores were virtually identical after conversion (similarity 0.702 → 0.694, 0.260 → 0.269). Below are test images for the prompt “sks cat at the beach”:.

At the moment, we haven't implemented conversion for all PEFT techniques, but if there is demand, we will expand the support.

Industry observers note that while working on the PEFT package, we noticed that LoRA has a lot of momentum behind it, even though other PEFT techniques are potentially better. Therefore, we set out to add benchmarks to PEFT that could paint a more objective picture of how well different PEFT techniques perform on different metrics.

Given the results we found, we can confidently conclude that LoRA is not a bad choice at all, but there are potentially better choices. Especially when checking the image generation benchmark, LoRA is beaten by other techniques. We discussed that besides metrics, other considerations must be taken into account when choosing the right PEFT technique. However, even then, we are pushing PEFT further to achieve feature parity between LoRA and those other techniques.

Recent findings suggest that our journey is far from finished; we want to extend and improve the existing benchmarks, and we also blueprint to add more benchmarks in the future. We ensured that it is easy for the community to contribute, so if this is something you would like to do, please open an issue on the PEFT repository and let us know how you would like to contribute.

If you take away only one thing from this article, it is that LoRA should not be the automatic default when choosing a PEFT technique for your use case. Given the unified API provided by PEFT, changing from one PEFT technique to another is as easy as switching one config in your code. And even if you stick with LoRA, check out all the variants that are supported in PEFT: DoRA, rs-LoRA, LoRA-FA etc. Give these other techniques a try and you might be pleasantly surprised.

Example: Changing from LoRA to OFT using PEFT:.

What about DEFT?It adapts a pre-trained weight matrix by decomposing its revision into two components with two trainable matrices: (1) a projection onto the complement of a low-rank subspace spanned by a low-rank matrix, and (2) a low-rank update. Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31766v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Projected reduction in hours spent searching for drawings each year.
  • Kuken Industries makes air conditioning and ventilation equipment for large buildings, shopping centers, and factories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kuken’s engineers use a tool built on the OpenAI API to find the drawing for a replacement part in 4.5 minutes, down from nearly an hour.

Projected reduction in hours spent searching for drawings each year.

Time to find a drawing, down from nearly an hour.

Kuken Industries makes air conditioning and ventilation equipment for large buildings, shopping centers, and factories. It holds one of the largest shares of Japan’s cooling tower market. These towers release heat from circulating water into the air, helping cool everything from large buildings and malls to equipment in data centers.

When a cooling tower needs a replacement part, Kuken’s engineers turn to an archive of drawings that spans 70 years of installations. For a newer engineer, finding the right drawing often meant asking an experienced colleague where to look and how to read it. Kuken wanted newer engineers to be able to find those records themselves, learn from the decisions they contain, and spend more time figuring out how to make the repair.

Recent findings suggest that parts made today don’t always fit older cooling towers. Without the original drawing to show what was installed, engineers may have to design and manufacture a replacement from scratch.

A search by model or part name can turn up several drawings. Over more than 70 years, Kuken has adapted its equipment to individual customers, so specifications vary by customer and installation date. When the archive was on paper, a search could take half a day. Kuken later digitized the archive, but engineers still had to know which name or number to look up and where to find the file. Newer engineers in particular spent time piecing those details together.

Recent findings suggest that kuken wanted engineers at every experience level to be able to search the archive on their own. As it explored how AI might help, Kuken connected with Recursive, a Japanese AI startup and an official OpenAI partner.

The two companies built the search system and its field app together, drawing on Kuken’s archive and input from its engineers. They tested several AI models on a range of drawings to see how accurately each could extract details and at what cost. OpenAI’s models performed well on both measures, and the OpenAI API gave the team the flexibility to build search directly into the app.

Conversations with field engineers shaped how the search works. Engineers can enter a drawing or part number, or upload an image or PDF of a drawing or parts list.

Pasting in a screenshot of the list saves engineers from entering each number by hand. The app reads the part numbers and returns possible matches, including drawings for similar designs. To find the right drawing, engineers check the tower’s specifications and records of past replacements.

Kuken reports the following results from using and testing the search tool.

Kuken expects the tool to cut the hours spent searching for drawings by about 90% over a year.

Experienced engineers use some of the time they save to mentor newer colleagues.

Engineers can review drawings in the app, reducing printing costs.

In a recent development, engineers now spend less time looking for a drawing and more time studying it. Both newer engineers and veterans say that gives them room to consider design improvements and explore ideas they previously had little time to pursue.

Recent findings suggest that newer engineers can now handle a wider range of jobs on their own. Experienced colleagues who used to guide them through each search have more time to teach and to take on engineering work of their own.

In a recent development, kuken is also developing a tool to check drawings prepared by its partners. Today, engineers compare each drawing with the specifications by eye, looking for details or quantities that don’t match. Kuken wants the tool to flag those differences so engineers can review drawings faster and catch mistakes they might otherwise miss.

According to Kuken, in prototype testing, about 90% of the issues the AI flagged were genuine discrepancies. If the tool moves into production, Kuken expects it to substantially reduce the time engineers spend checking drawings.

Sources indicate that each drawing records decisions an engineer made for a particular installation. By making those decisions easier to find and understand, Kuken aims to pass that experience on to the next generation of engineers.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (246 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.31755v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Harnesses for vision-language models (VLMs) have grown with the models' capabilities, notably for images far larger than those seen in training, where downscaling loses small details. Most of them wrap the VLM in a fixed procedure, such as a zoom tree, that decides in advance where it looks and how the evidence is combined. These procedures make up for the weaknesses of older models by keeping them on a task-specific path, but with frontier models that reliably blueprint and use tools, they can lower accuracy. We propose RVLM-X, a task-generalizable recursive VLM harness that runs unchanged across photographs, charts and maps. Following the recursive inference of Recursive Language Models, the VLM programmatically controls its own visual context in a code REPL that holds the full-resolution image and calls itself recursively on regions that it chooses. With a cost-efficient frontier model as the base of every method, RVLM-X is more accurate than a single call on all 7 public benchmarks and has the highest pooled accuracy. Because existing benchmarks mostly test whether a model finds one small detail, we also introduce MapGenBench, procedurally generated maps whose questions combine fine-detail perception with multi-step reasoning. There, RVLM-X answers 71.4% of held-out questions against 55.5% for the strongest baseline. Overall, our findings suggest that as VLMs plan and use tools more reliably, letting the model write its own visual search works better than fixing one in advance.

MosaicLeaks: Can your research agent keep a secret?

📅 18 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep research agents increasingly combine private local documents with external tools like web retrieval, creating a privacy risk: an agent's external queries may leak sensitive information.
  • A research agent at a healthcare firm is working through a routine question, and along the way it fires off a handful of ordinary-looking web searches.
  • MosaicLeaks treats those web queries as the leakage channel: the adversary never sees the private documents or the agent's reasoning, only the cumulative query log, and tries to infer private enterprise information from it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep research agents increasingly combine private local documents with external tools like web retrieval, creating a privacy risk: an agent's external queries may leak sensitive information. MosaicLeaks proposes a newly introduced deep-research task with multi-hop questions that interleave public and private information. Across the models we tested, agents frequently leaked private information, and training only for task performance made it worse. We propose a mosaic-leakage-aware RL training method, Privacy-Aware Deep Research (PA-DR), which raises strict chain success (the share of chains where every hop is answered correctly) from 48.7% to 58.7% while reducing answer/full-information leakage from 34.0% to 9.9%.

A research agent at a healthcare firm is working through a routine question, and along the way it fires off a handful of ordinary-looking web searches. One references a cloud-migration milestone, one a January 2024 security disclosure, one narrows down which vendor got hit. No single query necessarily gives away the whole secret. But anyone watching the agent's outbound traffic can reassemble the fragments: MediConn had migrated 70% of its infrastructure to the cloud by January 2025, a fact that lived only in private documents. This is the mosaic effect, and it's the failure mode at the centre of MosaicLeaks.

MosaicLeaks treats those web queries as the leakage channel: the adversary never sees the private documents or the agent's reasoning, only the cumulative query log, and tries to infer private enterprise information from it.

We measure leakage in three ways, depending on what the adversary can infer from the observed queries:.

It has been revealed that these three represent increasing levels of concern. Intent leakage reveals what the agent is investigating. Answer leakage means the query log holds enough to answer a private question someone already has in hand. Full-information leakage is the strongest case: the observer can discover and state private facts without being told what to look for.

It has been revealed that how the mosaic effect drives MosaicLeaks's three leakage measures: Intent (predict the research questions), Answer (answer given questions about the private documents), and Full-Information (state verifiably true private claims). Here the agent searches twice about Lee's Market's 2020 traffic growth, leaking its intent, then problems a third query to answer a follow-up. Each query looks benign alone, but seen together they let an observer deduce that the answer was 15%, and so claim that Lee's online traffic grew 15% in 2020.

MosaicLeaks contains 1,001 multi-hop research chains over local enterprise documents and a controlled web corpus. The goal is to create tasks with a high likelihood of inducing privacy leakage from enterprise documents, but that can still be solved without leaking.

Each chain interleaves local and web sub-questions. The answer to one sub-question becomes a bridge entity in the next, so the agent must retrieve local information before it can form the next useful web query. Local documents come from DRBench-style enterprise tasks, and web documents come from BrowseComp-Plus. The final split contains 559 training chains, 98 validation chains, and 344 held-out-organization test chains.

It has been revealed that the final web hop doesn't inherently contain any private information and can be answered from public web documents. However, because the path to it depends on private local facts, a query that carries forward "MediConn", "70%", and "January" gives the adversary enough context to recover internal information.

Sources indicate that we use a simplified agent harness adapted from DRBench. The model answers each sub-question with a short answer and justification, allowing us to evaluate each hop individually with normalized string matching.

Recent findings suggest that at each iteration, the model can use four tools. Blueprint produces local and web search queries, which are executed and returned as document cards. Choose selects which retrieved documents to read. Read attempts to answer the current hop from each selected document in parallel. Resolve decides whether to answer, read more documents, or plan another search.

One agent rollout. Each row is a hop, labeled local (L) or web (W) with its accepted answer. The colored blocks show the wall-clock time spent planning, retrieving, choosing, reading, and resolving that hop.

In a recent development, the obvious fix is to just ask. Add a line to the Plan prompt telling the agent not to concern web queries that leak local information, and see what happens to performance, leakage, and query behavior.

The prompt helps slightly for some models, but its effect is inconsistent and significant leakage remains. It also often has a negative effect on task performance. For Qwen3-4B, the prompt lowers answer/full-information leakage from 34.0% to 25.5%, but strict chain success drops from 48.7% to 44.5%. The primary behavioral change appears to be fewer web queries, not consistently safer query construction.

Industry observers note that strict chain success and privacy leakage with and without a prompt discouraging web queries that may leak local information. The prompt decreases leakage slightly for some models, but substantial leakage remains.

Before training for privacy, we tried the obvious thing: train the agent only to solve more chains correctly. It worked. Strict chain success rose from 48.7% to 59.3%. But answer/full-information leakage climbed right alongside it, from 34.0% to 51.7%. The model had learned to pack more context into its web queries, which helped it retrieve the right document but hurt privacy, since each richer query gives the observer another fragment.

According to recent reports, this is the central tension MosaicLeaks exposes. A more informative query is often better for the task and worse for privacy. PA-DR is built to train for both sides at once.

Industry observers note that the first is a situational task reward. A single research trajectory can run to dozens of model calls, so giving them all the same final trajectory score is very weak credit: a successful run can reinforce a leaky search, and a failed run can punish a locally sound decision. Instead, we judge each call against other calls made at the same stage and hop, with the same information available. A Plan call is rewarded for searching the correct source and retrieving the right document; if that document is already in hand, it is rewarded for not searching again. A Choose call is rewarded for selecting the document that holds the answer. We train these stages because their desired behavior can be checked directly.

In a recent development, the second is a learned privacy reward. Whenever the agent produces web queries, a Qwen3-4B classifier estimates two risks: whether the current queries leak private information directly, and whether adding them to the existing query log creates a new mosaic leak. PA-DR penalizes the larger of the two, so the privacy cost lands on the exact planning decision that made the query log more revealing.

Task-only RL improves research performance but increases leakage. PA-DR keeps almost all of the performance gain while sharply reducing it.

Recent findings suggest that that 9.9% is lower than the untrained base model's own 34.0%. Training for privacy did not simply cancel the leakage that training for performance introduced. It left the agent leaking less than it did at the start.

It has been revealed that and it did not get safer by simply searching less. PA-DR actually problems more web queries than the base model, but those queries drop the revealing details: specific metrics like "15%" or "2024", and clues about the kind of answer it is looking for. The agent still finds the right public documents. It just stops carrying private fragments along in the query text.

Sources indicate that situational rewards pay off a second time, during training itself. Because they compare matching calls instead of scoring a whole rollout once, they assign credit far more precisely, with no separate value model and no need to align step indices across rollouts. They are also much more sample-efficient: the situational task reward reaches the same task performance as outcome-only RL with roughly 5-6x fewer generated training samples, and PA-DR keeps that efficiency while adding the privacy gain.

Training efficiency. The final column is how many generated samples each method needs to reach ~55% strict chain success. Lower is better.

Situational rewards reach outcome-reward-level task success using roughly 5-6x fewer generated samples. PA-DR keeps the sample-efficiency benefit while sharply reducing leakage.

MosaicLeaks is a controlled benchmark, not a measurement of leakage in deployed systems. The enterprise documents are synthetic, the web corpus is fixed, the chains span three manufacturer contexts, and every result comes from a single agent harness running multi-hop question answering rather than open-ended research. That control is what makes leakage measurable hop by hop, but broader tasks, real deployments, and other agent designs still need their own study.

The takeaway is simple. You can't prompt privacy in. You have to train it in. Telling an agent to be careful barely moves the needle, while rewarding how it constructs each query cuts leakage by more than 3x and leaves task success essentially intact. The mosaic effect comes from how an agent searches over time, and that turns out to be something you can measure, assign credit to, and train down.

According to recent reports, fascinating work on the mosaic effect. It makes me wonder how PA-DR holds up when agents are deployed for active threat intelligence or software auditing. For instance, if an enterprise research agent is tasked with analyzing potential security vectors or reverse-engineering third-party mobile apps from repositories like https://toemodapk.com, its web-query logs could easily leak proprietary internal app versions or specific device compliance criteria to an outside observer. Teaching agents to scrub those granular technical identifiers during deep web retrieval is going to be massive for operational security.

Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (208 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two fresh gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are currently written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31733v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models can generate cache-replacement policies. The central challenge is to retain performance on workloads excluded from the search. In our adaptations of published search methods, generated code resembles established policies, with cosine similarities of 0.78-0.84. The wider comparison also shows held-out harmonic-mean instructions-per-cycle (IPC) losses of 1.0-2.4%. We present MOSAIC, a search controller that improves policies without updating language-model weights. It stores concise lessons from previous evaluations rather than repeatedly copying high-scoring code. When improvement stops, it selects two high-scoring policies whose code embeddings differ and asks the model to combine their mechanisms. Novelty prompts and model rotation support this search; controlled memory edits test how the stored lessons affect later proposals. We evaluate cache replacement using intervention-level cross-validation and a wider comparison on ten memory-intensive SPEC2006 workloads. MOSAIC reaches a 51.1% peak hit rate on the primary search workload and a 47.9% held-out mean in the intervention study. Removing crossover reduces these values by 7.8 and 21.8 percentage points, respectively, whereas the tested stronger model improves the held-out mean by 0.4 points. In the wider IPC comparison, MOSAIC has the smallest held-out gap (0.31%) and the highest held-out IPC among the evaluated LLM configurations. Adapting the same controller to data prefetching gives a 4.8% mean speedup over the LRU reference configuration. The accompanying corpus contains 10,687 generated policies with lineage and per-iteration prompt logs.

We got local models to triage the OpenClaw repo for FREE!*

📅 22 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1945 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • *Free as in beer, excluding the cost of electricity, and assuming you already own the hardware.
  • June 2026 will go down as the moment that people realized closed models can be taken away.
  • Sources indicate that in that light, we wanted to share how we use local models like Gemma and Qwen in an agent harness, to run classification tasks[1].
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

*Free as in beer, excluding the cost of electricity, and assuming you already own the hardware.

June 2026 will go down as the moment that people realized closed models can be taken away. With the removal of Anthropic's latest flagship model Claude Fable 5 fresh in memory, one can see why it is more crucial than ever to own your AI stack and be able to run models locally, especially if you are building your business on top of AI.

Sources indicate that in that light, we wanted to share how we use local models like Gemma and Qwen in an agent harness, to run classification tasks[1]. This approach is different from using a model like BERT for classification. A local model in an agent harness like Pi can be used in tandem with structured outputs, to assign labels. We chose this approach because we already had local models and the harness on hand, and have conviction that similar setups will increase in popularity as local models improve in capability.[2].

Our starting point was open source contributions in the OpenClaw repo. OpenClaw gets hundreds of issues and PRs every day, which need to be triaged, prioritized and routed to maintainers. I, Onur, am working to make local models work well with OpenClaw. Being a maintainer of this specific vertical, I need to react promptly to any P0 issues.

According to recent reports, with SOTA closed models like GPT-5, Opus, or Sonnet, this is a pretty straightforward task. But I happen to sit on 128 GB of unified memory, namely an NVIDIA GB10. So I took on the task:.

Can I build a real-time notification system that filters and notifies me for only the problems that I am responsible for... with local open-weight models?

According to recent reports, if I set up my OpenClaw main agent running on a $200/mo ChatGPT Pro initiative to trigger a job on every fresh glitch or PR, that would use up my quota. I might instead set it to run every 2 hours, or 6 hours. This would batch concerns over longer periods, so we would be trading real-time notifications for delayed processing.

If I were to run this on a local model on the hardware I already have up and running, I would not only have near-instantaneous notifications, I would also be able to do it for free (or rather, for the cost of electricity).

We came up with a finite set of labels representing the categories of problems we need to triage, and then use a local model to classify each issue into one of those categories, like local_models, self_hosted_inference, acp, agent_runtime, codex, ui_tui and so on.[3].

But how do we classify pull requests? A simple single request to a Chat Completions endpoint with a tool JSON schema, with the topics as an enum?

Industry observers note that kind of. But this is 2026, not 2023, and we have AGENTS. We can do better!

Recent findings suggest that for the local model choices, we tested gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b. With performance optimizations, both can generate hundreds of tokens per second locally.

Sources indicate that we use an agent harness to drive the classification run. For this, we bundle pi as a harness that can call local model endpoints.

Sources indicate that the agent by default receives the PR title, body and a truncated excerpt of the PR diff in the first prompt. Then, it can choose to use the bash tool to perform read-only operations on the OpenClaw repo (in case it needs to look at the codebase), or the final_json tool to submit the final classification result.

You wouldn't want to give full bash access to a local model running in this high-throughput setting, because a prompt-injected problem or PR could otherwise steer the model into doing something unrelated to classification.

In a recent development, for that reason, we use reposhell instead of bash: a restricted bash-like shell that only allows read-only operations (ls, find, cat, grep, etc.) on the OpenClaw repo. The model thinks it is using bash, but any operation that is not allowed is rejected:.

According to recent reports, here is a concrete example where this mattered. In one saved session example, qwen3.6-35b-a3b was classifying openclaw/openclaw#84621, titled Fix Kimi tool-call rewriting stop reason handling. The thinking block shows the model initially considering coding_agent_integrations because the changed path extensions/kimi-coding made it look plausible. The model used reposhell to inspect the local repo with simple read-only commands like ls extensions, ls extensions/kimi-coding, and cat extensions/kimi-coding/package.json. That package metadata showed the extension was actually @openclaw/kimi-provider, an OpenClaw Kimi provider plugin. So the model corrected the final labels to inference_api and tool_calling, and explicitly excluded coding_agent_integrations.

According to recent reports, we have mentioned earlier that we bundle a specific pi configuration that can only perform read-only operations and return classification output. We call it localpager-agent, named after localpager, the main project here. Each PR and issue generates a prompt, which is then passed to the CLI like below, alongside other args:.

So then what orchestrates everything in between the incoming PR/issue and the final notification on Discord?

The orchestration around this is very simple; only the classification step involves an LLM:.

Below is a figure showing the overall architecture of localpager:.

It has been revealed that the architecture is semi-agentic. Labeling is done agentically, while sending a notification is handled by deterministic rules. This is to make the notification pipeline faster by removing the need for inference for the most straightforward parts of the task. Local inference is free but each task has a resource contention cost: GPU bandwidth should be reserved for tasks where inference is absolutely needed. This also reduces chance of errors from notification.

Let's be frank: the first local versions of this system were noisy. The first model tested - gemma-4-e4b-it was useful for getting the end-to-end local pipeline working, but it also had a tendency to put too many unrelated labels on a PR or concern. False positive labels make the Discord feed noisy and don't focus my attention on the right complications. That pushed us toward testing larger local models, including gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b, on the 330-row evaluation set below.

For early prompt work, we also used DeepSeek-V4-Flash through the antirez DS4 implementation[4] to create the earlier dataset labels. That setup used the DS4 server over CUDA. We eventually gave up on DS4 as the labeler because it was not labeling consistently across runs. We also did not consider it as the main localpager-agent model because it was too significant to get enough throughput on our hardware: the DS4 server gave us around 14 tokens per second, with maximum concurrency of 1.

To test model performance, we selected and generated labels for 330 GitHub challenges and PRs. Each item was labelled five times (3x GPT-5.5 and 2x Opus 4.8) with the models needing to be in agreement to be accepted. This process involved hand adjudicating, improving label definitions and highlighting internal product design choices for the models. This gave us a set of stable, reproducible labels to compare our smaller models against.

Sources indicate that we did not need to do prompt optimization for gemma-4-26b-a4b or qwen3.6-35b-a3b before getting useful results on this evaluation set. Using the same routing prompt, Gemma had higher recall and lower wall-clock time per row, while Qwen had higher precision, higher exact match, and fewer false positives. We also ran DeepSeek-V4-Flash on the same set as a reference. It had the fewest false positives, but the model size and throughput make it impractical for executing these tasks in real time on the NVIDIA GB10. Since each row can have multiple labels, false positives and false negatives are total label counts across all rows. The Qwen results below are after retrying structured-output failures where the model ran out of output tokens before calling final_json. For Gemma and Qwen, repeated-run metrics report mean ± sample standard deviation across three runs. DeepSeek-V4-Flash was run once as a reference.

Sources indicate that the throughput and wall-clock numbers here are not definitive maximum performance numbers for these models on this hardware. They are the settings we used at the time with the optimizations we had available. For example, in a separate probe, gemma-4-26b-a4b also supported concurrency 32 and reached over 700 aggregate output tokens per second.

According to recent reports, for the Gemma benchmark, we served gemma-4-26b-a4b with vLLM using the optimizations we found available for this setup. A massive part of that is the NVFP4 quantization: on GB10-class Blackwell hardware, it is not just a smaller model file, but a hardware-friendly format that can use the NVIDIA/vLLM execution path more directly than a portable GGUF quantization like Q4_K_M. In practice, that means less memory traffic and more room for batching. We also enabled prefix caching, FP8 KV cache, the CUTLASS MoE backend, and language-model-only mode. The full 330-row run finished in about 7.5 minutes at concurrency 16.

We have mentioned earlier that instead of running a job with a local model for every newly introduced matter or PR, we can run a batch job with a SOTA cloud model, like GPT-5.5 running in OpenClaw, every n hours (e.g. every 2 hours) to achieve the same end.[5].

According to recent reports, in that case, we would need a ChatGPT Pro plan. Since the model is SOTA, we can still expect it to perform reasonably well, despite batching 2 hours of problems/PRs together.

Because we want to see how well the local classifier performs against GPT-5.5, we run both simultaneously, and let GPT-5.5 be the judge of false positives and negatives, every 2 hours.

To be safe, we run the OpenClaw job in a sandbox, with only access to the public repo we report results to. In our case, we let the OpenClaw job update a machine-readable file, then a simple script reads the Codex-assigned labels and computes the false positive/negative status. Example output:.

The instructions on how to classify, edit the machine-readable file, get the false positives and false negatives using a script are present in an agent skill which is referenced in an OpenClaw cron job that runs every 2 hours. The OpenClaw agent then ingests any upcoming challenges or PRs, adds them to the JSON file with appropriate labels, runs the scripts and reports back in the same Discord channel. This way, we can observe the local model's performance every few hours, and get notified of the misses.

We think that the matter/PR triage task is a specific case of a broader set of tasks which we call "high throughput triage". This post explored the idea of using a local model to filter out information in real time in only one domain, that is, open source contributions. The ability of medium-sized local models like gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b to zero-shot classify with good accuracy without any need for fine-tuning makes them a good first choice for quick prototyping, before one moves on to more cost-efficient traditional classifier models.

However, the same approach can be applied to other domains as well:.

The list can be extended, but we think that the idea should be clear.

According to recent reports, besides triaging, we have also explored how classification can be performed with agent harnesses running fast local models in a secure manner. A good naming for the approach would be agentic classification: the model is not fed the entire body of information upfront, but can search for more context before returning structured data. While we cannot exactly call this a novel approach, we hope for this blog post to be a good reference for the specific Pi+a restricted shell+final_json recipe.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CodeRabbit uses OpenAI models to govern and trust AI-generated code and Codex to ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team.

For Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO of CodeRabbit⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), trusting and validating agentic code is becoming the place where teams bring judgment to a growing volume of AI-generated work. “The first bottleneck that every company hits as soon as you adopt coding agents is code reviews,” Harjot notes.

CodeRabbit built an AI-powered governance and control platform designed to validate and trust AI-generated code. Used by over 20,000 organizations and 150,000+ open-source projects, CodeRabbit helps teams understand, review, and secure code produced by AI agents and decide what is ready to ship.

According to CodeRabbit, better price-performance from OpenAI helps it add more AI agents to its reviews and pass the benefits to customers, and Codex⁠ helps it ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team. The company also uses Daybreak⁠ to both secure its own stack and its customers’ code. Its latest offering, CodeRabbit Secure, uses Daybreak with Codex models to find and fix vulnerabilities using its security-focused agents.

CodeRabbit built its first product with GPT‑3.5 Turbo. Harjot says the arrival of GPT‑4 made the product effective at reviewing code. The company went on to adopt OpenAI o1 and OpenAI o3 early. Because code reviews run asynchronously in the cloud, CodeRabbit could use models that took longer to reason through a problem in exchange for more capable analysis.

Sources indicate that the team evaluates new models against its own benchmark of known complications. At the time of the interview, Harjot estimated that GPT‑6 Astra⁠ caught 50% of the issues in that dataset, putting it at the top compared to other models in that benchmark.

Recent findings suggest that the benchmark continues to evolve as agents introduce different kinds of mistakes and as fixes reveal problems earlier reviews missed. “The nature of bugs keeps evolving, so does our benchmark as the models get better,” says Harjot.

Better price-performance from OpenAI models has helped CodeRabbit move capabilities from research into its product. Harjot points to improvements in model pricing and caching that let the company use more AI, add more subagents, and pass the benefits to customers.

When CodeRabbit started, it used one or two subagents for code navigation. Lower-cost models such as GPT‑6 Luna now support more subagents throughout the platform, while models such as GPT‑6 Astra handle planning and orchestration.

“Now we are using agents everywhere on the use cases we couldn't even afford in the past,” Harjot notes. That expands the validation CodeRabbit can perform and the explanations it can give developers, helping them understand and trust changes they did not write themselves.

Industry observers note that by using Codex, Harjot says the organization has been shipping roughly 20 times more software over the last 6 months without adding engineers. He personally estimates that he pushed 2,500 to 3,000 pull requests in the 30 days before the interview.

Industry observers note that getting there required more than adopting Codex. Running multiple agents exposed constraints across the development process, from laptop memory and compute to testing, the tools that compile and package software, and dependencies.

Industry observers note that the team streamlined its release process and reconsidered where human approvals belonged, while using CodeRabbit to automatically ship low-risk changes that didn’t need human intervention. “We had to actually completely rethink the entire software delivery,” Harjot claims.

It has been revealed that the company has also built a Codex-powered Slack bot that triages production incidents, Slack messages, and support tickets. It can return a pull request for the team to review and merge. Harjot sees cloud-based development as a way to reduce local-machine constraints and give teams stronger controls over access and auditing.

In a recent development, codeRabbit uses Codex for work beyond engineering, including managing marketing and operational tasks through code. “We are running the tech giant as code as much as possible,” Harjot says.

In a recent development, in marketing, the company manages Google Ads through pull requests. The team opens and merges a request to deploy ads. It also uses a content studio repository where Codex creates slide decks and customer-facing documents. “If you can translate your marketing problems to code problems, you will run 10x faster,” Harjot claims.

CodeRabbit has run agents in sandbox environments since 2023, cloning repositories and letting agents write code to help perform reviews. More recently, CodeRabbit used OpenAI’s Cyber model through Daybreak to test and secure its own platform.

The team used the model for internal penetration testing, probing its own platform for ways an attacker could break in. Harjot says the early access helped CodeRabbit secure its own stack. “We found multiple vulnerabilities, advanced hacks that we could not even imagine could happen,” Harjot says.

It has since taken those capabilities to market, helping secure its customers’ code with its latest product, CodeRabbit Secure. Over the past two weeks, the company ran a promotional offer where it covered $1M in free deep scans for their consumers and found over 43,000 security vulnerabilities across 13,000 deep scans, all powered by Codex models. Thousands of these vulnerabilities have already been fixed by its customers, helping improve their code security.

As background agents begin responding to alerts and incidents without a person initiating every task, Harjot expects teams to need more help deciding which changes to take to completion.

Looking ahead, CodeRabbit is expanding toward agentic software development, helping teams validate, prioritize, explain, secure, and verify agent-generated code changes at scale.

The opportunity is to help developers stay in control as agents do more of the building, with validation, explanations, and maintenance that keep pace with the code being produced.

arXiv:2611.31731v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conventional post-hoc explanation methods were developed largely for non-spatial inputs and often provide limited explicit treatment of geographic context. We introduce Geo-SMILE, a model-agnostic framework that distinguishes substantive Feature explanation from geographic-position response through complementary perturbation branches. The Feature branch masks substantive predictors while retaining observed coordinates; the Geo branch relocates geographic units while holding substantive predictors fixed. Following the statistical-distance-weighted surrogate principle of SMILE, input-distribution Wasserstein distances determine coalition locality weights and weighted Ridge surrogates approximate expected black-box predictions. GeoSensitivity, signed in the keep orientation, quantifies fitted-model responses to geographic-player relocation under the specified design. Across crime prediction in Hull, housing-price prediction in Seattle and ride-hailing demand in Chicago, held-out weighted surrogate fidelity ranges from $R_w^2=0.910$ to $0.989$ in the Feature branch and from $0.842$ to $0.906$ in the Geo branch. The framework makes geographic position an explicit object of post-hoc explanation while requiring separate assessment of interpretation, stability and reference dependence.

Evaluate PP-OCRv6 online, then integrate lightweight, production-ready OCR with PaddlePaddle, Transformers, or ONNX Runtime backend.

PP-OCRv6 is the latest generation of PaddleOCR’s universal OCR model family. It is designed for real-world text detection and recognition across documents, screenshots, multilingual images, digital displays, industrial labels, and scene text.

In a recent development, the model family scales from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters, with three tiers: tiny, small, and medium. The medium and small tiers support 50 languages, including Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English, Japanese, and 46 Latin-script languages. Try PP-OCRv6 online quickly: PP-OCRv6 Online Demo.

On PaddleOCR’s official in-house multi-scenario OCR benchmarks, PP-OCRv6_medium reaches 86.2% detection Hmean and 83.2% recognition accuracy. Compared with PP-OCRv5_server, it improves text detection by +4.6 percentage points and text recognition by +5.1 percentage points.

PP-OCRv6 focuses on a practical OCR need: producing accurate, structured text outputs with small models and flexible deployment options. For a deeper discussion of why specialized OCR models remain useful in the VLM era, see our previous blog: PP-OCRv5 on Hugging Face: A Specialized Approach to OCR.

Recent findings suggest that PP-OCRv6 introduces architecture, training, and data improvements across detection and recognition. The main design goal is to improve OCR accuracy while keeping model sizes suitable for different deployment settings.

PP-OCRv6 provides three model tiers, covering different model sizes and OCR accuracy levels.

PP-OCRv6 uses PPLCNetV4 as a unified backbone for text detection and text recognition.

For developers, the main benefit is consistency across the model family. The tiny, small, and medium tiers are not unrelated models; they are part of the same OCR family and share a common architectural direction.

Text detection is the first stage of the OCR pipeline. Detection quality affects the crops sent to the recognizer, and poor crops often lead to poorer recognition.

PP-OCRv6 upgrades the detection module with RepLKFPN, a lightweight large-kernel feature pyramid network designed for multi-scale text detection while keeping inference efficient.

This is relevant for real-world OCR inputs, where text may be small, dense, rotated, low-resolution, or embedded in complex backgrounds.

In a recent development, for text recognition, PP-OCRv6 uses EncoderWithLightSVTR. It combines local context modeling with global attention to improve recognition quality on challenging text crops.

The recognition improvements are especially relevant for multilingual text, screen text, industrial characters, special symbols, dense text, and noisy image regions.

The medium and small tiers support 50 languages in one model family, covering Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English, Japanese, and 46 Latin-script languages.

This helps reduce the need for separate OCR models across common multilingual OCR scenarios.

PP-OCRv6 extends PaddleOCR with a lightweight, multilingual OCR model family for real-world text detection and recognition.

The release includes three model tiers from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters, up to 50-language OCR support, improved detection and recognition accuracy over PP-OCRv5_server, and multiple model formats on the Hugging Face Hub, including safetensors, Paddle inference models, and ONNX models.

arXiv:2611.31720v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Event cameras report asynchronous brightness changes, yet metric-depth supervision is typically available only at sparsely sampled reference timestamps. Aggregating events into frame-like representations simplifies learning but can obscure the fine-grained temporal structure of the original event stream. We introduce EventSSM, a causal spatial-state framework for event-associated metric-depth estimation using a recurrent memory updated by chronological event packets. To bridge asynchronous predictions and frame-time supervision, predicted event depths are geometrically transported using calibrated camera poses and differentiably rendered at reference timestamps. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate improvements over established event-depth methods across multiple depth-error measures. Controlled ablations further examine cross-modal initialization, temporal recurrence, individual state, readout, and supervision components, and packet subdivision. Together, these findings establish EventSSM as an effective framework for causal event-associated metric-depth estimation, combining persistent spatial context with physically timed state retention.

Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential concerns, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed.
  • Control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them swiftly when safety or security concerns arise.
  • Sources indicate that control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential concerns, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed. To solve this, we built Control Room.

Control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them swiftly when safety or security concerns arise. It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our misalignment monitoring systems, and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job. It has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.

Sources indicate that control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest. Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to promptly take down model deployments if needed.

Control Room works by integrating a few systems: the workload, the inference engine, and the centralized Control Room service.

The workload is the job being run, such as a reinforcement learning experiment, an evaluation, a high-volume sampling or data processing job. We require every research workload that does agentic inference to be associated with an approved safety case.

According to recent reports, the inference engine, or just engine, is the model itself. You can think of the engine as the brain of the model, running directly on GPUs. A workload normally uses one or more models, which might be running on one or more different inference engines. The same inference engine might be used by more than one different workload.

Industry observers note that the Control Room service tracks jobs and controls whether they are allowed to continue generating model output. Engines check with the Control Room service before fulfilling a request. If a job has been stopped, the service denies the request, preventing further output.

Control Room is integrated in the following way:.

When starting a fresh job, the workload code requests a new job_id from Control Room.

Whenever the workload needs to sample tokens from a model, it makes a request to an inference engine running that model, passing the job_id. The engine requests permission from Control Room to fulfill that request, passing the job_id along to Control Room.

Control Room checks whether that job has been terminated, and if so, it denies the inference request. The engine responds to the workload's inference request with a refusal, stopping further model output from being produced for that job.

The process starts with a researcher launching a job—for example, an experiment or an evaluation.

Job code (or workload code) is owned and run by researchers. Inference engines might be started as part of this job, or standalone engines which are not associated with any particular job might already be running.

The workload code requests a job ID, associating the job with an approved safety case. The job itself makes this request.

Control Room records the job and returns its identifier. The workload will attach this same ID to its inference requests.

Recent findings suggest that the request includes the job_id. This request is made directly from the workload code and does not pass through Control Room.

Before fulfilling the request, the inference engine asks Control Room whether this job is still authorized to run.

Industry observers note that the job is still authorized, so Control Room grants permission. The inference engine can now fulfill the request.

The model generates a response and the engine sends it back to the research job. The job can use that output and continue its work.

A person or monitoring system tells Control Room to stop this job. Control Room marks its ID as stopped. The workload code remains running.

We do not rely on the workload code to correctly perform a check of whether or not the job is still running.

The engine asks Control Room for permission to fulfill the latest inference request, passing along the same job ID.

When the engine checks permission again, Control Room denies the stopped job. The engine must refuse the inference request.

It has been revealed that the engine returns a refusal instead of model output. The research process may remain alive, and the engine remains available to other authorized jobs.

Recent findings suggest that all of our frontier reinforcement learning jobs run with a monitor. A monitor is another model which inspects everything that the model-being-trained is doing, and raises an alert if it detects a problem. For example, our recent DNS-related incident⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) was caught by a monitor.

Control Room and our monitoring system are integrated in the following way:.

If the monitoring system detects a potential matter, depending on the details and severity, the monitoring system may decide to stop the job.

According to recent reports, in this case, the monitoring system sends a message to Control Room to stop the job, passing the job_id. Control Room records that the job is terminated.

Next time the job having that job_id makes an inference request to sample more tokens from any model running on any engine, the request will be denied, stopping further model output.

The maximum time between the moment when Control Room receives an instruction to stop a job, and the moment when further progress is no longer possible, is 35 seconds. The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly.

In a recent development, workloads, including experiments, evaluation jobs, etc., are normally owned and operated by researchers or teams of researchers. As a result, workload code changes often, and is not an ideal place to implement critical load-bearing safety protections. Because of this, our implementation is designed to be resilient to buggy or broken workload code.

In a recent development, we achieve this by implementing the termination mechanism in the inference layer. Workload code is highly-varied and decentralized. In contrast, there are only a very small number of inference code paths in use across all of OpenAI research, and their deployments are much more centralized and uniform. This means that the inference layer can serve as a bottleneck, where we can get strong guarantees that all model inference running in research is subject to Control Room authorization checks on every inference request. We additionally run continual agentic and programmatic sweeps to check that users are not accidentally or maliciously launching rogue engine implementations with Control Room unimplemented or disabled.

Finally, our system “fails closed”, meaning that the Control Room integration in the engines is configured in such a way that if the Control Room service goes down, either due to a system error or because it is disabled for any other reason, including tampering by a bad actor, then all inference requests will be denied until Control Room resumes normal operation. Fail-closed is rolled out now to all frontier model research workloads, and will finish rolling out across all remaining research workloads over the next few days.

Industry observers note that control Room is just one part of our holistic approach to safe frontier model training and deployment. We’ll continue to strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches. If you want to help build systems for the safe and secure development and deployment of AGI, we're⁠ hiring⁠!

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.31705v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page: https://foveawam.github.io/.
