⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure.
  • We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services.
  • In a recent development, the intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one vital way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system - and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.

We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services. We are still completing our assessment of whether any partner or customer data was affected, and we will contact any affected parties directly as required. We have found no evidence of tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and our software supply chain (container images and published packages) was verified clean.

In a recent development, the intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.

Sources indicate that the campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness - used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services. This matches the "agentic attacker" scenario the industry has been forecasting.

We are working with outside cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the glitch and review our security policies and procedures. Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.

Industry observers note that as a precaution, we recommend rotating any access tokens and reviewing recent activity on your account. If you believe you are affected, or want to report a security concern, contact us at security@huggingface.co.

It has been revealed that we are grateful to the teams across Hugging Face who responded around the clock, and we are sorry for any disruption this caused. Security is never finished; we will keep raising the bar.

It has been revealed that the attack was initially surfaced through AI-assisted detection. Our anomaly-detection pipeline uses LLM-based triage over security telemetry to separate real signals from the daily noise, and it was the correlation of those signals that flagged the compromise.

To understand what a swarm of tens of thousands of automated actions did, we ran LLM-driven analysis agents over the full attacker action log, comprised of more than 17,000 recorded events. This allowed us to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, map the credentials touched, and separate genuine impact from decoy activity. Thanks to this approach, we were able to do in hours what would usually take days, and match the adversary's speed.

The choice of models we could use for this analysis was constrained in a way we did not anticipate; we describe this below.

According to recent reports, when we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.

In a recent development, this experience points to a gap worth planning for. We do not know which model powered the attacker's agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. This is not an argument against safety measures on hosted models, and we are sharing this feedback with the providers concerned.

Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical. It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed. Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defense to keep pace. We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.31261v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The application of Item Response Theory (IRT) for data selection in benchmarks has mostly been limited to monolingual settings. In this work, we ask: how does IRT generalize when the same benchmark is translated across languages? We conduct experiments on Multilingual GSM and Global MMLU, covering over 100 language models and 11 languages. Fitting 1PL, 2PL, and 3PL IRT models per language, we assess cross-lingual consistency of parameters and whether IRT-filtered subsets preserve model rankings across languages: item difficulty emerges as the most stable parameter followed by guessing and then discrimination. A differential item analysis also shows that lack of stability can be tracked to specific items shifting under translation across languages. Our findings suggest IRT-based selection in multilingual settings must be both parameter-aware and item-aware, validating model choice and screening individual items before assuming cross-lingual generalization.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.31260v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transformers are widely used in various language tasks, with limited understanding of their internal mechanisms. Motivated by the recurrent structure of many linguistic rules, we study the capability and interpretability of Transformers through a controlled family of linear recurrence tasks over finite cyclic groups. These tasks range from executing a single fixed rule to identifying a latent rule from context and switching between explicitly specified rules, with and without input masking. Through extensive experiments across different configurations, we find that switching specified rules is simpler than identifying latent rules for Transformers in general. We also identify how several key factors affect the generalization capability of Transformers, including the depth, width, and the algebraic structure of the linear recurrence. Curriculum training is extremely useful when the number of rules is large. With standard tools in mechanistic interpretability like linear probing and input patching, our study reveals how Transformers represent, identify, and execute multiple rules.

arXiv:2611.31259v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Question-answering recipe recommendation tasks lack datasets with ground-truth labels. Existing methods often generate datasets from simple combinations of ingredient or tag constraints, leading to unnatural expressions and unreasonable constraints that are hard to reflect users' real preferences. This paper proposes a construction method for a benchmark-style QA dataset for natural-language recipe recommendation. Driven by real user behavior, our method integrates external user query and review data to extract fine-grained preference signals by LLMs and maps them onto a knowledge-graph-based tag schema, thereby constructing QA data consisting of preference and ingredient constraints. Besides, a greedy strategy for constraint selection is also used to control the answer size, while tag-based re-ranking is applied to improve data quality. The generated dataset RecipeADQA contains natural-language questions, structured constraints, and answer sets, resulting in 128,465 instances. Experiments compare RecipeADQA with baseline datasets from two perspectives: data quality and retrieval-recommendation performance. The results show that ours outperforms existing methods on the same recipe knowledge graph in coverage, higher question quality in naturalness and constraint rationality, and better queryability. Moreover, we design a noise-augmented retrieve-and-rerank model, in which a lightweight parser first retrieves candidate recipes, and a small language model then selects and ranks relevant recipes from a noisy candidate pool. The model trained on RecipeADQA outperforms the same model trained on the baseline datasets. The relevant construction code and data have been open-sourced at a GitHub repository https://github.com/MorimoLab/RecipeADQA.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we’re starting the OpenAI science blog to give scientists and academic researchers a place to share what they’re discovering with AI and how they’re doing the work. Our mission is to ensure that AGI benefits all of humanity, and accelerating scientific discovery is one of the most impactful ways we can work toward that goal.

We’ll publish work across a broad range of scientific disciplines, including:.

Research and discoveries: New scientific results and updates on ongoing research from OpenAI, our collaborators, and the broader scientific community.

Methods and practical guidance: Examples of how scientists use our models for tasks such as scientific computing, data analysis, exploring literature, and planning experiments. We’ll share approaches others can adapt, including how to check the work and where a method falls short.

Recent findings suggest that perspectives from the scientific community: Firsthand accounts from researchers using AI, what they are learning, and how these capabilities are affecting their disciplines. We’ll also discuss open questions about scientific practice and how to make these tools useful to more people.

Industry observers note that science expands our understanding of the world and makes advances possible, from better medicines to new sources of energy. Many of those advances begin with fundamental questions whose practical significance becomes clear only years later.

In recent months, we’ve seen an expanding range of scientific problems our models can address. In September, an internal OpenAI system produced a proof addressing the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem⁠, a longstanding question about the equations describing fluid motion. In early October, we released a broad range of mathematical results⁠. Among them was a result on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis⁠(opens in a upcoming window), with a result that gives a tighter bound on the error in a classical formula for estimating how many primes lie below a given number. Later that month, we shared results across mathematics, computer science, and physics⁠ concerning how waves concentrate, the limits of efficient computation, and the mathematical foundations of interacting quantum field theory.

In biology, researchers are using AI to analyze complex datasets, connect findings across fields, and develop upcoming hypotheses to test in the lab. Working with PerturbAI and Scripps Research⁠, thousands of agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind analyzed existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells in 32 minutes. By connecting the effects of gene disruptions with scientific literature, they identified possible biological mechanisms for scientists to test. Researchers are also developing their own approaches: César de la Fuente’s team uses ChatGPT and Codex⁠ to build algorithms that identify potential antibiotic molecules, which they then make and test in the lab.

Industry observers note that these capabilities bring new possibilities and changes to scientific practice. In mathematics, systems that generate proofs raise questions about how new arguments are checked, explained, and incorporated into the field. In experimental sciences, exploring more hypotheses creates opportunities — and challenges — in deciding which experiments to pursue. Across disciplines, researchers are considering what these tools mean for training, attribution, and the skills their work requires. The implications will differ by field, and scientific communities should help shape how these tools are used.

We hope this blog helps more people understand how AI is changing science and how they can use it to explore newly introduced questions and make discoveries of their own.

#36297. Newer Models, Same Advantage

Newer Models, Same Advantage

📅 16 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models.
  • It has been revealed that the training pipeline was built in two stages.
  • In a recent development, the combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models. The objective was specific: optical character recognition engineered for Brazilian Portuguese.

It has been revealed that the training pipeline was built in two stages. The first was a supervised fine-tuning step, drawing on a broad collection of Portuguese-language files from different sources, formats, and levels of complexity. This stage aligned the model's weights to the specific vocabulary, syntax, and document structures of Brazilian Portuguese — concentrating representational capacity on the target language rather than distributing it across a broader multilingual space. The second stage applied Direct Preference Optimization: rather than training only on correct transcriptions, the model learned from comparative preference data between competing outputs, teaching it to consistently select the better extraction at inference time. This stage addressed a different problem: not accuracy, but stability. By suppressing the failure modes that cause generative models to produce repetitive or incoherent output, DPO reduced inference time and cost, and materially improved the reliability of what the model delivered in production.

In a recent development, the combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark. Both stages were necessary. The fine-tuning stage built domain competency; the DPO stage ensured that competency held under the conditions where models tend to fail.

OCR models have been moving quickly. But the gaps that originally motivated DharmaOCR's design (in extraction quality on complex documents and in model stability under production conditions) have not closed. They have, if anything, become more instructive as the field has changed.

The proliferation of multimodal generative models made language model-based OCR widely accessible, and the wave of fine-tuned OCR variants that followed reflects how fast that adoption has moved. That proliferation has not, however, changed the fundamental character of the technology. Every OCR system built on a generative model is probabilistic. Transcription errors are an inherent variable of this probabilistic technology. What differentiates models is how many errors they make and of what kind. That is determined by two things: the structure of the model (its architecture and parameter count) and how those parameters were trained for the task.

Architecture and parameter count establish the ceiling on what a model can learn. Training determines how that capacity is allocated.

In a recent development, this distinction is where specialization becomes a structural question rather than a design preference. When a model is trained on a restricted domain — a single language, a bounded document type, a specific task — All of its parameters are dedicated to that specific task. When a model is trained to cover a broader range of domains — a multilingual model handling N languages, for instance — those same parameters must be distributed across all of them. The distribution is not linear: the neuron superposition principle means individual parameters can encode multiple features simultaneously. But the division is real, and its consequences are real. A model covering more ground commits less to any given part of it.

Recent findings suggest that dharmaOCR was trained to accept that constraint in reverse. The model is not designed to be the best option for other languages, and was never intended to be. In exchange, every parameter available to the network could be oriented toward the specific vocabulary, morphology, and orthographic patterns of Brazilian Portuguese — the most directed possible use of the model's resources for that domain.

That concentration is the structural basis of an inherent advantage over multilingual and broader-domain models. The advantage does not depend on having a larger architecture or a more sophisticated training procedure than competitors use — new architectures and new training techniques improve what any model can do. It depends on where those resources are directed: at one domain rather than spread across many.

Three months later, newer models have arrived. Whether the case for specialization holds when those models are newer and more capable is a different question.

Sources indicate that three months after the DharmaOCR paper appeared, two newly introduced OCR models attracted significant attention from the research community: Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR. Both represent genuine technical advances — new training techniques, new datasets, and strong results across multiple languages on a range of benchmark evaluations. They are the kind of models that raise the competitive standard for what OCR systems are expected to deliver.

When we ran both against the DharmaOCR benchmark — an evaluation designed exclusively around Portuguese — the results were conclusive.

DharmaOCR scored 0.925. Mistral OCR4 scored 0.798. Unlimited-OCR scored 0.7587.

The difference is significant. Mistral OCR4 falls approximately 13 points below DharmaOCR; Unlimited-OCR falls more than 16 points below. Both were released after our model, both backed by substantial research resources. On a task where DharmaOCR's fundamental design decision was to concentrate entirely on Portuguese, the specialization advantage is measurable and significant.

The benchmark is the central finding. What follows illustrates why the gap takes the specific shape it does.

According to recent reports, processing non-trivial Portuguese documents reveals precisely where multilingual models tend to break. ENEM essays (Brazil's national high school examination) combine handwritten text with vocabulary, proper nouns, and cultural references that are specific to Brazilian Portuguese. They are exactly the kind of documents where language-specific training produces a return.

Figure 1: ENEM essay manuscript used in benchmark evaluation with outputs of the each model. Misreads marked in red.

Mistral OCR4, evaluated on documents of this kind, transcribed the name Chico Buarque (one of Brazil's most widely recognized musicians and poets) as "Chico Barque." Unlimited-OCR rendered the same name as "chico bique." Confronted with the phrase "O Brasil não exclui, assimila" ("Brazil does not exclude, it assimilates", a Chico Buarque quotation embedded in the same document) Unlimited-OCR returned: "a dose de chico bique, 'o Brasil no exclu, eliminila.'.

Sources indicate that these are not random errors. A model with insufficient exposure to Brazilian Portuguese does not fail arbitrarily — it fails at precisely the vocabulary and proper nouns that distinguish Brazilian Portuguese from the broader multilingual corpus. Chico Buarque is not an obscure reference; the name is nationally recognized. Its systematic corruption across outputs is not an edge case. It is a diagnostic: evidence of where the model's training did not go.

DharmaOCR, evaluated on the same documents, handles these cases correctly. The reason is direct: the model's training was concentrated on this linguistic space, orienting its resources toward the vocabulary and proper noun distributions that characterize Brazilian Portuguese rather than spreading them across many languages at once.

Sources indicate that the examples illustrate the benchmark rather than replace it. The benchmark establishes the magnitude of the gap; the examples show why it is concentrated in language-specific recognition rather than in general capability.

It has been revealed that extraction accuracy, however, is only one dimension of production performance. Stability under visual difficulty is another — and operationally, it is the more consequential one to fail on.

Industry observers note that when a generative model encounters a document it cannot clearly resolve — small fonts, degraded scan quality, dense handwriting — it faces uncertainty in its input signal. Models trained primarily on next-token prediction objectives face a specific vulnerability here: when the visual signal becomes ambiguous, the model can continue generating from prior learned patterns rather than from the source document. The result is text degeneration — output that is repetitive, incoherent, and semantically disconnected from the page.

Presented with a document with small fonts, Mistral OCR4 produces output with no connection to what is written.

Figure 3: DharmaOCR output and Mistral OCR4 degenerated output.

It has been revealed that this is not a low-quality transcription of the source. It is a failure of an entirely different category.

Sources indicate that the operational consequence is distinct from that of a transcription error. An incorrect transcription is wrong in a recoverable way — it stands in a relationship to the source document, and the error can in principle be identified and corrected. Degenerated output has no such relationship. It cannot be corrected because there is nothing to correct toward. For downstream processes that depend on structured OCR output — document classification, information extraction, compliance workflows — degenerated output is not inaccurate data. It is structurally unusable data. The efficiency that automation was meant to deliver is negated at precisely the point where output stops being information.

Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR are good models with significant technical advances behind them. The degeneration behavior described here does not define them; it identifies a specific failure condition that their current training has not addressed for this domain. The question is what a training pipeline designed to address it looks like.

In DharmaOCR, the answer is the DPO stage.

Supervised fine-tuning concentrates the model's resources on the target domain — the stage that builds the linguistic alignment described above. But SFT trains on individual token predictions: the model learns to produce the correct next token given the context preceding it. Under visual complexity, this creates the condition that produces degeneration. If an early token in the output diverges from the source document, each subsequent prediction is conditioned on that divergent state, and the output continues to drift. Repetition loops and incoherent sequences are an inherent characteristic in this context — they are the predictable result of an objective optimized step by step without accounting for the coherence of the full extraction.

DPO trains against a different signal. Where SFT trains token by token, DPO trains the model against the quality of complete outputs — teaching it to discriminate between competing responses based on the coherence of the full extraction rather than the accuracy of individual predictions. The effect is stabilizing: on documents where visual complexity would otherwise trigger drift, the model is less likely to commit to a divergent path, because its training penalized outputs that lost coherence at the extraction level.

The result is what the original benchmark demonstrated: lower degeneration rates alongside higher extraction accuracy, on the same documents where models without this training stage lose coherence.

In a recent development, the benchmark establishes what is true today. It is less precise about what will be true in two years.

Industry observers note that it is possible — and likely — that newer models will eventually outperform the current DharmaOCR even in Brazilian Portuguese. Architectures will improve. Training techniques will advance. Datasets will expand. The field moves toward higher capability at every level, and there is no reason to expect that trajectory to stop. This is expected, and it is welcome.

What changes with each architectural generation is the ceiling on absolute performance. What does not change is the structural logic that determines which systems come closest to their ceiling in a given domain.

Recent findings suggest that available resources — compute, parameters, training data — are finite. They must be directed somewhere. A system that directs them at a single domain will extract more from them in that domain than a system distributing the same resources across many. This relationship holds regardless of how capable the generalist model has become. The gap between specialist and generalist may evolve as architectures improve. The structural dynamic does not reverse. We explored this principle in more depth in an earlier piece on why specialization continues to produce an advantage as AI systems advance (Why Specialization Is Inevitable).

Industry observers note that this is what shapes how Dharma approaches what comes next. The objective is not to defend the current model's benchmark position. It is to remain at the frontier of emerging techniques — new architectures, new training methods, new approaches to alignment and evaluation — and adapt them toward the same end: a specialized system for Brazilian Portuguese OCR that makes the best possible use of available resources, at the lowest possible cost and the shortest possible inference time.

Recent findings suggest that better tools do not work against specialization. They expand what it can achieve.

Three months ago, we showed that concentrating a model's training on a specific domain produces a measurable advantage over generalist systems, including ones that are newer and better-resourced. That advantage held. The same principle will determine how DharmaOCR continues to evolve — not by staying fixed, but by applying whatever progress the field makes to a domain that remains fixed.

arXiv:2611.31258v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Context compaction enables large language model agents to tackle long-horizon tasks within limited context budgets by replacing interaction histories with compressed summaries. However, learning effective compaction jointly with the agent policy remains challenging, as summaries affect task success over many subsequent interactions. We introduce RECAP, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework based on the principle that a summary should preserve the behavior induced by the original interaction history. We formalize this principle with a behavior distortion objective that measures the divergence between the agent's subsequent behavior under compressed and original contexts. We show that the gradient of the distortion objective decomposes into two complementary learning signals: distortion-based reward for summary generation and self-distillation for subsequent actions. Experiments on Qwen3.5-4B show that RECAP consistently outperforms the task-reward-only RL baselines on both environments, leading to an absolute improvement of 4.6% and 4.3% on BrowseComp-plus and SWE-bench Verified, respectively. Ablations further highlight the value of jointly supervising summary generation and post-compaction behavior for RECAP.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.31257v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Motivation: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for single-cell annotation, but existing training methods mainly rely on scalar outcome rewards that provide limited supervision for intermediate biological reasoning. Batch-level annotation is particularly challenging because it requires jointly resolving local cell identities and a global one-to-one matching constraint, such that one local error can affect the entire assignment. Moreover, a single inference pass provides insufficient evidence for locating uncertain predictions. These limitations call for fine-grained reasoning supervision during training and uncertainty-aware refinement during inference. Results: To address these challenges, we propose scOPD, an on-policy self-distillation framework for LLM-based single-cell annotation. After reasoning fine-tuning, scOPD adaptively routes qualified rollouts to reward-based optimization, while erroneous rollouts receive privileged token-level supervision from successful sibling trajectories. During inference, rollout disagreement triggers constraint-aware pairwise refinement of uncertain assignments. Across CellPuzzles and four out-of-domain disease datasets, scOPD consistently improves the performance of diverse LLM backbones, achieving average cell-level and batch-level accuracies of 81.71% and 44.49% with Qwen3-8B. Availability and Implementation: Code and data are available at https://github.com/YuZhiyin/scOPD.

A step toward defining the Standard Model on a lattice

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in the first guest post on our science blog, physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model.
  • The Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism.
  • I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the first guest post on our science blog, physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, describes how he worked with GPT‑6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics.

The Standard Model of particle physics is an extraordinarily successful theory of nature, describing the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces—the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. The success of the theory rests on outstanding agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen’s 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. And yet for all of its successes over the more than fifty years of its existence, a foundational problem remains: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition, one that does not rely on treating its interactions as small corrections. In an October preprint⁠(opens in a latest window) prepared with the aid of GPT‑6 Astra, I proposed a candidate definition on a lattice—a grid representing spacetime.

I had a strategy for tackling this problem, but had not been able to prove that it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. To explain what we did, it helps to start with what is missing from our existing description of the Standard Model.

It has been revealed that what does it mean to say that we lack a definition of the Standard Model? Quantum mechanics and special relativity tell us how the particles and forces of the Standard Model interact. Unfortunately, we don’t yet know how to make complete predictions based directly on these interactions. Instead, we often start by imagining that the interactions are turned off, so that electrons would no longer repel each other. We can solve that problem exactly, then put the interactions back in as a series of small corrections. When the corrections get progressively smaller, a few terms can give a remarkably precise answer—for example, it has allowed physicists to predict the strength of the electron’s magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. This approach is known as perturbation theory.

However, much of the richness of the Standard Model lies outside the realm of perturbation theory. Take the mass of the proton: the proton is made up of three quarks, but its mass comes primarily from the motion and interactions of the quarks and the strong force-carrying gluons inside it. If you turn off the strong force, the proton falls apart entirely, so perturbation theory is not a useful guide to understanding the size of the proton’s mass. More powerful methods are needed to access information about the theory nonperturbatively, where the interactions are present from the start and not treated as small corrections.

For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, we don’t have a nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined. A promising alternative is to discretize spacetime into a grid of points, known as a lattice. The spacing of the grid defines the shortest distance our theory can resolve, and studying a finite grid allows us to give a rigorous nonperturbative definition of the theory at a given spacing. It also enables us to put the theory on a computer, where we can calculate its predictions directly without resorting to perturbation theory. This approach, known as lattice field theory, has led to remarkable progress in our understanding of the strong force over the last few decades, including a quantitative understanding of the mass of the proton from first principles.

Industry observers note that if lattice field theory has been so successful for the strong force, why haven’t we extended it to a nonperturbative lattice definition of the entire Standard Model? Here a crucial difference stands in the way: the Standard Model is an example of what is known as a chiral theory.

A chiral theory is one that looks different under reflection in space. Think of gloves in a mirror: the mirror image of a left-handed glove is a right-handed glove. If you have one of each kind, the mirror image does as well, so your collection of gloves looks the same under reflection in space. But if you only have a left-handed glove, the right-handed glove in the mirror is different.

This notion of handedness extends to many of the fundamental particles in the Standard Model, known as fermions, including quarks and electrons. Most forces in the Standard Model are not chiral: the strong force and electromagnetism, for example, treat left-handed and right-handed fermions in the same way. Such theories can be put on a lattice more readily.

But the third fundamental force of the Standard Model, the weak force, lacks this reflection symmetry. It treats left- and right-handed fermions differently, and so does not look the same under mirror reflections that exchange left and right. This treating of different-handed particles differently is what makes the Standard Model a chiral theory. And it turns out that putting chiral theories on a lattice is profoundly challenging. If we try to put a left-handed fermion on the lattice, the most natural rules give you a right-handed partner you never asked for. This is a surprising outcome, which we’ll unpack momentarily. Whatever the reason, this means a straightforward lattice formulation of the Standard Model gives the wrong particle content for the weak force. Doubling is one reason a complete nonperturbative definition of the Standard Model has been missing since the theory took shape.

Recent findings suggest that to understand doubling, consider an analogy with light. Light has two polarizations, which describe the orientation of the electric field as the light moves through space. (This is familiar if you wear polarized sunglasses, which block the horizontally-polarized light that reflects off water or roads while letting through vertically-polarized light.) Although polarized sunglasses pick out a basis of horizontal and vertical polarizations, for our analogy it will be more useful to pick a basis where these two polarizations are left-circular and right-circular, meaning that the electric field is rotating either clockwise or counterclockwise around the direction of motion. As we’ve said, electromagnetism is reflection-symmetric, so its actual laws are the same for both left-circular and right-circular polarizations. (For the technically inclined, left and right refer to chirality when we talk about fermions. In our analogy with light, they refer to the photon’s helicity, which tells us whether its spin points along or against its direction of travel.).

But imagine you wanted to emulate a world with only left-circular light, akin to the way the weak interactions single out left-handed fermions. To study this in the lab, you could put a laser producing left-circular light into a box with a mirror at either end. The light could build up as it bounced back and forth, allowing you to study it carefully—kind of like putting the Standard Model on a lattice. In each case you are bounding the accessible length scales of the theory to gain control—the lattice bounds the shortest accessible distances, while the box bounds the longest distances.

In a recent development, if you built the box using ordinary mirrors (like putting a chiral theory on the lattice in the most straightforward way), you’d be in for a surprise: the left-circular light coming out of the laser becomes right-circular when it bounces off the mirror at the other end, so now the box contains both polarizations of light. This occurs because the mirror reverses the direction of the light without changing how the electric field is rotating (as seen from the same end of the box), which flips the polarization. This is a bit like the appearance of doublers when you put a left-handed fermion on the lattice. You supplied only left-handed light, and the box supplied the other hand.

In a recent development, there is a clever fix. You can make a chiral mirror using special films whose molecules line up in layers. The alignment turns a little from one layer to the next, tracing a spiral down into the film. For light whose wavelength and handedness match the spiral, the small reflections from different layers reinforce one another, flipping the rotation of the electric field in the light that bounces back. The film sends left-handed light back left-handed and lets right-handed light pass through. Such chiral mirrors have been around for more than a decade, and the phenomenon even occurs in nature: some scarab beetles have a similar spiral in their shiny shells. If you constructed your box using chiral mirrors, then the light traveling in both directions would be left-circular.

According to recent reports, A similar trick works on the lattice: decades ago, Paul Ginsparg and Nobel laureate Ken Wilson1 worked out the lattice rules analogous to the requirement that chiral mirrors reverse the rotation of the electric field upon reflection. Rajamani Narayanan and Herbert Neuberger2 built the analog of the chiral mirrors by finding the necessary definition of fundamental particles on the lattice, known as overlap fermions. Finally, Martin Lüscher3 indicated how to tell the difference between left-handed and right-handed overlap fermions on the lattice, while Yoshio Kikukawa4 and collaborators explored how this might be used to describe weak interactions in the Standard Model. However, one piece was still missing.

Recent findings suggest that to identify that piece, let’s come back to our box with chiral mirrors. The circular polarization of light tells us which way the electric field turns as light propagates, but there’s another important property of the light in our experiment: the optical phase. Imagine water waves rolling past the pilings of a dock, and watch the water rise and fall at one piling. The wave’s phase is the stage of that rise and fall you catch it in when you look, perhaps just past its highest point and on its way down. For our circularly polarized light, the optical phase tracks the same kind of cycle at a fixed spot in the beam, with the electric field pointing up at the “crest” and down at the “trough.”.

The relative phase of two waves determines how much they add or cancel at the same point. At one piling of a dock, two waves arriving in phase lift the water higher as their crests meet, while a crest arriving with a trough can leave the water close to its usual level. Similarly, light with the same phase in the same place builds up, while light with different phases can cancel out. In our box with chiral mirrors, left-circular light is now bouncing back and forth inside the box. After a lap, the returning light meets fresh light from the laser going in the same direction. If their electric fields are in step, they reinforce and the light builds up inside the box. If the fields are half a cycle apart, they point in opposite directions and the returning light cancels some of the fresh light. To build up a strong beam, we want the phase of each return to arrive in step with the source.

To get the phase right, we can rotate one chiral mirror relative to the other. Imagine a mark at twelve o’clock on the rim, and spin the mirror about the beam as though the beam were its axle. Moving the mark to three o’clock turns every layer of the film by a quarter turn and shifts the phase of the reflected light by half a cycle. We can set the angle to make up for the phase accumulated on the rest of the trip. Once the returning light arrives in step with the laser, we have a splendid laboratory for studying purely left-handed light.

Sources indicate that imagine changing the force fields until they return to where they started. The orange arcs show the phase the left-handed fermions pick up on that round trip, first on the original grid and then on finer ones. Each bracket pairs two neighboring grids. Adding up the differences between their arcs recovers the phase shift on the original grid. The teal arrow undoes that shift, bringing the fermion measure back to its starting phase.

On the lattice, overlap fermions give us a way of keeping only the left-handed fermions that we want, and getting rid of the doublers. But this doesn’t tell us how to set the phase. (The phase in question is quite different from the one we’ve encountered in our chiral mirror thought experiment, but the analogy is good.) On the lattice, this becomes tricky because the phase depends on what the forces of the Standard Model are doing at every grid point. Lüscher worked out the phase prescription for a simpler class of theories such as a chiral version of electromagnetism, but the alignment for the full Standard Model remained open for more than 25 years.

Recent findings suggest that we can try to assign a phase by starting with one configuration of forces on the lattice and following the allowed left-handed fermions as we change the force fields in small steps. Now take a series of steps that bring the force fields back to where they started. The same states are allowed at the end, yet the way we carried them around the loop can leave us with a different phase. In the box, we adjusted the mirror to compensate for the phase the light picked up on a lap. On the lattice we have to work out how to compensate for the phase picked up around every loop.

According to recent reports, my idea was to take the force fields on the grid where we want to define the theory and represent those same fields on a succession of finer grids. Comparing the allowed fermion states on two successive grids tells us one part of the phase correction for a small change in the forces. Adding up those parts gives us the phase rule on the original grid. The proof reveals that it gives the right correction around every allowed loop. The correction for a change at one spot depends mainly on the fields nearby, and different mathematical descriptions of the same fields give the same answer. This supplies the measure for the Standard Model at finite lattice spacing, under a bound on field strengths at the scale of the grid.

In a recent development, developing this refinement strategy into a proof required several rounds of work with Astra and discussions with outside experts. GPT‑6 Astra was essential to turning the refinement idea into a working construction. It suggested the right way to carry a given set of force fields onto finer grids, revealed that the comparisons on finer grids would converge to a definite answer, and took the lead in developing the detailed proof. Human experts also played a key role; lattice field theorists Maarten Golterman, Andreas Kronfeld, and Yigal Shamir graciously spent time looking over Astra’s proof and asking probing questions that helped me to build confidence in the result. Their experience with the problem and the questions they asked were invaluable as the construction took shape.

The result is a candidate nonperturbative lattice definition for the Standard Model, potentially answering a question that had been open for more than fifty years. As with all scientific progress, however, this construction is much more a beginning than an end. Scientific dialogue among experts is required to decide if this prescription has all the properties we desire. The method that Astra and I proposed is far more an answer in principle than an answer in practice; much work lies ahead to make it useful for realistic lattice simulations. Right now I’m thinking a lot about whether this construction satisfies reflection positivity at finite lattice spacing, a condition that helps connect calculations in this lattice model to a quantum theory in which probabilities are conserved.

The construction also leaves open the question of defining the interacting theory in continuous spacetime. OpenAI’s recent proof of the existence of Yang-Mills theory (of which the strong and weak forces of the Standard Model are examples) provides the missing puzzle piece. This enabled them to prove the existence of the simplest unified Yang-Mills theory that includes the gauge fields and fermions of the Standard Model by starting with overlap fermions on the lattice and taking the continuum limit. I’m optimistic these developments will lead to fresh progress in our understanding of the Standard Model.

Grabette: an open system to record robot-manipulation data

📅 21 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.
  • It has been revealed that robot learning has a supply problem.
  • Teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.

It has been revealed that robot learning has a supply problem. We have capable policy architectures (transformer-based VLAs, diffusion and flow-matching policies, and even world models) and the GPUs to train them. What we lack is large, diverse, real-world manipulation data.

Teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot. And depending on the teleoperation method, data collection can be tedious for the user if it takes hours and involve significant hardware and logistical challenges. That is difficult to scale with the wide variety of tasks and environnements required.

But you don't need a robot to collect robot data. Just a human hand, a gripper, a camera, and a way to recover the 6-DoF trajectory of what the hand did. Capture the demonstration and you have data a robot can learn from.

That's what we're releasing today: Grabette, an open, low-cost system for recording manipulation data. Pick it up, record a task with your own hand, and get back a clean, robot-ready dataset. No robot, no lab, no teleop rig.

It has been revealed that and that's the bigger goal: if recording a demonstration is as easy as shooting a video, anyone can contribute. We want Grabette to seed a large, open, collaborative manipulation dataset. One no single lab could ever build alone.

Grabette is directly inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) from Stanford: a handheld gripper with a fisheye camera that records demonstrations "in the wild", recovers camera trajectories with SLAM, and trains visuomotor policies from them.

UMI proved the recipe works. Other (closed source) devices exists like Agibot's MEgo gripper, Genrobot's DAS gripper and Sunday Robotics skill capture glove. Our goal was to make it effortless to use, to get the barrier from "I have a task" to "I have a trained model" as low as possible.

It has been revealed that grabette is built into the modern open ecosystem: LeRobot for datasets, the Hugging Face Hub for sharing, and a processing pipeline you run from your browser with nothing to install. Grabette is something anyone can build on a workbench, use in the field, and contribute data from.

Industry observers note that we have been developing Grabette for months, and we feel it has become usable enough to share. We are excited to share it now with you!

Grabette is a handheld gripper instrumented with everything needed to reconstruct a manipulation demonstration.

It carries two cameras, each with a distinct job. Splitting the two roles is deliberate: the cheap wide fisheye gives the policy the context-rich, wrist-camera-style view it needs, while the RGBD camera does the heavy lifting of robust 6-DoF tracking.

Sources indicate that and while Grabette records data during tasks performed by a user, it relies on its robotic counterpart to execute the movements it has learned after training. So, meet Gripette, the robotic arm end-effector twin of Grabette.

The family shares the same hardware DNA:.

Grabette hand held recording device (left) and Gripette robot gripper (right).

Components. Standard sensors you can buy, no closed pipeline, no fork lock-in. A Raspberry Pi, a standard Pi camera, an off-the-shelf OAK-D depth camera, magnetic encoders. The whole point is that anyone can build one from parts you can just order.

Robot-agnostic by design. Nothing in the capture or the data format assumes a particular arm. Demonstrations are stored as camera-local 6-DoF cartesian pose plus gripper state, the output is a standard LeRobot dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, so the same data can drive different robots and different learning methods. You will still need the matching Gripette gripper on your arm though.

This release enables anyone to go from "I want to demonstrate a task" to "I have a training-ready dataset" swiftly and without prior expertise.

Press the button, and data from the observation camera, the tracking camera (color, depth, and IMU), and the gripper’s encoder joint values are recorded simultaneously, using a single shared clock to ensure proper synchronization. Press the button again to stop the episode, and the data is saved locally on the Raspberry Pi.

Open the Grabette dashboard in your browser. Select the episodes you want to add to the dataset, and with one click, post-processing begins.

Everything is now ready to start training!

According to recent reports, A dataset is only interesting if it trains something. So, to show the loop end-to-end, we ship a complete example. But to be clear, this is an example of what is enables, not the product: the release is the recording system. Your Grabette data works with any method that consumes LeRobot datasets.

Our example takes 200 recorded demonstrations such as :.

Dataset available on this HF Dataset.

Policy available on this HF Model.

The data bottleneck doesn’t get solved by one lab, but by a community recording demonstrations everywhere. You can now help build the dataset: build a Grabette, record tasks you are interested in, and share them on the Hub. Every episode makes the open dataset bigger and more diverse, and every contributor makes robot learning a little less gated behind expensive hardware.

In a recent development, this release is only the start of the project! Grabette will keep evolving. We already have more coming, including Casquette, a head-mounted POV device to complement Grabette for egocentric capture (still a work in progress). But the most key next step isn’t only ours, it’s also yours: start recording, and let’s build the dataset together.

Breaking: Directly Maximizing On-policy Expected Accepted Length for Speculative Decoding

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (186 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.31256v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by using a lightweight draft model to propose tokens for verification by a target model. Draft training commonly optimizes token-level distribution alignment, but this does not directly optimize the length of the accepted prefix: once a draft token is rejected, all subsequent draft tokens are discarded. We propose FreDraft, an on-policy training method that directly maximizes the expected accepted length of drafts sampled from the current draft model. This objective accounts for first-rejection truncation and induces prefix-aware credit assignment, weighting each token by its contribution to the acceptance of the current and subsequent tokens. To optimize the objective efficiently, we analytically marginalize token-level acceptance rate, using the target model's vocabulary distribution to reduce gradient variance. We further redistribute part of this distribution-level gradient into an explicit penalty for sampled tokens whose probabilities are overestimated by the draft model, while preserving the expected gradient. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and target models show that FreDraft improves accepted length and decoding speedup over strong baselines, achieving faster on-policy training convergence.

The day after Holiday Extras⁠(opens in a new window) debuted a new feature in its app, Liam Thompson, the firm’s VP of AI Innovation, got a report on how it was performing. He hadn’t asked for one. His dot, which he calls Beast, noticed the launch, pulled data from Google BigQuery via the ChatGPT plugin, and brought him the results.

Sources indicate that holiday Extras is a UK travel technology organization that helps travelers book the practicalities around a trip, from airport parking and hotels to lounges and transfers. Its promise is simple: less hassle, more holiday.

It has been revealed that the promise of simplicity extends to employees too. ChatGPT Enterprise gives them a foundation for using AI, Codex helps them turn their expertise into working software and better customer experiences, and dots⁠ simplify all the work in between.

Liam and his colleague David Lee, Director of Innovation & Growth, shared how they use their dots as assistants and thought partners: to talk through what’s ahead, catch challenges they might miss, and do work that would otherwise wait until they got back to their desks.

Recent findings suggest that david named his dot Brian and he calls him on his morning commute. They talk through the meetings ahead, and David can ask Brian to run a report using connected manufacturer data. “By the time I get into the office and sit at my desk, the report is there and it’s ready to go,” he claims.

Sources indicate that when some API keys needed to be retired, Brian flagged the concern, went back through David’s email, and surfaced a list of people who might be affected. David could see who might need a heads-up without having to reconstruct it from old threads.

“My dot is my orchestrator of everything,” says Liam. Beast reminds him about replies he hasn’t sent and finds answers from past conversations. Instead of scrolling through his chat history, Liam can ask Beast when they talked about something and what the answer was.

“It relaxes me having Beast there, because I know that if I miss something, he’s probably already covered it, and he is keeping an eye on all the things that are going on,” claims Liam.

Liam had tried two other assistants, OpenClaw and Hermes, but says he wasn’t comfortable giving them much information. “With anything OpenAI in our tech giant environment, I know I can trust it,” he says. He gave Beast access to his Slack, inbox, Drive, and laptop, which made it more useful to him.

Liam talks with Beast for his morning and evening briefings. “Voice is my favorite. Bidirectional voice is the game changer for interaction with OpenAI,” he indicates. “It’s like having a natural conversation. I spend at least two hours a day in a voice conversation with Beast.”.

In a recent development, dots are also a design partner. Liam, who trained as a designer, turned to Beast to animate 3D characters for an app he was working on. He gave Beast access to After Effects and Rive on his laptop, and then watched it work.

Beast animated the characters and put them in the app. Liam says the job would have taken him several days; he estimates Beast did it in about ten minutes. “I went to university for three years to learn design,” says Liam. Watching Beast work, he thought, “Well, it’s done a better job than me.”.

In a recent development, for Holiday Extras, the next opportunity is to help more people put their dot to work. David wants the people experimenting with dots to share what they’re learning, helping others see what’s possible and try it for themselves. The next idea could come from anyone, whether they start with preparing for a meeting, building something, or making everyday life a little easier.

That builds on the ambition behind the organization’s work with OpenAI: giving people across the business the confidence and tools to work differently and helping useful discoveries spread.

According to recent reports, for anyone getting started, Liam’s advice is to simply create a dot and start a conversation. “There’s no excuse not to get started. Really, just go.”.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (234 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.31255v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Current multilingual benchmarks cover only a fraction of the languages represented in modern pretraining corpora and often conflate language proficiency with the ability to answer questions grounded in specific regions and communities. We introduce INCLUDE-2.0, a large-scale benchmark for region-aware multilingual factual evaluation, which covers 91 languages from 86 countries (127 total language--country pairs), comprising over 220K curated samples drawn from native regional sources. Unlike existing benchmarks that often treat language as a proxy for region, IINCLUDE-2.0 distinguishes between questions whose answers are independent of context, vary by country, concern widely documented facts about a place, or depend on knowledge primarily expressed through local linguistic and cultural sources. Each item is annotated with its regional knowledge type and domain, and paired with an English translation, enabling controlled analysis of the relationship between language proficiency and possession of regional knowledge. Evaluating frontier and open-weight models on IINCLUDE-2.0, we find that aggregate multilingual accuracy masks substantial variation across regional knowledge types, languages, and regions. We find that frontier models perform worse on locally embedded knowledge than on widely documented facts about regions, with an average drop of ~14.5 points. We also show that for open-weight models, scale improves accuracy but does not reliably make performance invariant to whether a question is asked in English or its original language. INCLUDE-2.0 is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/epfl-nlp/include-2.0.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs.
  • It has been revealed that most of these backends are weight-only.
  • Industry observers note that SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs. Quantization is a powerful solution to this problem, and Diffusers already integrates several quantization backends such as bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, and Quanto, which we covered in Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers.

It has been revealed that most of these backends are weight-only. This means that they store the weights in low precision and dequantize them back to high precision at compute time. This reduces memory usage significantly, but it usually does not make inference faster, and can even add a small latency overhead.

Industry observers note that SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach. It runs the main transformer layers with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), reducing memory while also speeding up the denoising loop. The details are covered below, but until now, using these checkpoints required a separate inference library.

Industry observers note that with current Diffusers, loading a Nunchaku checkpoint is as simple as calling from_pretrained(), with no local CUDA compilation required thanks to the kernels package. In addition, the companion diffuse-compressor toolkit lets you quantize new architectures yourself and publish them as regular Diffusers repositories.

First, install the requirements. You need a recent version of Diffusers and the Hugging Face kernels package:.

Then load a pre-quantized pipeline like any other Diffusers model:.

No custom pipeline class or separate inference engine is needed, and there is nothing to compile locally. The NVFP4 kernels are downloaded from the Hub through the Nunchaku Lite kernels page the first time they are used. This checkpoint pairs a Nunchaku NVFP4 transformer with a bitsandbytes NF4 text encoder, and generates a 1024x1024 image in about 1.7 seconds on an RTX 5090 with a peak memory usage of about 12 GB, compared with about 24 GB for the BF16 pipeline. You can find more details about the Nunchaku Lite checkpoint format in the official Diffusers documentation.

It has been revealed that NVFP4 checkpoints require an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU (RTX 50 series, RTX PRO 6000, B200). For earlier generations, use the INT4 variants. See the hardware support table below for details.

Sources indicate that SVDQuant is the quantization method behind Nunchaku, its reference CUDA inference engine. Standard 4-bit quantization is difficult for diffusion transformers because both weights and activations contain large outliers. SVDQuant handles this by moving activation outliers into the weights, representing the hardest part of each weight matrix with a small 16-bit low-rank branch, and quantizing the remaining residual to 4 bits. Nunchaku makes this fast with fused kernels for the 4-bit path and the low-rank branch.

It has been revealed that the original Nunchaku engine gets much of its speed from model-specific fused execution paths, such as fused QKV projections and fused GELU/MLP kernels. Those optimizations are tied to each architecture's module layout and checkpoint format, so supporting a new model family usually requires model-specific integration work.

Nunchaku Lite is the new integration path in Diffusers. With it, Diffusers can load Nunchaku-style checkpoints without a custom pipeline or a separate inference engine. Under the hood, Nunchaku Lite patches the relevant nn.Linear modules of a stock Diffusers model with runtime SVDQ/AWQ linear layers before the checkpoint is loaded. The CUDA kernels come from the Hub through the kernels package. Two kernel families are used:.

According to recent reports, the trade-off is that, without architecture-specific fused kernels and modules, Nunchaku Lite cannot match the speedup of the original Nunchaku engine. However, the bare-bones implementation still delivers around 30% speedup while retaining the same level of VRAM reduction.

Industry observers note that if you have used bitsandbytes or torchao in Diffusers, the mechanics will feel familiar. A Nunchaku Lite model repository is an ordinary Diffusers repository. The only special part is a quantization_config block inside the transformer's config.json:.

This config tells Diffusers which modules were quantized, which scheme they use, and which Nunchaku Lite runtime layer to instantiate (SVDQW4A4Linear or AWQW4A16Linear).

Because the quantized model keeps the exact module structure of the dense one, everything downstream (schedulers, LoRA loading hooks, offloading, torch.compile) sees a normal Diffusers model.

Nunchaku Lite uses different kernel variants depending on the GPU generation and checkpoint precision:.

It has been revealed that volta and Hopper GPUs are currently not supported by the 4-bit kernels. The quantizer validates the GPU's CUDA capability at load time and raises a clear error instead of producing incorrect outputs.

Nunchaku Lite can be combined with other Diffusers memory and speed optimizations.

torch.compile. Compiling the transformer improves the end-to-end speedup from 1.35x to 1.8x:.

Quantized text encoders. The transformer is not the only component with a large memory footprint. Text encoders such as T5 or Qwen3 can occupy several gigabytes on their own. Further quantizing the text encoder with bitsandbytes NF4 reduces peak VRAM by about 22% in our benchmark.

Industry observers note that offloading. Diffusers offloading helpers such as enable_model_cpu_offload() and enable_sequential_cpu_offload() work as usual if you need to fit the pipeline onto a smaller GPU.

All numbers below were measured on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell) at 1024x1024 using rootonchair/ERNIE-Image-Turbo-nunchaku-lite-int4-bnb4-text-encoder.

Sources indicate that as shown above, Nunchaku reduces peak VRAM by up to 50% while still improving latency by roughly 30%. The remaining overhead comes largely from extra kernel rolls out, which torch.compile can mitigate, bringing the full pipeline down to 1.68 s, or 1.8x faster than the BF16 baseline.

Nunchaku Lite support in Diffusers is architecture-agnostic, and the diffuse-compressor toolkit provides an end-to-end SVDQuant workflow for Diffusers models: calibrate, quantize, package, and publish.

Recent findings suggest that below, we walk through quantizing FLUX.2 Klein 4B as an example. It covers the main steps: inspect the model, calibrate and quantize the transformer, package the result as a Diffusers pipeline, then verify and push it to the Hub. The full tutorial covers every flag in detail.

The generic scanner walks the model and decides what to target: compatible linears inside the repeated transformer-block stack become SVDQ W4A4 targets, recognized modulation linears become AWQ W4A16 targets, and everything else stays dense.

Always read this report before quantizing. For FLUX.2 Klein 4B, the expected result is 100 SVDQ targets, 3 AWQ targets, and 6 dense outer linears, with no missing patterns or duplicate names.

The following command runs SVDQuant on the transformer and writes the quantized checkpoint to outputs/checkpoints/svdq-int4_r32-flux-2-klein-4b.safetensors:.

Replace --precision int4 with nvfp4 to build Blackwell-native weights.

The converter combines the quantized transformer with the base pipeline's other components, writes the compact nunchaku_lite configuration into transformer/config.json, and can optionally convert text encoders to NF4:.

Industry observers note that once the outputs look good, run pipe.push_to_hub("your-name/your-model-nunchaku-lite-int4"). Other people can then load it with the same from_pretrained() pattern shown above.

Note that the generic path assumes the architecture can be quantized without structural rewrites. For additional speedup, the original Nunchaku engine rewrites groups of Diffusers layers as fused modules. The generic path cannot infer these changes on its own, such as combining separate Q, K, and V projections into one module or splitting a fused projection across several modules.

FLUX.1-dev's QKV projection is a concrete example. Diffusers defines three separate modules:.

The Nunchaku FLUX module combines those layers into one quantized to_qkv module:.

According to recent reports, this grouped module is required because Nunchaku's fused operator consumes the QKV projection, Q/K normalization, and rotary embeddings together. By comparison, the default Diffusers path executes them separately:.

The Nunchaku path supplies the grouped projection, normalization modules, and rotary embeddings to one fused operator:.

Industry observers note that this is the structural rewrite that the generic path cannot infer. Diffusers has three destination modules with to_q, to_k, and to_v parameter prefixes, while Nunchaku has one grouped module under to_qkv. A model-specific target config or adapter must state that the Q, K, and V parameters should be concatenated along the output dimension, in that order, and loaded into to_qkv.

Structural rewrites like these are described by a model-specific target config during quantization and handled by a small runtime adapter when the checkpoint is loaded. The FLUX.2 Klein 4B quantization script provides a concrete target-config example for producing a structurally rewritten checkpoint, while rootonchair/nunchaku-lite provides the runtime adapters needed to load grouped QKV tensors, split fused projections, and other fused operations. For the complete workflow, you can check the Adding A Latest Model guide.

To get started right away, check out the following repositories:.

According to recent reports, nunchaku's SVDQuant kernels are one of the most effective ways to run diffusion transformers efficiently on consumer hardware, and they are now natively supported in Diffusers. Pre-quantized checkpoints load with from_pretrained(), and the diffuse-compressor toolkit makes it possible to quantize new architectures without waiting for engine support. By quantizing both weights and activations, the W4A4 path lowers memory use while improving denoising latency, keeping image quality close to the BF16 original.

If you quantize and publish a new model, we would love to hear about it. Share it on the Hub and let us know! If you have any questions about this feature, feel free to join our Discord.

arXiv:2611.31254v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The system prompt of many instruction-tuned models carries a date, usually today's, filled in automatically for conversational and agentic requests alike, so an unchanged evaluation can send a different prompt each day. In this paper, we explore how much this hidden input changes evaluation outcomes. Across six instruction-tuned models and four benchmarks, with prompts, decoding, and configuration fixed, every model is affected: two plausible dates (2024--2026) switch a median $6.6\%$ of test items between correct and incorrect. Even rerunning the evaluation one day later flips about as many items as changing the batch size, although nothing in the setup was changed. In addition, using a grammar-constrained variant of Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) to search dates of any year, we find dates that cost the Llama-3.x models up to $36.5$ points of held-out accuracy. Beyond accuracy, switching to another plausible date alters LLM-judge verdicts and undoes $15$--$32\%$ of reproduced jailbreak successes on Llama-3.2-3B. Yet none of the eleven evaluation stacks we audit pins the date. With the date and the rest of the setup fixed, reruns reproduce byte-for-byte; we therefore recommend pinning, logging, and reporting the date.

The King’s Trust⁠(opens in a upcoming window) has revealed a major partnership with OpenAI designed to help up to 25,000 young people build AI skills for work, prioritizing those not in education, employment or training.

OpenAI is making a £1m donation to the youth charity to support this work.

This is part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications that The Trust will launch in the coming months, designed to help young people stay ahead of a changing labor market.

The announcement comes as The King’s Trust marks its 50th year and looks to the future, helping ensure young people are supported to succeed in an increasingly AI-enabled world.

The King’s Trust and OpenAI have launched a £1 million partnership to help young people across the UK build AI skills for work, prioritizing those who are not in education, employment or training (NEET). The program aims to support up to 25,000 young people over the next 18 months, helping them develop practical skills and confidence to move toward education and employment in an AI-enabled economy.

The program will help address a gap in young people’s experience of AI while responding to their appetite to learn. The Open University’s Business Barometer 2026⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) found that 68% of 16–24-year-olds surveyed who were not in education, employment or training would be willing to train or upskill to improve their job prospects.

The partnership will help prepare young people for the opportunities and challenges of a rapidly changing world of work by combining opportunities to learn AI skills with recognized qualifications and practical experience. It forms part of a wider program of nationally recognized AI qualifications being developed by The King’s Trust, designed to equip young people with the skills employers need as AI transforms the world of work.

Working with employers, AI specialists and young people, The King’s Trust is exploring the skills young people will need in a world of work where AI is becoming part of everyday life, and how these can complement the employability skills already embedded across its programs.

Building on a 50-year legacy of supporting more than 1.3 million young people, The King’s Trust wants to ensure the next generation gains the skills and confidence needed to thrive in an AI-enabled economy.

Ahead of the final report of the independent Young People and Work review, the Rt Hon Alan Milburn welcomed the partnership, reflecting on the shared ambition to improve young people’s opportunities to learn and earn.

Industry observers note that for OpenAI, the partnership forms part of a broader commitment to helping young people develop the skills and confidence to benefit from AI. It builds on wider efforts to make practical AI learning more accessible, including through OpenAI Academy, which provides free learning resources for students, job-seekers and other learners.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31253v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) models are increasingly embedded in everyday visual culture, yet little is known about how they translate abstract human values into visual scenes. We address this gap by introducing a framework, grounded in Schwartz's theory of basic human values, for studying value instantiation: the process by which ideals such as success, care, or freedom are visually realized. Using person-centered prompts from 70 positive and negative value items, we generate 28,000 images across four state-of-the-art T2I models. We identify visual prototypes, recurring combinations of subjects, actions, and settings, and use them to quantify how narrowly models instantiate these values and how this breadth compares with human descriptions of the same items. We then map these prototypes onto a taxonomy of social configurations spanning setting, sociality, mode of engagement, and social register, revealing what is systematically foregrounded or omitted. Our results show that T2I models produce far more concentrated representations than humans do when describing the same values. They default to a hyper-individualistic, adult-centric worldview, reproducing value-specific associations, such as achievement tied to formal institutional settings or hedonism rendered as affluent consumption, while marginalizing everyday labor, relational care, and non-adult perspectives. As a proof of concept, we show that these structural gaps can guide a steering method that diversifies outputs without modifying the original prompt.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A companion technical writeup to our incident disclosure.
  • We are publishing this level of detail because the technique matters more than the incident, as it reveals the emerging attack capabilities of the frontier agents, how they could be used by rogue actors, and how everyone should be prepared as defenders.
